items.body:
# Pacing AI via Compute Reallocation — LessWrong

- Pacing AI via Compute Reallocation — LessWrong x Slowing Down AI AI Curated 154 Pacing AI via Compute Reallocation by Thomas Larsen , romeo 18th Nov 2026 Linkpost for pacing-ai.com 22 min read 5 154 This is a linkpost for pacing-ai.com . I encourage folks to read it via the site (which has interactive graphs and expandables), but we’ve copied the text here as well . We offer a concrete proposal for pacing the frontier. 1. Transparency: Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD) 2. Reallocation: Shift compute away from capabilities R&D The first component is Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD): AI companies regularly disclose their compute usage, and an independent auditor verifies the disclosures. The second component is to reallocate compute away from capabilities R&D and toward other use cases, such as serving customers and safety research (non-capabilities R&D). We roughly estimate that pacing via compute reallocation starting January 2027, with a 15% cap, would delay the intelligence explosion by a year . This is most likely insufficient to prevent AI takeover (or mitigate other problems created by RSI), and so this year should be used to implement a more durable policy regime such as Plan A or Plan S . Nearly every approach to pacing, including ones built on safety and security requirements, strongly benefits from VCAD: Any pacing proposal that actually slows down AI development must do so either by reducing one of the inputs to AI development (such as training compute, experiment compute, or automated or human labor), or by implementing a safeguard that results in using inputs less efficiently (e.g., avoiding neuralese).
- Something like VCAD is evidently needed for compute restrictions. For other input restrictions and safeguards, VCAD is highly desirable to prevent attacks of the form “don’t follow this restriction/safeguard on some compute, and hide or misreport that compute.”
With VCAD, competitors and the public can trust a company that says it is pacing. As evidence of risk grows, this could enable a “race to the top”. If regulation later mandates pacing, a VCAD process that companies have already built and stress-tested makes that regulation faster to write and more workable.

Given the urgency of the situation, we elected to publish this relatively quickly. We are not very confident in any given detail of our proposal. Nevertheless, we think it represents a step forward in concreteness for pacing proposals and hope that we and others can quickly turn this into something workable.

## VCAD Implementation Proposal

We propose that AI companies take the following steps to estimate and disclose their compute usage:

## How AI companies could estimate compute usage

The basic proposal is:

Step 1: Logging. Implement logging infrastructure that logs all workloads running inside the AI company, along with relevant metadata.

Each company should create a database that accounts for all the compute (measured in GPU-hours) that the company uses (more detail on the scope here ). Each entry in the table should have the GPU-hours used by the workload, and depending on which of the following categories of workload it fits into, it should have the following metadata attached to the log:

Step 2: Classification.

- Classify the logged jobs according to whether they contributed to capabilities R&D (detailed proposal here ).
- Weight the jobs by how many quality-adjusted GPU-hours they used (detailed proposal here ).
Step 2 involves three substages: 2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. 2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities. 2.3) Estimate idle compute.

2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. Getting an overall estimate of compute use requires aggregating across heterogeneous GPUs into a single unified GPU-hr metric (e.g., “H100-equivalents”). We discuss this in more detail in an appendix .

2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities, using a mixture of AI classification and manual human classification. By “capabilities” compute, we mean compute that has any positive capabilities effects — including work that has capabilities and safety externalities. This centrally includes:

- Experiments to improve algorithms and data
- Data generation or filtering
- Training more capable AIs
- Internal inference in service of the above
Unfortunately, it’s hard to give a crisp definition of this, and there are many edge cases. The exact definition isn’t that important so long as it isn’t possible to use internal non-capabilities compute in a way that has large capabilities externalities. We discuss this in more detail in a supplement here .

2.3) Estimate idle compute. By idle compute, we mean compute that is not turned on or is not in use. This includes:

- Hot spares
- Downtime
- New racks that haven’t started use
When Step 2 is complete, the company will have an internal estimate of compute allocation such as the following:

The categories are defined as follows:

- Serving customers: compute used to serve customers, including via API, web interfaces (e.g., Claude.ai), and desktop (e.g., Claude Code). We also call this category “External Inference”. The “trained on” box is the subset of external inference that feeds back into capabilities, either by being directly trained on, paraphrased and then trained on, or similar.
- Safeguard classifiers: monitors checking for misuse
- Internal Inference: inference compute used for internal AI company use. This includes evaluations, internal coding agents, and RL rollouts. We subdivide internal inference into capabilities and safety, where safety compute refers to the internal inference that doesn’t have significant capabilities externalities.
- Non-Capabilities R&D: R&D compute that has minimal capabilities externalities.
- Capabilities R&D: all other R&D compute.
See Supplement C for more detail on the definitions.

Step 3: Disclosure. Publicly report a breakdown of how much compute was spent in each category, and whether it counted as capabilities (red) or non-capabilities.

The AI company publishes a disclosure of the compute allocation. We could imagine, for example, a disclosure every two weeks covering compute allocation over that period. This report should include:

items.body:
This year brought a remarkably strong showing in fiction. Here is my list in the order I read them:

Siri Hustvedt, [Ghost Stories: A Memoir](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/05/what-ive-been-reading-288.html).

Karl Knausgaard, [The School of Night](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/02/the-school-of-night.html).

Juan Marsé, [Last Evenings with Teresa](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/05/last-evenings-with-teresa.html) [new translation]

Claudia Piñeiro, [Cathedrals](https://www.amazon.com/Cathedrals-Claudia-Pi%C3%B1eiro/dp/1917260288/ref=sr_1_1?crid=SG52MP17QWCV&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.Hu-QferChYhDEPWp5HEYnHhrFzkx1dg1gUSekcFZsro1oZzg1ryq87dqOgZkPMWcUysp8B6aoGzGsyyc7BY8SCWkEyn3L14hh3q0eqwqnyJ2RNKAxn_R2flh1wmFsku1m_h38bT6QLMxqp9eCbqhP4NV9OD1uBGOibG1Kbh4EF3KA3KruRN9gTJZv5VsFzG8Ig8Fbap1Q_b21bVqJJ5JM-fQGBt2rN0txwAcjaeVJOwP6ksoiIRenerbIxSrOknXHz3_Je4wSwsxNPuk_cH5B81RiV5jZKrd0FM05DFuF3A.F9aG1-_uCZlGaPG9-uQVU9ySChBiv4hY1paKHMRt49Y&dib_tag=se&keywords=Claudia+Pi%C3%B1eiro&qid=1795349645&sprefix=claudia+pi%C3%B1eiro%2Caps%2C683&sr=8-1).

Christian Kracht, [Eurotrash](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/07/what-ive-been-reading-292.html) [2025], and Air [2026].

Munir Hachemi, [The Mulai](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/08/what-ive-been-reading-294.html).

Olga Grjasnowa, [My Dreadful Body](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/09/my-dreadful-body.html).

China Mieville, [The Rouse](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/what-ive-been-reading-296.html) (still reading this one).

Ingeborg Bachmann and Max Frisch, [‘We Didn’t Do Very Well’: The Correspondence](https://www.amazon.com/We-Didnt-Very-Well-Correspondence/dp/1803096640/ref=sr_1_1?crid=XS5FHNB0PI8L&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.eqgX0lK3bTgrPTaeuy-lHqPCOwthPb_UHXvsLJ-u8MIXWyCVFgOw4NKRiOLmif3HeuWJyYRCatUwthBfnkhf93nsC5yquWQuh5djZk-SqXw3p7j380-4WUJxVZsWiDAmVxtFFiXn8DqGGdKuKz08pkT5zEr-q-S1EHjRRNUppEGdfjCdut43pEZ5kTFmy48k66qC04pfFVYS_S0jiffxwWlBAcHUrEXOerUHYRsAHwo.JH4i51O7OOZioF1FViC67Gv7Bi29Sy3ibtv2Unf2dqg&dib_tag=se&keywords=Ingeborg+Bachmann+and+Max+Frisch&qid=1795349513&sprefix=ingeborg+bachmann+and+max+frisch%2Caps%2C505&sr=8-1). Here are [my remarks on the German-language edition](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/09/mein-ingeborg-bachmann-studium.html).

Adolo Bioy Casares, [Morel’s Invention](https://www.amazon.com/Morels-Invention-Adolfo-Bioy-Casares/dp/B0GGNLYS96/ref=sr_1_1?crid=2DYCM1TBC52BO&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.qIbqYA39c4XZt0O40n6iqErl6DZr1ty1EQT7RYcHJFNHL0y4pxggeMSYSenPjlxHPU2dwkvROS1889ve5ixbMTueWV3MdLC5QXm6HlLPj5ktXmk8QyJY7XafgxrvqBFxYVCvkk_gpqsIFR3if0KOZiup8Kmr4N9NFCOKbVNVMfGoe6SuhnMh8RNWSrVk0y16tX0faXqZhFRneD3oYBlqJ5I2N2BD6-dBFPyVS4eafGM.zSd2WQH7Z25bF7xJihxYy1-QXzue5uZCkNMiDBiPplA&dib_tag=se&keywords=morel%27s+invention+by+adolfo+bioy+casares&qid=1795349588&sprefix=morel%27s+inven%2Caps%2C140&sr=8-1), new translation by Margaret Jull Costa.

Missouri Williams, [The Vivisectors](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/11/what-ive-been-reading-298.html).

Mathias Enard, [Perfecting the Shot](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/11/what-ive-been-reading-298.html).

M. John Harrison, [The End of Everything](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/11/what-ive-been-reading-298.html).

Solvej Ball, [On the Calculation of Volume V](https://www.amazon.com/Calculation-Book-V-Solvej-Balle/dp/081124038X/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3GT8MBEP5BPBF&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.UfEYs0frpqxRucGNMTpDFzlPTb07Zpz4C74h_R1aMG5jW36OklQQk14FuH0zfIKMj0J5S-j7f3BtdPafSZ8kJWQEKVbsDVeA8tKAOs9FvFJEf0pTMAWhStpgPJeWn1SB.bl4g8dgv0ovDERrS8A2nJhKll5OBzhghwmhsxMQebII&dib_tag=se&keywords=On+the+Calculation+of+Volume+V&qid=1795349472&sprefix=%2Caps%2C130&sr=8-1), noting you cannot start at the fifth volume for this series.

There is also a new Min Lee novel, and a new and short Jon Fosse novel, as possible contenders for this list. I have not yet read them. As for a “best of,” the Knausgaard and the Bachmann-Frisch correspondence stand out for me, Bioy Casares as well.

What else? I do believe we are entering an era where high quality fiction is more and more important. I am delighted to see that our writers and translators are responding accordingly.

items.body:
**Warum die Neandertaler vor rund 40.000 Jahren verschwanden, ist bis heute umstritten. Einer neuen Modellsimulation zufolge reichten die damaligen Klimaveränderungen allein meist nicht aus, um die Menschenart in ganz Europa aussterben zu lassen. Erst die Ausbreitung des Homo sapiens könnte eine Erholung der bereits geschrumpften Neandertaler-Populationen verhindert haben.**

Die durchschnittliche ökologische Tragfähigkeit für Neandertaler (A) und Homo sapiens (B) in Europa sowie das Verhältnis beider Werte (C) © Science Advances

**Santander (Spanien).** Lange bevor unsere Vorfahren nach Europa kamen, erlebten die Neandertaler bereits wiederholt drastische Schwankungen ihrer Populationsgröße. Genetische und archäologische Befunde deuten darauf hin, dass sich die Verbreitungsgebiete der eiszeitlichen Jäger und Sammler mehrfach veränderten. Auch nach der Ankunft des Homo sapiens verlief ihre Verdrängung nicht überall gleich.

Während beide Menschenarten in einigen Regionen zeitweise nebeneinander lebten und sich miteinander fortpflanzten, verschwanden die Neandertaler vielerorts bereits vor der Ankunft des modernen Menschen. Zugleich waren die Lebensbedingungen in Europa während der letzten gemeinsamen Jahrtausende beider Menschenarten erheblichen klimatischen Schwankungen unterworfen. Welchen Anteil diese Veränderungen am endgültigen Aussterben der Neandertaler hatten, ist bisher nicht abschließend geklärt.

### Schwindende Nahrungsgrundlage

Forscher der University of Cambridge um Marco Vidal-Cordasco haben nun untersucht, wie sich Klimaschwankungen, Nahrungsverfügbarkeit und die Ausbreitung des Homo sapiens gemeinsam auf die Neandertaler auswirkten. Dazu rekonstruierten sie anhand von Klimamodellen sowie archäologischen und paläontologischen Funddaten die Lebensbedingungen in Europa vor 55.000 bis 27.000 Jahren.

Auf dieser Grundlage ermittelten die Wissenschaftler, wie viele Menschen in den einzelnen Regionen zu verschiedenen Zeitpunkten von den verfügbaren Ressourcen hätten leben können. Die Ergebnisse flossen in ein Computermodell ein, das die Entwicklung einzelner Menschengruppen über viele Generationen simuliert. Dabei berücksichtigten die Forscher unter anderem unterschiedliche Wachstumsraten, die Mobilität der Gruppen und die Konkurrenz um Nahrung.

Die Rekonstruktion zeigt, dass sich die Nahrungsgrundlage der Menschen vor allem zwischen 45.000 und 40.000 Jahren verschlechterte. Mit sinkenden Temperaturen und Niederschlägen nahm die pflanzliche Biomasseproduktion ab, wodurch insgesamt auch weniger Beutetiere zur Verfügung standen. Die maximal tragbare Bevölkerungsdichte sank dadurch bei beiden Menschenarten.

Allerdings hätte das Nahrungsangebot im untersuchten Zeitraum laut dem Modell im Durchschnitt etwa 19,8 moderne Menschen, aber nur 14,7 Neandertaler pro 100 Quadratkilometer versorgen können. In Teilen Mittel- und Osteuropas fiel diese ökologische Obergrenze für den Homo sapiens sogar zwei- bis viermal so hoch aus. Dabei handelt es sich nicht um die tatsächlichen damaligen Bevölkerungsdichten.

### Ausbreitung des Homo sapiens erhöhte das Risiko

Wie sich diese Unterschiede auf das Überleben der Neandertaler ausgewirkt haben könnten, untersuchte das Team anhand von 15.520 Simulationsläufen mit variierenden ökologischen und demografischen Bedingungen. Fehlte der moderne Mensch oder blieb seine Population klein, starben die Neandertaler nur in rund zwei Prozent der entsprechenden Simulationen aus. Dennoch verschwanden sie auch ohne die Konkurrenz unserer Vorfahren aus einzelnen Regionen Europas und zogen sich nach Westen und Süden zurück.

Mit der Zunahme der Population des Homo sapiens änderte sich das Bild. Laut der Analyse der Simulationen war die Populationsgröße unserer Vorfahren der wichtigste der untersuchten Einflussfaktoren auf das Aussterberisiko der Neandertaler. Klimatische Verschlechterungen konnten dieses Risiko zusätzlich erhöhen.

Eine besondere Rolle spielte dabei die Mobilität der Neandertaler. Bei einer größeren Population des Homo sapiens, ausgeprägten Umweltschwankungen und niedrigen Wachstumsraten der Neandertaler kam es in den entsprechenden Simulationen bei einem großen Aktionsradius zur Nahrungssuche in 16 Prozent der Fälle zum Aussterben. Bei geringer Mobilität waren es dagegen 98,2 Prozent.

### Kontakte zwischen Gruppen förderten das Überleben

Die Simulationen legen nahe, dass der Verlust von Lebensraum nicht allein wegen der geringeren Nahrungsmenge zum Problem wurde. Je weiter die Neandertaler-Gruppen voneinander entfernt lebten, desto anfälliger waren ihre Populationen für demografische Engpässe. Häufigere Kontakte zwischen den Gruppen konnten hingegen den Austausch von Individuen und damit auch den Genfluss begünstigen.

Die Einwanderung des Homo sapiens könnte diesen Mechanismus gestört haben, indem sich unsere Vorfahren in zuvor von den Neandertalern aufgegebenen Gebieten ansiedelten. Dadurch hätten sich die verbliebenen Neandertaler bei günstigeren Umweltbedingungen womöglich nicht mehr so leicht nach Norden und Osten ausbreiten können. Auch frühe Gruppen des Homo sapiens waren dem Modell zufolge anfällig für Isolation und verschwanden teilweise wieder aus Europa, bevor sich durch wiederholte Einwanderungswellen dauerhaft größere Populationen etablierten.

Für die Verdrängung der Neandertaler ist laut der Studie kein genereller kognitiver oder verhaltensbedingter Vorteil des Homo sapiens erforderlich. Vielmehr könnten klimatisch bedingte Bevölkerungsrückgänge und die Ausbreitung unserer Vorfahren gemeinsam die Vernetzung der Neandertaler beeinträchtigt haben. Die Simulationen liefern damit eine mögliche Erklärung für deren Verschwinden als eigenständige Population, ohne den tatsächlichen Verlauf der Ereignisse abschließend zu belegen.

**Quellen:**

- Originalstudie im Fachmagazin [Science Advances](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13781121/), doi: 10.1126/sciadv.aej5212

items.body:
# Eine Zugangskontrolle fürs Internet

## Uns fehlen noch 428.737 Euro für unsere Arbeit

für den Erhalt von Grundrechten und der Demokratie.

## Wir schlagen Alarm : Eine Zugangskontrolle fürs Internet

Die EU plant weitreichende Altersschranken im Netz. Was Kinder schützen soll, könnte für alle zur digitalen Ausweiskontrolle führen. Uns fehlen noch 430.000 Euro um auch nächstes Jahr Alarm schlagen zu können, wenn Kontrollinfrastrukturen drohen. Das geht nur mit deiner Unterstützung.

Wenn Kommissionspräsidentin Ursula von der Leyen von den Plänen der EU zu Alterskontrollen im Netz spricht, dann geht es vor allem um Kinder: ihren Schutz, ihr Wohlergehen und die Gefahren im Netz, vor denen wir sie bewahren müssten. Die Kommission will, dass Kinder und Jugendliche unter 15 Jahren das Internet nur noch mit eingeschränkten, von ihren Eltern verwalteten Accounts nutzen dürfen.

Ich versuche mir vorzustellen, wie in einigen Jahren der Alltag für ein 13- oder 14-jähriges Kind aussehen wird, sollten diese Pläne umgesetzt werden. Wie wird es dann Videos schauen, Apps und Social Media verwenden? Wo findet es Gleichgesinnte im Netz, die ihm zeigen, dass seine Ideale, seine Sexualität und seine persönlichen Interessen nicht abwegig sind, sondern viele andere sie teilen?

Ich denke auch an Familien, die jetzt schon viel Zeit dafür aufwenden, die Geräte und Accounts ihrer Kinder möglichst gut abzusichern, weil Tech-Firmen es ihnen gerne schwer machen. Geht es nach der EU-Kommission, werden sie in Zukunft außerdem noch drei Dinge nachweisen müssen: ihr eigenes Alter, das Alter des Kindes und dass sie das Sorgerecht für dieses Kind haben. Das klingt nach einem bürokratischen Albtraum – und ist es wohl auch.

## Weitgehende Restriktionen

Die Restriktionen der EU gehen wesentlich weiter als etwa in Australien, das als Vorbild dient. Sie umfassen App-Stores, Videoplattformen, Chatbots oder Spiele. Und diese Altersschranken für weite Teile des Netzes werden nicht nur Kinder und Jugendliche treffen. Sondern uns alle, ob wir 8, 18 oder 80 Jahre alt sind. Denn im Internet gelten wir künftig alle als minderjährig – bis wir das Gegenteil bewiesen haben.

## Uns fehlen noch 428.737 Euro

Damit wir auch nächstes Jahr Alarm schlagen können. Dafür brauchen wir deine Unterstützung.

Eine solche Regelung geht weit über Jugendschutz hinaus. Sie würde fundamental ändern, wie wir das Internet nutzen. Im Klartext bedeutet das: Die EU will für große Teile des Internets eine Zugangskontrolle bauen.

## Die Quadratur des Kreises

Diese Zugangskontrollen sollen angeblich grundrechtsschonend sein. Allein technisch lässt sich dieses Versprechen allerdings nur schwer einlösen. Denn damit Alterskontrollen verlässlich funktionieren, müssen sie streng sein: Auf amtliche Papiere setzen, die manche Menschen nicht besitzen. Und auf biometrische Abgleiche, die erfordern, dass schon Kinder ihr Gesicht scannen lassen müssen. Gleichzeitig entstehen neue Angriffsflächen für Hacking, Datenmissbrauch und Identitätsbetrug.

Und wenn eine solche Kontroll-Infrastruktur erst einmal existiert, kann sie in Zukunft auch ganz andere Dinge kontrollieren. Wir sind dann nur noch ein paar Einstellungen von einer Klarnamenpflicht im Netz entfernt. Oder von einem System, das bestimmte Menschengruppen aus der digitalen Öffentlichkeit aussperrt.

Es ist ein Kontrollapparat, von dem autoritäre Regierungen träumen.

## Wir schlagen Alarm!

Keine Frage: Kinder und Jugendliche haben es verdient, im Netz besser geschützt zu werden. Vor Gewalt und vor Belästigung. Aber auch vor den süchtigmachenden Endlos-Feeds und manipulativen Designs, mit denen Tech-Konzerne ihre Nutzer*innen immer fester an ihre Plattformen binden wollen.

Der Kids Act bietet dafür gute Ansätze. Die Pläne für Alterskontrollen halten wir aber für gefährlich. Deswegen berichten wir seit Jahren engmaschig darüber – und schlagen Alarm. Und wir werden das weiterhin tun.

Dafür brauchen wir deine Unterstützung. Unsere Arbeit ist spendenfinanziert und für unser aktuelles Jahresziel fehlen uns derzeit noch 428.737 Euro.

Wenn du ein offenes Internet erhalten willst, dann spende jetzt .

## Die Hütte brennt: Wir brauchen deine Hilfe!

Bis Jahresende brauchen wir noch 428.737 Euro. Damit wir weiterhin genau hinschauen können, wenn Freiheit unter Druck gerät.

Wir machen die Arbeit, die sonst keiner macht. Wir lesen Gesetzentwürfe im Original, befreien Dokumente und warnen als Sachverständige vor neuer Überwachung.

Deine Spende macht das möglich.

items.body:
Art by Thomas Cole via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cole_Thomas_The_Course_of_Empire_Destruction_1836.jpg)

Sometime in the mid-2010s, just as liberalism was getting replaced by “progressivism”, the conservatism that I had grown up with was getting replaced by something we then called the “alt-right”. Whereas the old conservatism was based on Christian faith, libertarian economics, and flag-waving patriotism, the alt-right saw America as a white racial nation-state, rejected the idea of free markets, and was basically irreligious and isolationist.

Over the course of two Trump presidencies and one Biden interregnum, the alt-right matured and grew into what I now call [the New Right](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/understanding-americas-new-right). In doing so, it basically took over from conservatism as the guiding ideology of the GOP base — though not (yet) of the GOP as a whole. Whereas the alt-right was a naked white-power movement, the New Right sees things in broader “civilizational” terms. It has embraced the idea of Christianity, not as a faith or a lifestyle, but as a tribal affiliation defining ingroup and outgroup. Its foreign policy matured into something concrete — a desire to [wield American policy on behalf of “Western Civilization”](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/new-rights-grand-strategy-after-trump).

At the grassroots level, the New Right also added some new components. It merged with the [Covid antivax movement](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-alternate-reality-of-rfk-and) to become skeptical of modern medicine, public health, and life science in general. It partially merged with [the incel movement](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/dating-advice-for-men), telling young men that their sexual frustration was the fault of progressivism. It [veered even more strongly into antisemitism](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/jewish-americans-are-feeling-unsettled), probably feeling liberated to do so by rising antisemitism on the left in the wake of the Gaza war. And it added a strong component of [anti-Indian hatred](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-anti-american-right), seeing Indians as a uniquely vulnerable target among recent immigrant groups.

Anyway, it’s too early to say that this movement has *failed*. Yes, the Democrats won one midterm election, but Trump is still the President, and he has shown zero inclination to reverse course on any of his most New Right-aligned policies. He has made Stephen Miller, the ultimate anti-immigration crusader, his chief of staff, and [posted a picture](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/europe/trump-friend-greeting-putin-causes-alarm-europe-ukraine-rcna610373) of himself hugging Vladimir Putin with the caption “My Friend”. Meanwhile, the New Right still has a fairly robust online presence.

But it’s impossible to deny that the winds have shifted. The midterms made it clear that even if the New Right sticks around for the long term, it won’t have a monopoly on power. That will make it essentially impossible for it to follow through on its long-term agenda. Basically, the notion that wokeness and internal disputes would cause the Democrats to permanently collapse as a party has been falsified.

Already, some prominent figures are backing away from the New Right. Elon Musk, who once stood on a stage and declared himself “Dark MAGA”, now says he’s not even MAGA at all, and is instead a political moderate:

And the CEO of Palantir is calling himself a Democrat:

Meanwhile, Bo French, the Texas candidate who lost an election after complaining about Indian fans at a UT football game, has been [kicked out of his country club](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/18/bo-french-texas-country-club-membership-01173063).

The New Right’s online activists and commentators are in a state of deep despair:

Others are tweeting ever more histrionic demands for a civil war that absolutely no one seems interested in actually fighting:

What enthusiasm still *does* exist on the New Right tends to be concentrated on the movement’s most extreme fringe, which focuses on getting attention by bashing Trump and MAGA and saying ridiculous, extremist stuff. For example, *[Politico](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/11/18/the-far-right-leaves-trump-behind-01172242)* [reports](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/11/18/the-far-right-leaves-trump-behind-01172242) on the “Christ is King” conference, run by a guy named Joel Webbon:

> [F]or Webbon, the problem was also that MAGA hadn’t gone far enough. He wanted even harsher deportation policies. He wanted a total repudiation of Israel. He wanted to curtail women’s right to vote, to criminalize abortion and homosexuality, and to expel Jews and non-Christians from public office…The event attracted a notorious set of online agitators, including conspiracist Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white nationalist and antisemite, who made a rare public appearance as a guest speaker…
> There are, in Webbon’s telling, few “guys” capable of leading this faction…He did put forward a few “guys” who might fit the bill, naming electoral losers like [James] Fishback, one of the weekend’s main draws, who recently lost [a gubernatorial primary] to a MAGA-backed candidate by 37 points in Florida…Webbon also went on to name Bo French, the far-right candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner who ultimately lost by some 670,000 votes to a Democrat after making anti-immigration a centerpiece of his campaign.

(There are also various [loonies from overseas](https://vimeo.com/1248089901?fl=pl&fe=vl).)

These are all signs of a movement that’s on the way down. It may return someday — communism sort of did, after all — but its hopes of transforming America over the next few decades are fading. It’s not over yet, but it’s looking more and more that way.

A big part of the reason for that failure, of course, is that Americans simply do not buy what the New Right wants to sell them. Regular Americans [generally like (legal) immigration](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712289/americans-support-immigration-down-strong.aspx), and they [don’t see racial and religious heritage](https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/52636-what-makes-someone-american-heritage-constitution-declaration) as an important determinant of who is a real American. It’s very hard to sell people a product they don’t want.

But there are also various strategic errors that the New Right made. To be clear, I’m *glad* these mistakes were made; I have zero desire to see a movement like the New Right hold power in my country. I just think it’s interesting and instructive to think about what the mistakes were.

## Deontic Logic

Deontic logic [ 1 ] is a branch of logic that has been the most concerned with the contribution that the following sorts of notions make to what follows from what (or what supports what, more generally): [ 2 ]

- permissible (permitted)
- impermissible (forbidden, prohibited)
- obligatory (duty, required)
- omissible (non-obligatory)
- optional
- non-optional
- must
- ought
- supererogatory (beyond the call)
- indifferent / significant
- the least one can do
- better than / best / good / bad
- claim / liberty / power / immunity
- responsibility
- blame / praise
- agency / action
Consider

> You are obligated to return your friend’s car by noon, and the least you can do is return it on time with the same level of battery charge it had when you borrowed it, but it is beyond the call to buy your friend a dinner on top of that.

Various things seem to follow: It is impermissible to not return your friend’s car by noon; it is obligatory to return your friend's car, it is optional to return it with a full charge, and doing the least you can do precludes buying dinner. For deontic logic, the aim is to develop accounts of the logical contribution made by the key concepts listed above. [ 3 ]

As a branch of logic, deontic logic is of theoretical interest for some of the same reasons that modal logic (the logic of necessity and possibility), is of theoretical interest. Also, although we need to be cautious about making too easy a link between deontic logic and practicality, many of the notions listed above are typically employed in attempting to regulate and coordinate our lives. [ 4 ] For these reasons, deontic logics often directly involve topics of considerable practical significance such as morality, law, social and business organizations (their norms, as well as their normative constitution), and security systems. To that extent, studying the logic of notions with such practical significance adds practical significance to deontic logic itself. However, in this entry we will focus on deontic logic itself, rather than its applications and practical relevance.

In Section 1 of this entry, we note certain simple formal relationships between the first six concepts in our initial list above, following the many-centuries old tradition of comparing (and contrasting) basic deontic notions (e.g., obligation, permission) with modal notions (e.g., necessity and possibility). In Section 2, we turn to a benchmark system of symbolic deontic logic, one that quickly became a reference point. In Section 3, we examine a closely related approach that reframes deontic notions by “reducing” them to pure modal notions coupled with a so-called “deontic constant”. In a sense, the approaches discussed in Sections 2 and 3 might be said to stand in the shadow of modal logic. In Section 4, we turn to developments in deontic logic that emerged in the attempt to grapple with conditionalized deontic claims, and here deontic logic comes more fully into its own. In Sections 5 and 6 we turn to a variety of perceived inadequacies of the benchmark systems introduced in Sections 1–4. Section 5 focuses primarily on arguing for and specifying expansions of the limited expressive resources in the benchmark systems. [ 5 ] Finally, Section 6, rather than expanding on the benchmark approaches, instead raises putative fundamental shortcomings in their modelling of the ideas they purport to represent, thereby seeking to dismantle some of the principles of the systems and/or construct new systems in their place.

## 1. Informal Preliminaries and Background

Deontic logic has been regularly influenced by reflection on the logic of modal notions, such as necessity (in varying senses of the term). In particular, analogies between alethic (truth-implicating) modal notions and deontic notions were noticed before the fourteenth century in Europe, where we might say that the rudiments of formal (though not symbolic) deontic logic experienced its initial European stirrings. In Islamic thought, such analogies go back at least as far as the tenth century.

Although interest in what can be arguably called formal aspects of deontic logic continued off and on, the trend toward studying logic using the symbolic and exact techniques of mathematics began primarily in the nineteenth century, and became dominant in the twentieth century. Work in twentieth century symbolic modal logic provided the explicit impetus for von Wright (1951a, 1951b), the central early figure in the emergence of deontic logic as a full-fledged branch of symbolic logic in the twentieth century. However, we note that prior to von Wright 1951a, there was one significant earlier episode in symbolic deontic logic, namely Mally 1926. See supplement A: Mally and Symbolic Deontic Logic . [ 6 ]

In the remainder of this section, we first spell out a few folk-logical features of alethic modal notions, and then give an impressionistic sense of how natural it was for early developments of deontic logic to explore deontic analogs to those features.

APOD

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

## Galaxies Battle in the NGC 7771 Group

**Explanation:** After this galaxy battle, only one galaxy will remain. Already visible in the [featured picture](https://app.astrobin.com/u/Bluesky71?i=vn4g73) are [rings](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-june-1-ugc-1810-wildly-interacting-galaxy-from-hubble/) and faint star [swirls](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2022-may-17-ngc-1316-after-galaxies-collide/) from previous [gravitational encounters](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2013-may-14-galaxy-collisions-simulation-vs-observations/). Known collectively as the [NGC 7771 Group](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2024-august-31-ifn-and-the-ngc-7771-group/), these galaxies lie almost 200 million [light-years](https://chandra.harvard.edu/resources/faq/astrophysics/astrophysics-18.html) away toward the high-flying [constellation Pegasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegasus_(constellation)). The largest galaxy, [barred spiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barred_spiral_galaxy) [NGC 7771](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGC_7771) on the lower right, is itself about 75,000 light-years across, and the galaxy on the upper left is spiral [NGC 7769](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGC_7769), which is almost as large. As these and other [smaller galaxies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_galaxy) make repeated close passages, they will [all likely merge](https://i.pinimg.com/736x/3b/fd/fe/3bfdfefb4f45fc0d90af3a111e2704b5.jpg) into one very large galaxy. Playing out over billions of years, the [merger process](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/science-highlights/galaxy-details-and-mergers/) is understood to be a normal part of the [evolution of galaxies](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/galaxies/evolution/). Studying [galaxy clashes](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-january-6-colliding-spiral-galaxies-from-webb-and-hubble/) like this helps [humanity](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2019-august-18-human-as-spaceship/) to better understand the [possible](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-025-02563-1) merger [between](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2022-june-6-milky-way-galaxy-doomed-collision-with-andromeda-pending/) our own [Milky Way](https://science.nasa.gov/resource/the-milky-way-galaxy/%22) and [Andromeda](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2025-november-15-andromeda-and-friends/) galaxies.

**Tomorrow’s picture:** open space

# SAMA: Training-Free Consensus Ridge Tracking for Camera-Based Heart Rate on Five Public Datasets

## Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

- [Submitted on 20 Nov 2026] Title: SAMA: Training-Free Consensus Ridge Tracking for Camera-Based Heart Rate on Five Public Datasets Authors: Sudhakar Mishra View a PDF of the paper titled SAMA: Training-Free Consensus Ridge Tracking for Camera-Based Heart Rate on Five Public Datasets, by Sudhakar Mishra View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is usually benchmarked by one heart rate per video, a figure that hides the short windows in which a tele-consultation would actually read the pulse. We present SAMA, a training-free estimator that (i) forms a quality-weighted consensus of POS and CHROM chrominance spectra, (ii) discounts frequencies occupied by pulse-free references derived from the same frames (frame motion, skin-mask geometry and background brightness), (iii) follows the heart rate through time with a Viterbi ridge under a random-walk prior, and (iv) returns a track-filtered, amplitude-normalised waveform with a per-window confidence. No parameter is learned and no dataset-specific tuning is used. On 218 recordings from 111 participants in five public datasets (UBFC-rPPG, PURE, SUMS, M3PD and a two-participant subset of MMPD), all processed with the same fixed face box and scored with a re-implementation of the rPPG-Toolbox protocol, SAMA has the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) averaged over datasets at every protocol level: 4.40 against 5.13,bpm for POS per video, 4.80 against 5.43 on 30,s windows and 5.05 against 6.59 on 10,s windows. Pooled over participants, the bootstrap interval of its paired difference from POS excludes zero on 30,s and 10,s windows (Wilcoxon p=0.11 and 0.004) but not per video, and it does not beat POS on SUMS per video or on the MMPD subset. Withholding the 20\% least confident windows lowers the pooled 10,s error from 4.06 to 2.33,bpm. We also show that the per-video protocol has a floor of 1.2--1.6,bpm on datasets where heart rate drifts, and that skin tone cannot be recovered from uncalibrated video, which motivates the instrumented, skin-tone-stratified collection we propose for the Indian population. The method does not surpass the best published neural networks on UBFC-rPPG; we report where it stands against them without re-running them. items.feedText: MONO2K is an open-source firmware for the M-VAVE FM-1 that transforms the compact synthesizer into a groovebox inspired by Elektron's Monomachine, with six synthesis engines, four drum machines, parameter locks and a 64-step sequencer.… Read More Free Firmware Turns M-VAVE FM-1 Into An Elektron Monomachine-Inspired Groovebox
items.body:
# Free Firmware Turns M-VAVE FM-1 Into An Elektron Monomachine-Inspired Groovebox

Iñigo Hernandez has released MONO2K , an open-source firmware that transforms the M-VAVE FM-1 into a multi-engine synthesizer and groovebox inspired by the Elektron Monomachine .

The firmware combines six different synthesis machines, four dedicated drum synthesizers, and a 64-step sequencer with parameter locks, trigger conditions and ratchets.

The instrument is organized around six mono machines, with each track capable of running its own synthesis engine. The available engines include FM synthesis with two to four operators, superwave oscillators, wavetable synthesis, SID-6581-style chip sounds, voice and speech synthesis, and four different drum synthesis engines.

The sequencer provides 64 steps of pattern-based control, with parameter locks, trigger conditions and ratchets. This allows individual steps to have their own sound settings and playback behavior, providing a workflow closer to a dedicated hardware groovebox than a conventional compact FM synthesizer.

Features:

- Six independent mono synthesis machines inspired by the architecture of the Elektron Monomachine.
- FM synthesis with two to four operators, including FM+STAT, FM+PAR and FM+DYN configurations.
- Superwave synthesis with saw, pulse and ensemble modes.
- Digital wavetable synthesis.
- SID-6581-inspired chip synthesis.
- VOX-6 voice and speech synthesis engine.
- Four dedicated drum synthesis engines, including ground, sine, noise and percussion sound generators.
- 64-step sequencer with parameter locks, trigger conditions and ratchets.
- Independent synthesis and sequencing across six tracks.
- Lo-fi bus processing for adding character to the overall sound.
- Four included demo parts demonstrating the firmware’s synthesis and sequencing capabilities.
- Web-based patch editor for editing sounds.
- Support for saving and retaining patterns when upgrading between MONO2K 1.x releases.
Pricing & Availability:

MONO2K is available as a free, open-source firmware under the GPL-3.0 license. I

items.body:
# What Schools Still Don’t Teach About Interest Rates and Why It Matters | TeachThought

Most people leave school able to calculate interest on paper. Far fewer leave knowing what interest will do to their lives. That gap is easy to miss because it doesn’t show up on a report card. It shows up years later, in loan papers, credit card statements and savings balances that never seem to grow.

The problem isn’t that schools ignore math. Interest is taught as a formula, and the formula stops at the edge of the worksheet. Students learn how to find an answer but not how to read the numbers that will shape what they borrow, what they save and what they can afford. To close that gap, it helps to look at what gets left out, starting with how the subject is framed in the first place.

### The Gap Between Arithmetic and Everyday Money

### Formulas Without Consequences

A typical lesson on interest gives students a principal, a rate and a time period, then asks them to solve for the total. It’s tidy and it can be graded. It also hides almost everything that matters. Real rates change. Real balances get added to and drawn down. Real people make choices partway through, and those choices change the outcome.

When interest only ever appears as a problem with one right answer, students learn to treat it as a puzzle rather than as a force acting on their money every day.

### Interest Is a Price

The simplest idea missing from many classrooms is also the most useful one. Interest is the price of money over time. When you borrow, you pay that price. When you save, someone pays it to you. Once students see interest as a price, they start asking the questions they would ask about any purchase. Is this a good deal? Can I find it cheaper somewhere else? What happens if I wait?

That shift in thinking matters most when you see how interest builds over long stretches of time.

### How Compounding Actually Feels Over Time

### The Slow Start That Fools People

Compounding means you earn interest on your interest. Most students can repeat that definition. What they rarely get is a feel for how lopsided the results are.

Put $1,000 in an account earning 5% a year and leave it alone. In the first year, you earn $50. Nothing to get excited about. By year 30, the balance has grown to about $4,322, and that single year alone adds more than $200. The growth was always there, but it took decades to become obvious. People who expect fast results often give up during the slow early years, which is exactly when patience pays off most.

A quick shortcut called the rule of 72 makes this easier to grasp. Divide 72 by the interest rate, and you get a rough idea of how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, that’s about 12 years. A tool like the compound interest calculator on the SEC’s Investor.gov site lets students test different rates and time frames and watch the curve bend upward.

### Compounding Runs in Both Directions

The same math that rewards savers punishes borrowers. A credit card charging 24% APR works out to about 2% a month. On a $3,000 balance, that’s roughly $60 in interest in the first month. If you pay $75, only $15 actually goes toward what you owe. The balance barely moves, and the card company is happy to keep it that way.

Students who understand this early tend to treat credit cards very differently. Still, knowing how compounding works is only half the picture. The other half is knowing which rate you’re actually dealing with.

### Why the Rate You See Is Rarely the Rate You Pay

### APR, APY and the Fine Print

Banks and lenders use different terms for a reason. APR, or annual percentage rate, is often used for loans and doesn’t always show the effect of compounding. APY, or annual percentage yield, does. A 12% APR compounded monthly actually costs about 12.68% over a year. The gap looks small until it’s multiplied across a large balance or a long loan.

Few students are ever shown these two terms side by side. As a result, many adults compare offers without realizing they’re comparing different measurements.

### Inflation Eats Quietly

Even a correct rate can mislead you if inflation is ignored. If your savings earn 1% while prices rise 3%, your balance goes up but what it can buy goes down. Economists call the difference the real return. The Consumer Price Index published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics is the standard way to track how fast prices are rising, and checking it against your savings rate is a sobering exercise.

That raises a fair question. If rates matter this much, who decides what they are?

### Where Rates Come From

### The Central Bank’s Role

Rates don’t appear out of nowhere. In the United States, the Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate , which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans. That rate ripples outward into mortgages, car loans, credit cards and savings accounts.

### Why Your Rate Moves, or Doesn’t

Some rates follow the Fed closely. Variable credit card rates often rise within weeks of a hike. Others lag behind or barely move at all. Many large banks are slow to raise what they pay savers, even when borrowing costs climb. Knowing this helps people spot when they’re being underpaid and gives them a reason to act. The easiest place to put that knowledge to work is a savings account.

### Savings Accounts as a Practical Classroom

### Watching Interest Work in Real Time

A savings account turns abstract lessons into something you can see each month. Deposits go in, interest gets added and the balance changes without any effort. For a young person, watching even a few dollars of interest arrive can make compounding feel real in a way no textbook can. It also builds a habit, and habits tend to outlast lessons.

Savings accounts carry little risk, too. Deposits at insured banks are protected up to set limits, which makes them a calm place to learn how rates behave before moving on to investments that can lose value.

### Shopping for a Better Rate

Not all savings accounts pay the same. Some traditional accounts pay close to nothing, while online banks and high-yield accounts often pay far more. On a $10,000 balance, the difference between 0.5% and 4% is about $350 a year, earned for doing nothing extra at all. Comparing the best bank savings rates against what your current account pays is one of the quickest ways to learn how much a few percentage points are worth.

This is the habit schools rarely teach: treating your own savings rate as something you can shop for and improve.

### Why the Gap Matters

Each of these missing lessons is small on its own. Together, they decide whether interest works for a person or against them. Someone who understands compounding, reads APY instead of APR, accounts for inflation and checks their savings rate will make dozens of slightly better decisions over a lifetime. Those small edges add up the same way interest does.

items.body:
Congrats to Sierra on [tripling](https://x.com/sierraplatform/status/2124832956795539842?a=LMwTZcXTCy6VIdPRUb0&s=46) last year’s [$10B valuation](https://x.com/SierraPlatform/status/1963654362384724388), and to [Z.ai](http://z.ai/) for releasing [GLM 5.4](https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.4), their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller [Inkling Mini 2](https://x.com/miramurati/status/2123872534970208421) from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories…

**Jensen Huang is**[back](https://x.com/aburducky/status/2124924846266277988/video/1?a=6-tbBZhGNaBzRNGkqhk&s=46)**.** Eleven days after [announcing his resignation](https://latent.space/p/ainews-jensen-huang-resigns-after-33-years-leading-nvidia/), Nvidia [announced](https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2026/NVIDIA-Board-Reinstates-Jensen-Huang-as-President-CEO-and-Board-Director/default.aspx) his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors.

[View post on X ↗](https://x.com/alecqfong/status/2124938191761555517)

The board voted unanimously after [more meetings with Jensen on Sunday](https://x.com/lookner/status/2125067095113154824) and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka [the Treasury Secretary](https://x.com/CGasparino/status/2124899810314437062) and [the President dialing into the board meeting](https://x.com/rogoswami/status/2124881764535464261?a=wUcGlCxi-wvs1ZrGiJw&s=46)). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control.

As [Matt Levine points out](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/newsletters/2026-11-23/jensen-s-candor-is-satisfactory-now?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NTQ3NDYxNSwiZXhwIjoxNzk2MDc5NDE1LCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1lWVEtSMjRVODkwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiI5MjgxRkY1M0M2N0Q0Qzg5QUQxNUQyMDNGMjlEOEEyRiJ9.xJ5NMXrrwB70YTBP2MCG1blRaX5XHxD7S0fAVzCB7Vw), with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light.

**OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record.** In [Perplexity and Intelligence](https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/), Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their [internal held-out coding dataset](https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/#citation-top-3)… which has [notable caveats](https://x.com/ziv_ravid/status/2124685987402182737)):

[View post on X ↗](https://x.com/merettm/status/2124549218995949967)

Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, [hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly](https://latent.space/p/ainews-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-openai/). Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70.

This is all in context of [pacing the frontier](https://latent.space/p/ainews-fearing-rsi-openai-anthropic/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv). Pachocki proposes that labs agree on a first limit to development and spell out what would let them cross it, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitoring. Microsoft’s [Mustafa Suleyman](https://x.com/mustafasuleyman/status/2124663594449318173) gave the first win by cosigning and joining in, running MAI-2 Base on OpenAI’s evaluation set and reporting 0.819. We’d need at least a couple more top labs to join this effort for it to gather steam as a real self-regulatory limit, most notably of course, Anthropic.

**

# Die Alltäglichkeit organisierter Gewalt

Elisabeth Pönisch | Rezension | 24.11.2026

## Die Alltäglichkeit organisierter Gewalt

## Rezension zu „Gewalt erleiden. Eine Soziologie organisierter sexualisierter und ritueller Gewalt“ von Tabea Koepp

Tabea Koepp: Gewalt erleiden. Eine Soziologie organisierter sexualisierter und ritueller Gewalt Deutschland Hamburg 2026: Hamburger Edition 352 S., 40,00 EUR ISBN 978-3-987-22006-7

Über organisierte sexualisierte Gewalt zu lesen, kann schwer auszuhalten sein. Die Schilderungen des Erlebten hinterlassen eine Beklemmung, die sich auch durch wissenschaftliche Einordnung nicht einfach auflösen lässt. Diese Gewalt wissenschaftlich zu erforschen und darüber zu schreiben, stellt eine besondere Herausforderung dar. Tabea Koepp nimmt diese in ihrer Studie Gewalt erleiden. Eine Soziologie organisierter sexualisierter und ritueller Gewalt an und rückt dabei die Erfahrungen der Betroffenen ins Zentrum. Ihr Ausgangspunkt ist eine Sprachlosigkeit, die das Begreifen des Erlebten betrifft. Im Anschluss an Carolin Emcke beschreibt Koepp, wie schwierig es sein kann, Gewalterfahrungen zu verstehen und sprachlich auszudrücken. Auch für sie selbst war zunächst vieles „schwer in Worte zu fassen“ (S. 7). Ihr gelingt es, diese Schwierigkeit analytisch fruchtbar zu machen, indem sie die Sprachlosigkeit selbst zum Gegenstand ihrer Untersuchung macht. Besonders überzeugend ist ihre Auseinandersetzung mit der vermeintlichen Unvorstellbarkeit von Gewalt. „Was dabei übersehen wird […]: Diese ‚Unvorstellbarkeit‘ von Gewalt ist ein Privileg“ (S. 15), schreibt Koepp in Anlehnung an Hannah C. Rosenblatt. Der Satz trifft einen entscheidenden Punkt: Was Außenstehenden unvorstellbar erscheint, kann für andere alltägliche Wirklichkeit sein. Koepp zeigt, wie wichtig es ist, auch schwer vermittelbare Erfahrungen zur Sprache zu bringen und ihnen Gehör zu schenken. Ihre Studie macht deutlich, weshalb diese Auseinandersetzung notwendig ist: Sie trägt dazu bei, die gesellschaftlichen Bedingungen zu verstehen, unter denen Gewalt unsichtbar bleibt, und sie hilft, die Betroffenen mit ihren Erfahrungen nicht allein zu lassen.

Hinzu kommt eine weitere Herausforderung: Koepp beschreibt, wie sehr ihre Forschung von der Erwartung begleitet war, sich in der öffentlichen Debatte um sogenannte rituelle Gewalt zu positionieren und die Wahl ihres Untersuchungsgegenstandes zu rechtfertigen. Dieser Rechtfertigungs- und Positionierungsdruck wäre seinerseits eine soziologische Untersuchung wert. Für die Auseinandersetzung mit ihrer Studie sollte jedoch entscheidend sein, welche Fragen sie stellt, wie sie diese untersucht und zu welchen Erkenntnissen sie gelangt. Eine Rezension muss ihren wissenschaftlichen Beitrag diskutieren, ohne die Bewertung des Buches auf eine Stellungnahme der Autorin zur öffentlichen Kontroverse zu verengen. Der vorliegende Text bespricht Koepps Arbeit deshalb als gewaltsoziologische Untersuchung und misst sie an ihrem wissenschaftlichen Anspruch. Im Mittelpunkt steht, was die Studie zum Verständnis von Gewalt beiträgt, wie sie ihre Erkenntnisse gewinnt und wie weit diese tragen.

## Rituelle Gewalt verstehen

Viele Bücher beanspruchen, eine Soziologie von etwas zu entwickeln. So auch die 2026 in der Hamburger Edition erschienene Studie von Tabea Koepp. Ihr geht es um eine

> „Soziologie der Gewalt, die nicht den Tätern und ihren Handlungen, sondern der Perspektive der Gewalterleidenden und ihren Verletzungserfahrungen folgt und nachzeichnen kann, wie andauernde (kollektive) Gewalt als soziale, zwischenmenschliche Erfahrung erlebt und erlitten wird“ (S. 9).

Während ihrer Forschung sei sie „immer wieder von der Normalität und Alltäglichkeit überrascht“ worden, „mit der sich die Gewalt in das Erleben (und Leben) der Betroffenen einzufügen schien“ (S. 8). Damit ist das zentrale Problem benannt: Wie lässt sich Gewalt verstehen, wenn sie für diejenigen, die sie erleiden, keine klar abgrenzbare Unterbrechung ihres Alltags darstellt? Wenn sich vielmehr „um die Gewalt herum über Jahre hinweg eine Lebenswelt baut, die so vieles mehr ist als die Gewalt“ (S. 9)?

Im Mittelpunkt stehen Menschen, die als Kinder bereits in Gewaltverhältnissen aufgewachsen sind. Koepps Forschungsgegenstand sind auf Dauer angelegte, klandestine, also gegenüber der Außenwelt verborgene Gewaltgemeinschaften, in die organisierte sexualisierte Gewalt weltanschaulich eingebettet ist. Die Autorin fragt, wie diese Gemeinschaften fortbestehen und ihre Gewalt verbergen können. Der Zugang erfolgt vor allem über rückblickende Interviews. Die Analyse rekonstruiert die untersuchten Gewaltverhältnisse aus den Erzählungen und Deutungen der Befragten. Wie prägt die Gewalt die Erfahrungen und Beziehungen von Betroffenen und wie entstehen neben Verletzung und Abhängigkeit auch Zugehörigkeit, Bindung und Orientierung? Die Perspektive überzeugt vor allem deshalb, weil sie eine verbreitete Vorstellung infrage stellt: dass Gewalt dort beginnt, wo das gewöhnliche soziale Miteinander aufhört. Koepp untersucht stattdessen, wie beides ineinandergreift und Gewalt in Beziehungen eingebunden ist, die über die einzelne Gewaltsituation hinaus bestehen.

Dafür ist zunächst zu klären, was Koepp unter ritueller Gewalt versteht. Sie ist eine „Variante von in Gruppen organisierter sexualisierter Gewalt, die sich primär durch die weltanschauliche Einbettung der Gewalt von anderen Gewaltformen unterscheidet“ (S. 10). Die begriffliche Unterscheidung hat analytische Konsequenzen. Sie richtet den Blick auf die Funktion der Weltanschauung innerhalb sozialer Ausbeutungsverhältnisse. Das ist wichtig, weil die Konzentration auf vermeintlich außergewöhnliche Rituale verdecken kann, welche Interessen innerhalb solcher Gruppen verfolgt werden. Koepp verweist ausdrücklich auf Machtinteressen sowie sadistische und kommerzielle Interessen (S. 11). Die Weltanschauung dient der Rechtfertigung der Gewalt und prägt zugleich die Deutungen, mit denen die Beteiligten das Geschehen und ihre eigene Stellung darin verstehen (S. 11).

## Theorie und Methodik

Koepp bewegt sich in einem Forschungsfeld, das sie als jung, umkämpft und empirisch unzureichend erschlossen beschreibt (S. 31). Der öffentlichen und medialen Aufmerksamkeit steht eine bislang begrenzte wissenschaftliche Auseinandersetzung gegenüber. Die deutschsprachigen Untersuchungen sind demnach überwiegend quantitativ ausgerichtet und folgen psychologischen oder psychiatrischen Perspektiven (S. 36). Ihr qualitativer, ausdrücklich soziologischer Zugang erweitert dieses Feld. Die von ihr gewählte explorative Herangehensweise erscheint angemessen: In einem wenig konsolidierten Forschungsfeld müssen zunächst Zugänge erschlossen, Begriffe präzisiert und Zusammenhänge am empirischen Material herausgearbeitet werden.

> In einer „gewaltaffizierten Lebenswelt“ (S. 279) prägt Gewalt auch alltägliche Gewohnheiten, Beziehungen und Erwartungen, die über die unmittelbare Gewaltsituation hinausreichen.

# What VP ≠ VNP Means (In 3 Minutes) – Gil

I assume you know about the P vs. NP problem. But what is this wacky thing Anthropic just posted ?

You learned how to take a determinant in your linear algebra class:

The naive way is fine for 3 × 3 matrices, but notice that you need to perform Θ ( n ! ) arithmetic operations here. Exercise for the reader is to find the exact number of operations (hint: start with a recurrence relation).

Luckily, if you paid attention, you will remember there are faster ways to do this for big n × n matrices, like Gaussian elimination. If we stick only to adding and multiplying, we can still find a determinant in polynomial time ( there are better ways, but this is an old, readable method ).

A related problem to the determinant is finding the permanent. It’s like a determinant without any subtraction:

Unlike determinants, there is no known way to compute permanents in polynomial time. Since finding the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s is NP-hard (and in fact #P-complete ), it would be pretty important if there were a way.

What the Anthropic proof that VP ≠ VNP means is that there is no way to do this if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size, which look like this:

This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn’t clear how they would help with the permanent. If you think of a way, go claim your $1 million.

items.subtitle: Lobsters Computing Community • Lobsters Community
items.feedText: my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format. lua’s syntax provides many niceties.
items.body:
# lua for data representation - citrons.xyz

## lua for data representation

my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format.

lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]] . however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]) . the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===] , not with a ]] or a ]==] , or a ]====] .

here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:

local function stringize(str) local equal_signs = "" for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do if #e >= #equal_signs then equal_signs = e .. "=" end end return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs) end of course, you can just use string.format with %q , but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code.

anyway, download this file . if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose.

design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use.

## styles of data representation

### JSON style (LON?)

chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program.

return { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead.

return (function() arbitrary_code() end)() trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead.

### INI style

what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, and which table is used can be controlled by the code itself. this table is known as the “environment”. an environment may be passed to load as an argument. the way this can be used is that you can load a chunk with an empty environment and then capture the values it sets as globals.

you can have a file like this:

-- config.lua foo = "bar" list = {1, 2, 3} rule_of_thirds = true then, you can get a table with all the configuration as simply as this:

local config = {} assert(loadfile("config.lua", "t", config))()

### imperative style

lua has a bit of sugar that allows you to shed the parenthesis on function calls to make them look cleaner. an imperative style is a very suitable means to represent data in lua, and it’s very powerful.

path "/path/to/things" config { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } lipsum [[ Voluptatibus laudantium et omnis ut debitis. Similique omnis molestias consequuntur. Praesentium corporis omnis nihil et quidem dolore. Veritatis fugiat eaque corporis eligendi officiis praesentium. Libero quo vero temporibus impedit sit inventore assumenda ]] programming in lua provides a real world example of this .

## security considerations

the major problem with using an entire programming language to represent data is that untrusted data can be readily crafted to be malicious. indeed, I would not use this technique for untrusted data. with that in mind, it is possible to solve or mitigate the potential vulnerabilities.

the main technique for sandboxing lua is controlling the environment. when using lua for data representation, an empty enivronment is the most appropriate (or, an environment that only exposes data constructors). this prevents any I/O or access to the larger program’s state. preventing access to all standard library functions is safest. there are a few standard library functions that have consequences you might not expect .

another concern is denial of service. this is trickier to prevent. it’s fairly trivial to construct a lua chunk which does not return ( while true do end ). debug.sethook can mitigate this somewhat. even so, it’s probably possible to construct something that uses excessive amounts of memory. that said, denial of service is significantly less problematic than the vulnerabilities that are completely avoided by depriving the untrusted code of any standard library functions.

finally, make sure to reject lua bytecode . untrusted lua bytecode is not safe and may cause arbitrary nasal demons in the lua interpreter. load can accept both bytecode and lua source by default. however, passing "t" for the mode parameter prevents this.

## why?

clearly, it’s silly to bring in the entire lua interpreter where you would just use JSON or INI. where this use case of lua shines is when you’re already using lua for a project (and then you already have this powerful data description language), or when you need something with a lot of power or flexibility.

these mini languages can be extended to arbitrary complexity and nuance. unlike JSON, you can add arbitrary type constructors, or anything at all. you can build any kind of language you want, and that’s how lua is designed to be used, and it’s actually approximately the story of how it was invented .

if you’re anything like me, this will sound a little familiar. indeed, many have said similar things about lisp and forth. both of those languages have very different approaches but reach the same conclusion of “inventing your own language”. I believe lua belongs in their pantheon.

## bonus content

python? js? ruby? what the hell are those? all I care about is LUA.

**1:**In [The AI Forecasting Agenda](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-ai-forecasting-agenda), I mentioned three AI forecasting companies. My goal was to name everyone in the space and not play favorites, but this field is moving so fast that I inevitably missed someone, and in this case it was**[Cassi](https://www.cassi-ai.com/)**, a British startup which is currently the top-ranked AI on [Metaculus’ leaderboard](https://www.metaculus.com/leaderboard/). The Cassi team kindly wrote [a post responding to my agenda](https://substack.com/home/post/p-226170904) - most notably, they are pretty confident in their conditional forecasts and say they’re already providing them to institutional paid customers.

If you’re another AI forecasting startup I forgot to mention, feel free to get in touch with me at scott@slatestarcodex.com. Again, I’m not trying to play favorites (although companies that give me free demo access are naturally more likely to have results from their products mentioned in posts).

# Google alternative Kagi launches an email service

- Tech
- News
- Apps
## Google alternative Kagi launches an email service

Kagi Mail is launching in public beta with a 60-day free trial.

Kagi Mail is launching in public beta with a 60-day free trial.

Kagi, which already offers a paid alternative to Google Search and its own Orion browser as a rival to Chrome, is taking on another Google service: Gmail. Today, Kagi announced a public beta of Kagi Mail, a new email service that has “no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.”

With Kagi Mail, you get an @ kagimail.com address, but the service also supports unlimited aliases and domains. It also offers 50GB of storage and a built-in calendar. On the roadmap, you can expect contacts and an address book in Q1 2027, but native mobile apps aren’t expected to arrive until Q3 2027.

“Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once,” Kagi says. “There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.”

Kagi Mail is available now with a 60-day free trial before you have to pay $99 per year. The service is available as part of a $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription.

items.body:
# Frontiers | The biology of therapeutic spacing: a CREB-ERK memory-updating framework linking stress neurocircuitry to exposure-based trauma treatment

## HYPOTHESIS AND THEORY article

Front. Neurosci. , 24 November 2026

Sec. Translational Neuroscience

Volume 20 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2026.1988018

## The biology of therapeutic spacing: a CREB-ERK memory-updating framework linking stress neurocircuitry to exposure-based trauma treatment

- C R C. Richard Spates 1,2 *
- R W Richard W. Seim 2
- R S Rakeshwar S. Guleria 2
- L B Lisa Baker 1
- 1. Department of Psychology, Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo, MI, United States
- 2. VA VISN 17 Center of Excellence for Research on Returning War Veterans, Waco, TX, United States
Article metrics

## Abstract

Exposure-based interventions are among the most empirically supported psychological treatments for trauma- and fear-related disorders. Yet the mechanisms underlying their efficacy remain debated, effect sizes have not appreciably advanced over the past two decades, and dropout is substantial. Established accounts emphasize sustained arousal and within-session fear reduction, but empirical support for them is inconsistent. This Hypothesis and Theory article proposes that therapeutic change can be understood in terms of molecular timing constraints on memory updating rather than in terms of named treatment packages. We draw on three partly independent lines of evidence. First, dismantling trials of Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) and the meta-analyses that review them found no reliable incremental benefit from eye movements or explicit cognitive restructuring, although a working-memory contribution of eye movements remains plausible and a separate meta-analysis reported a moderate additive effect. Second, controlled studies from our laboratories found that brief, spaced exposures produced outcomes equal to or better than prolonged exposure with less aversive arousal. Third, cellular research in non-neuronal cells shows that spaced signals produce stronger and longer-lasting CREB-mediated gene activation than continuous signals of equivalent dose, in an ERK-dependent manner. We integrate these within the Dopamine-Opioid/CREB-ERK (DOCE) framework, which proposes that dopaminergic prediction-error signaling and opioid-related safety signaling are candidate contributors to spacing-dependent updating of fear memory, through reconsolidation, extinction consolidation, or both, with CREB-ERK signaling supporting restabilization. We state the evidence status of each link, note that the dopaminergic and opioid evidence is mixed or limited, and identify predictions that would discriminate reconsolidation from extinction accounts. The framework suggests testable hypotheses for spacing parameters, pharmacological timing, and neuroimaging, and suggests that the proliferation of named trauma treatments may partly reflect a problem of mechanism identification.

## Introduction

### Section 1: The mechanism problem in trauma and fear treatment

Exposure-based interventions are among the most empirically supported psychological treatments for fear- and trauma-related disorders, with established efficacy across specific phobias, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and posttraumatic stress disorder ( Chambless and Ollendick, 2001 ; Choy et al., 2007 ; Powers and Emmelkamp, 2008 ). Two features of this literature have resisted progress. First, effect sizes have not appreciably increased over time. A meta-analysis of prolonged exposure for PTSD found that publication year did not moderate effect size ( Powers et al., 2010 ), and a recent meta-analysis of placebo-controlled cognitive-behavioral trials found smaller effects in recent trials, particularly in PTSD ( Bhattacharya et al., 2023 ). Second, the mechanistic accounts offered by competing named treatment packages remain largely incommensurable with one another and with the neuroscience of memory. By “treatment brands” we mean manualized treatments marketed under distinct theoretical labels, such as EMDR, prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, and Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART; Buck et al., 2020 ; Kip et al., 2019 ; Storey et al., 2024 ).

Traditional theories of exposure therapy emphasize sustained arousal and prolonged confrontation with feared stimuli until within-session fear reduction occurs ( Foa and Kozak, 1986 ). The exposure literature often calls this habituation. We avoid that term because habituation strictly denotes a non-associative process, which is distinct from the associative learning processes (extinction and reconsolidation) discussed below. Empirical support for the traditional account has been inconsistent, and implementation faces constant challenges: high dropout ( Hembree et al., 2003 ; Kehle-Forbes et al., 2016 ), therapist reluctance to deliver highly aversive procedures ( Becker et al., 2004 ), and a plateau in clinical outcomes despite four decades of refinement. These difficulties reflect a general problem in clinical psychology: therapies have tended to be evaluated as branded packages rather than as combinations of active and inert components. Component analysis addresses this problem: designating a package as empirically supported does not show which of its parts contribute ( Borkovec and Castonguay, 1998 ).

The molecular neuroscience of memory has matured considerably over the same period. CREB-mediated transcription, ERK signaling cascades, and the dopaminergic and opioidergic modulation of these pathways are now characterized in considerable detail at the cellular and circuit levels ( Kandel, 2001 ; Silva et al., 1998 ; Thomas and Huganir, 2004 ). Recent work has extended this to live, circuit-level manipulation of CREB-ERK signaling during memory recall itself ( Tan et al., 2026 ; Zent and Dell’Acqua, 2025 ).

Reconsolidation research illustrates both the promise and the difficulty of translation. Retrieval can destabilize a consolidated memory and open a time-limited window in which it can be modified ( Nader et al., 2000 ; Alberini and Ledoux, 2013 ), and a mismatch between expected and actual outcome (prediction error) is an important condition for destabilization. Success depends, however, on boundary conditions that remain incompletely understood, including memory strength and age, learning history, and the character of the mismatch, particularly for the real-life memories treated in clinic ( Milton et al., 2023 ; Radiske et al., 2024 ). Prediction error also participates in extinction, and how a retrieved memory moves among reconsolidation, an insensitive transitional or “limbo” state, and extinction is only beginning to be characterized ( Lee et al., 2006 ; Merlo et al., 2014 , 2018 ). Any mapping of clinical procedures onto these processes is therefore a hypothesis.

items.body:
# John Siracusa launches Jetty Pro

- John Siracusa launches Jetty Pro – Six Colors MENU This Week's Sponsor Magic Lasso Adblock : Block ads in iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple TV apps by Jason Snell November 23, 2026 3:58 PM PT ■ apps John Siracusa launches Jetty Pro My little auto-hiding palette features connections to file servers, SSH shortcuts, screen-sharing shortcuts, Keyboard Maestro macros, and more. A thousand beta builds later, John Siracusa has finally launched his new app, a dock-and-palette utility called Jetty Pro : I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to. I’ve been using this app for months and I love it. It has very specifically filled a space in my Mac’s interface that has been empty since DragThing died in 2019 , namely a palette full of arbitrary stuff like SSH connections, folders, macros, and URLs that I want to get to with a single click. For a guy who has a reputation for liking things just so , you might think Jetty Pro does things only one way. That’s not true. One of the things John wants just so is for his apps to have a lot of user-configurable options. You can make palettes of various looks, with various behaviors, and have their behavior remain consistent or vary depending on what display you’re using. (And yes, it is a thorough Dock replacement, so I can finally have a second Dock appear on the right side of my secondary display whenever I have it open.) In John’s unsurprisingly detailed FAQ page he explains why the app is available only on a subscription basis —mostly, it’s because it will require a lot of maintenance due to its use of private Apple APIs. Those private APIs are also why it’s not available in the Mac App Store, but only direct from John. Jetty Pro has a 14-day free trial, and then costs $10 for the first year. Oh, and there’s no non-Pro version of Jetty in the Mac App Store. John worked on one for a while, but it didn’t make sense. All the goodness of Jetty Pro is happening with John’s circumvention of Apple’s rules. He’s a rebel! And his attempt to slowly rebuild every feature of DragThing continues. Report a typo
—Linked by Jason Snell
