items.body:
*Housekeeping:*

- There will be a reader meetup in SF on December 10: [RSVP here.](https://luma.com/mk1c03jk)
- I’ll be in Stockholm on November 26 and made [a Luma event if someone wants to meet up](https://luma.com/8ga6l729). You can also dm me on Substack.

If you read writing advice, you’ll often stumble upon all of these rather abstract rules, such as “show, don’t tell,” “open the essay with a concrete story to engage people,” and so on. I don’t find advice like that useful at all. These sorts of maxims remind me of the small notes I might jot down to myself to remember the directions to a friend’s house—“left, right, past the oak tree, right.” Well, that might describe the right way, but it is a very rough map of the terrain, and if it turns out that the person who wrote the notes forgot to mention something—or perhaps was going somewhere other than you—their advice will lead you completely astray.

To develop a good toolbox, I find it much more fruitful to take the texts that I feel do whatever I want to learn best and read them slowly, repeatedly, with a pencil in hand. It’s like taking a slow, attentive walk around the neighborhood, getting a deep *feeling* for the landscape, for what it means to write at the highest levels. I will usually form a few theories about why the text is so powerful and I might spot a few techniques I can put into my toolbox, but these theories and techniques will be much more idiosyncratic and tentative than the ones I get from consuming writing advice: I will create tools that are meaningful to *my* projects, and my taste, and I will hold the tools with a light hand, knowing full well that they are just a rough guess, derived from a limited reading.

Last weekend, I did such a close reading of the piece that David Foster Wallace wrote about John McCain’s failed campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2000—the one that was originally published as “The Weasel, Twelve Monkeys and the Shrub,” a sprawling ~15,700-word essay in the April 13 issue of *Rolling Stone,* and later republished in a three-times-as-long “director’s cut” ebook called, first, *Up, Simba*, and later, *McCain’s Promise*. It is a New Journalism-derived sort of essay-reportage hybrid, where DFW travels around with the McCain campaign’s press bus, fails to interview any of the main players, and instead hangs around with the cameramen and sound technicians, but does little of the standard journalistic scene-setting and interview-quoting, in favor of a kind of writing that is a crossover between diary and essay.

I have read the book-length version of *McCain’s Promise* four times, I think, and the short version, once or twice. The immediate excuse for the last two + one rereads was that I wanted to understand how DFW integrates interviews and scene-setting into his essayistic reflections (and for the answer to that see this footnote1), but what I ended up focusing most on during the actual reading was the question: how on earth does he manage to make the reading so engaging and have such strong narrative momentum when most of it is just very long and detailed descriptions of the interior of a bus and the different kinds of phones people use on the bus and so on?

#### How DFW creates narrative momentum

items.body:
The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on.

Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up.

Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ([slides](https://natolambert.com/slides/2026/fireworks/talk.html), [recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zsO5RktNB7k)). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside.

The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is.

The downside is that the true *long-term* benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where [inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/ai-inference-startups-quietly-buying-chips) (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s [DeepInfer](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepinfer) release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in [my recent piece on the open model economy](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/how-well-can-we-measure-open-model).

Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen’s support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out.

Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models.

There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards [candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety”](https://www.axios.com/2026/10/14/ai-safety-regulation-election-spending-50-million). Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been [one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/6-months-to-live-for-open-models) since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting.

Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work.

As a brief aside, the extent to which the media ecosystem is revolving around timing today, rather than exact availability of information, is incredible. All of these Jensen affairs were known, but getting them out at the right time, right after the midterm political swing, took down the king.

The same goes for the Jacob Coxon brouhaha this summer. All of that safety culture around top labs was well known, but the right timing around datacenters and the Overton window made it a national issue. This could very well happen at some point for open model safety, as it tends to be harm, risk, or safety-related narratives that drive the modern media algorithms. I cannot imagine my work on open-science driving such a media cycle, because it will never happen.

[Share](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/open-source-ai-without-jensen?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

The only lasting solution to this is to incubate a truly frontier open model player in the US. For example, I agree completely with Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, on a core problem in the US open model ecosystem. From a recent ChinaTalk + SemiAnalysis [emergency podcast](https://youtu.be/2jqSNHWdHEY?t=1737):

> Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it.
> Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot? No. Moonshot skill-wise is probably just as good as the US labs. They just have a big deficit in compute and deployment. So I think if we don’t have a scale advantage, then you don’t win. Yes, these smaller labs have spent a lot of money on models. But DeepMind, Grok, Meta have regularly fallen behind the frontier of Chinese labs, and they’re spending more. So it’s not just, oh, spend a few billion dollars and you can make a model that’s better.

items.body:
After a months-long investigation, Channel 4 News’s FactCheck team has obtained a dossier of exclusive new files on UK arms export licences to Israel.

The files give us major new insights into UK companies’ arms sales to the Israeli government during its war on Gaza, which has killed at least 75,000 Palestinians.

Our revelations raise questions about the former Conservative government’s policy on arms sales, as well as the current Labour government’s stated policy on the ongoing export of military aircraft parts.

We’re going to take you through the files step by step.

## The basics – what is an export licence?

When a UK company wants to sell arms abroad, it needs to apply to the UK government for an arms export licence – this document is like a permission slip.

Public data on these licences is limited. It doesn’t tell us whether the licences have actually been used to export weapons, or who in a given country would be using them.

But through repeated Freedom of Information requests to the Department for Business and Trade, FactCheck has now obtained several line-by-line snapshots of active arms export licences for Israel. The snapshots are from July 2024, July 2025 and July 2026.

Our new data captures which licences were active, not just for the country of Israel, but specifically for use by the Israeli government – which we understand means the Israeli military. And it also includes “usage notes”, which tell us whether a given licence has been used to export goods during a specific period of time.

## The Conservative government

On 7 October 2023, attacks on Israel by Hamas – which is proscribed as a terror group by the UK – left 1,200 people killed and 251 taken hostage. Israel then began its biggest ever bombardment of Gaza.

It was then that the International Court of Justice ruled there was a plausible risk of genocide in Gaza. Soon after, in April 2024, hundreds of UK lawyers, including former Supreme Court justices, issued a legal opinion saying that the UK must urgently suspend arms sales to Israel.

The then-Conservative UK government did not suspend arms sales.

Our first snapshot of new data reveals that, as the Conservatives were leaving office in July 2024, there were still 67 military export licenses left active where the Israeli government was an end user.

Those licences permitted the sale of a wide range of items – including parts for:

- combat aircraft
- military helicopters
- combat vehicles
- equipment for the launch and control of munitions
- military communications equipment
- military navigation equipment
- other military aircraft
- training ammunition, and more.

The total value of the active licences was around £164m. That represents an upper limit on what could have been exported under single issue licences. But the data also includes other types of open licence, which allow an unlimited value of exports.

We can reveal for the first time that, by July 2024, at least 25 of those 67 active licences had actually been used to send military parts to the Israeli government, since October 2023.

The licences that were used by UK companies to export goods during the war included licences for parts for:

- targeting equipment
- military aero engines
- combat aircraft
- military aircraft
- trainer aircraft
- parts for surface-to-air missiles.
- Targeting equipment refers to equipment which allows you to find, and aim weapons at, a target on the ground.

One of the used licences was a high value £25m licence for parts and software for “military aero engines”, which could include engines for military aircraft or drones. The data does not reveal the exact value that was actually exported. Another was an £88m licence for parts of “combat aircraft”.

The combined value of the used licences was around £150m. Again, this represents an upper limit on what would have been exported, and the actual value of the items sent was likely lower.

Two of the licences had been exhausted, meaning their full value was exported. These included one worth around £66,000 for trainer aircraft parts, and another worth around £109,000 for combat aircraft parts. It’s not clear whether the full value was exported during the war on Gaza.

We spoke to Professor Janina Dill, Dame Louise Richardson Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government, University of Oxford. She told FactCheck that the UK “should have used [its] leverage” as a major arms exporter to Israel and “while there is a great deal of contestation around the question whether Israel is commiting genocide in Gaza”, it was “hardly contestable in 2024” that it was “committing grave breaches and war crimes”.

The Conservative Party did not respond to our repeated requests for comment about this story.

Israel has repeatedly denied the accusations that it has committed genocide or breaches of international law in Gaza.

## The Labour government

In July 2024, Keir Starmer’s Labour government entered power.

And by September 2024, the new administration said it wanted to suspend around 30 arms export licences for Israel, citing concerns over breaches of international law.

It said it was suspending exports that could be used by the Israeli military in Gaza. And it explicitly mentioned targeting equipment, and parts for military aircraft, including helicopters, fighter jets and drones.

But there were two big carve outs in the policy.

Firstly, Labour said it would continue to allow the sale of military training items, because they wouldn’t be used directly in conflict.

And secondly, the Labour government said it wouldn’t try to stop all exports of parts for the F-35 — a type of fighter jet used by Israel and NATO allies — because the exports went to a global pool that benefited multiple countries.

The Labour government refused to give us the full list of licences it suspended – even under Freedom of Information laws. It cited commercial sensitivity and confidentiality. It said if we figured out the names of the companies holding the suspended licences, we might, “potentially incorrectly”, link those firms to potential war crimes.

But by looking at the snapshots which the government did release, and comparing the active licences before and after Labour’s suspensions, we can corroborate some of what Labour announced about its suspensions.

For example, targeting equipment did disappear from later lists of active export licences, after Labour’s suspensions. As did other licences covering parts for military helicopters and combat vehicles. So that data fits with what Labour said it would do.

But many export permissions remained active under the Labour government.

Some of the licences that remained active for the Israeli government under Labour included parts for:

items.body:
Cover Image by [Gustavo Fring](https://www.pexels.com/@2206740/) from Pexels

*By Althea Need Kaminske*

Perhaps one of the more obvious pieces of advice that I give medical students about learning is to remember that our brains are in our bodies. Yes, I know that these are very smart, high achieving students who know quite a bit about anatomy and biology. But I also know that in an educational system and society that focuses so much on productivity, it can be easy to compartmentalize our lives. To become so focused on maximizing spaced retrieval practice (yay!) that we forget to prioritize sleep, nutrition, and exercise (boo!). In high-stress and fast-paced environments it can be difficult to remember that we are, ultimately, animals. Creatures that need sleep, a healthy diet, and daily walks.

A recent meta-meta-analysis by Singh et al. (2025) examined the effectiveness of exercise for improving cognition (1). The analysis included 133 meta-analysis, which themselves comprised a total of 2,724 randomized control trials. I’ll break down the results, but the overall finding was pretty notable: **exercise, even light intensity, benefits general cognition, memory, and executive function across all populations.**

The meta-meta-analysis classified outcomes into three categories: general cognition, memory, and executive function. General cognition was measured by scales like the Mini-Mental State Examination, Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale - Cognitive Subscale which are used in medical settings to assess overall cognitive functioning. Memory was measured by instruments like the Wechsler Memory Scale and Verbal Learning Test which measure short-term memory and episodic memory. Executive function was measured by tools like the Digit-Span Test, Digit Span-Backwards, Digit-Span Forwards, and Trail Making Test Part A and B which measure visual and verbal working memory and attention.

## General Cognition and Exercise

There was a significant effect of exercise for improving general cognition. This effect was found across all age groups. The effect varied as a function of exercise type, with a moderate-to-large effect for exergames, and a small-to-moderate effect for aerobic, dance, mind-body, mixed mode, resistance exercise, and other. The effect of exercise on general cognition did not vary as a function of exercise intensity, however interventions that lasted for 1-3 months had the greatest effect on general cognition compared to interventions lasting 4-6 months or greater than 6 months. Finally, the beneficial effects of exercise on general cognition did not vary as a function of session frequency, session duration, or weekly duration.

## Memory and Exercise

There was a significant effect of exercise on memory. This effect was stronger in children/adolescents than in older adults (though benefits were still present in older adults). The effect also varied as a function of exercise type, with large effects for exergames, small-to-medium effects for aerobic, dance, mind-body, mixed mode, and resistance exercise. The effect of exercise on memory did not vary as a function of exercise intensity or intervention length. Further, the beneficial effect of exercise on memory did not vary as a function of session frequency or duration (there was an insufficient number of studies to draw conclusions about weekly duration).

## Executive Function and Memory

There was a significant effect of exercise on executive function. This effect was stronger in children/adolescents than in older adults (though benefits were still present in older adults). The effect also varied as a function of exercise type with exercises categorized as “other” as having a greater effect compared to aerobic, dance, exergames, mind-body, mixed mode and resistance exercise. The effect of exercise on executive function did not vary as a function of exercise intensity or intervention length. Further the beneficial effects of exercise on executive function did not vary as a function of session frequency, session duration, or weekly duration.

## Why does exercise benefit cognition?

The authors propose two potential ways that exercise improves cognition. First, there are several physiological mechanisms that might lead to cognitive improvement. The release of neurotrophic factors, increased vascularisation of the brain, greater dendritic spine density, enhanced synaptic plasticity, and reduced systemic inflammation (1). Your brain is in your body! Exercise improves overall brain health.

Second, the authors highlight the fact that exergames appear to be a particularly potent form of exercise. They suggest that this particular mode of exercise not only confers some of the physical benefits listed above, but may be particularly potent because of the challenging cognitive aspect of the exercise. Exergames require you to recall movements, recognize cues, and memorize steps.

## Exercise and ADHD

While there were benefits of exercise for all populations, the authors note that the benefit appears to be greater for those with ADHD. They highlight a few potential reasons for this. First, many of the studies examining exercise and ADHD involved children and adolescents, which is a population that was more responsive to exercise in general. Second, given that the hallmark of ADHD is struggles with executive function, they suggest that ADHDers simply had more room for improvement. Finally, they point out that one of the proposed mechanisms for working memory deficits in ADHD are altered neural activity in areas of the brain associated with working memory. Exercise may improve neural activity in these areas through enhanced blood flow and neuroplasticity. While further research is needed to test these theories, and to extend them to adult populations, this provides some initial evidence for a relatively low-cost tool for helping with the management of ADHD.

## Takeaways

Overall, I think the results of this meta-meta-analysis are really encouraging. Exercise - any exercise - can benefit cognition. Whether it’s a 20 minute walk after dinner, lifting weights, or breaking out the Nintendo Wii, adding movement into your routine can improve your cognition, memory, and focus.

My dog, Oden, who reminds me to go for walks every day.

…

items.body:
Welcome to the latest edition of “What’s new in Swift,” a curated digest of releases, news, and discussions from the Swift project and community.

To start things off, our guest contributor shares a timely reminder for anyone relying on CocoaPods:

> Hi, I’m Dave Verwer, co-creator of the [Swift Package Index](https://swiftpackageindex.com/) and now part of a team at Apple working on a public, cross-platform package registry for Swift. How developers find, share, and manage dependencies across the entire ecosystem is something we think about a lot.
> CocoaPods is a dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C Cocoa projects. The project began in 2011, before Swift was publicly available and long before the Swift Package Manager (SwiftPM) existed. For many people who started developing with the iPhone SDK, it was a first look at what a dependency manager could do. Today, Swift has expanded across platforms, and SwiftPM has become the standard for managing dependencies everywhere Swift runs.
> Following a two-year sunset period that began in 2024, the [CocoaPods project will stop accepting new pods and pod versions on December 2nd, 2026](https://blog.cocoapods.org/CocoaPods-Specs-Repo/). With that date less than a month away, I wanted to make sure this milestone is on your radar, and to share what it means for your projects. If your project still uses CocoaPods, this change won’t immediately break your builds. All current pods and versions will still be available, just in a read-only state. However, with pod authors no longer able to publish updates, if you haven’t switched to SwiftPM yet, now is the time.
> Most pods in your dependencies that are still being maintained will already be compatible with SwiftPM, and the easiest way to check is to look for them on [Swift Package Index](https://swiftpackageindex.com). Every package in the index is a SwiftPM package, and if you find any incompatible pods, you can search for an alternative so you don’t leave yourself with unmaintained dependencies.
> I’d like to extend a personal thank you to everyone who worked on CocoaPods for creating and maintaining it for the last fifteen years. Their work shaped how the community shares code, and it helped lay the groundwork for the modern, cross-platform package ecosystem Swift has today. I also want to express my admiration for how the team managed this sunset and communicated the transition so clearly.

Now on to other news about Swift:

## Videos to watch

- Tim Condon’s ACCU 2026 talk, [Incrementally Migrating C++ to a Memory Safe Language with Swift](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LMQ21X6_2FQ), shows how Swift’s C++ interoperability lets you adopt memory safety incrementally, without rewriting everything at once.
- [Building Android App with Swift: First-Hand Experience](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AibwYt3esbk) is a conversation with Pierluigi Cifani, who describes how his team shares business logic and ViewModels between iOS and Android, with native UI on each and Skip bridging the two, in apps like Polymarket.
- Want to build Minecraft mods in Swift? A recent iOSDC Japan lightning talk, [Creating a Minecraft Java mod with Swift](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r_A44OiLASw), shows how, using swift-java to interoperate with Minecraft Java Edition. The speaker’s [blog post](https://note.com/1mash0/n/n107a49ec76a3) has the slides and more demo videos. The talk is in Japanese, with an auto-dubbed English track available on YouTube.

## Community highlights

- Did you know Optional has a take() method? John Sundell’s [Interesting ways of using Swift optionals](https://www.swiftbysundell.com/articles/interesting-ways-of-using-swift-optionals/) goes beyond if let, with take(), switching directly on optional enums, and a small isNil(or:) helper that works with key paths.
- What happens when you let the compiler check your whole website? Sindre Sorhus [rebuilt his site in Swift](https://sindresorhus.com/blog/swift-website), moving off Astro so that broken links and bad metadata become build errors.
- Two server-side frameworks, one team’s experience. [Don’t Underestimate Swift](https://wearecommunity.io/communities/mobilepeople/articles/8881) shares what engineers at EPAM learned building backends with Hummingbird and Vapor, and how those services compared against FastAPI and Node.js.
- A [preview of Embedded Swift support in Swift Testing](https://forums.swift.org/t/preview-embedded-swift-support-in-swift-testing/90281) shows nearly the whole API, including @Test, #expect(), and custom traits, running in Embedded Swift. It has been tried on WASI in Safari, a Raspberry Pi Pico 2, a Playdate, and a Game Boy Advance SP.

## New package releases

- [Swift Kafka Client](https://github.com/swift-server/swift-kafka-client/releases/tag/1.0.0) has reached 1.0.0. The client for Apache Kafka, the event streaming platform, is built on librdkafka and works with structured concurrency, with built-in metrics through swift-metrics and static Linux builds.
- Robotics meets Swift. [swift-ros2](https://github.com/swift-ros2/swift-ros2) is a native client library for ROS 2, the robotics framework. It runs on Apple platforms, Linux, Windows, and Android, and version 3.1.0 recently added a topic graph API for discovering what’s available on a robot network.
- [Perfect-NIO](https://github.com/PerfectlySoft/Perfect-NIO), the HTTP layer of the Perfect server framework, has been rewritten on SwiftNIO and Swift 6 concurrency. Version 0.1.0 uses async, @Sendable route handlers, and 0.2.0 adds WebSocket message size limits.

## Swift Evolution

The Swift project adds new language features through the [Swift Evolution process](https://www.swift.org/swift-evolution/). These are some of the proposals currently under review or recently accepted for a future Swift release.

**Under active review:**

- [SE-0559](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0559-unicode-bidi-class.md) Add bidiClass to Unicode.Scalar.Properties - If your code lays out or transforms text that mixes right-to-left and left-to-right scripts, you often need to know how specific characters behave. This proposal adds bidiClass to Unicode.Scalar.Properties, so you can look up a character’s bidirectional class in Swift without needing to bridge to external libraries like ICU.
- [SE-0560](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0560-swiftpm-build-configuration-conditional-target-dependencies.md) Build configuration conditionals for target dependencies - This proposal would let you conditionally include SwiftPM dependencies based on whether you’re building for debug or release. By adding a new configuration condition, you could link a debug menu only into your debug builds, or a crash reporter only into your release builds.

**Recently accepted:**

items.body:
Nicht viele Lieder haben mich in meinem Leben unmittelbar zu Tränen gerührt. Dass man eines davon als Karnevalslied bezeichnen kann, hätte ich vermutlich nie gedacht, bevor ich nach Köln gezogen bin. Aber keine Sorge, dieser Text wird keine lokalpatriotische Ode an die Domstadt.

Der Kölner Karneval ist eines der größten Straßenfeste Europas. Er ist ein riesiger Wirtschaftsfaktor für die Stadt Köln, sowie für zahlreiche Musiker:innen, deren Songs im Karneval rauf und runter laufen und die in der Karnevalszeit etliche Auftritte haben. Im Februar 2026 stand mit dem Song „Karnevalsmaus“ (Druckluft) sogar ein Karnevalslied an der Spitze der deutschen Singlecharts. Das hat vor Druckluft vier Jahre lang keine andere deutsche Band geschafft.

Oberflächlich betrachtet könnte man die gängigen Karnevalslieder für Malle-Party-Schlager in Mundart halten. Gemeinsamkeiten gibt es durchaus. Aber wer genauer hinhört, erkennt, dass sich in der Musik des Kölner Karnevals weitaus mehr finden lässt als plumper Exzess. Doch so progressiv sich die Kölner:innen ihren Karneval auch denken: Die Männerdominanz unter den im Karneval tonangebenden Musiker:innen zeigt beispielhaft, wie zäh sich Gleichstellung auch 2026 noch gegen gewachsene patriarchale Strukturen und die überzogene Angst um Tradition(en) behaupten muss. Aber beginnen wir bei den Tränen.

Anfang 2026, früher Mittag, ich stehe in meiner Küche und koche. Die Karnevalswoche steht vor der Tür, meine dritte als zugezogener Kölner, und ich will den Ausnahmezustand zwischen Weiberfastnacht und Aschermittwoch in diesem Jahr vollständig auskosten. Zur Vorbereitung höre ich mich durch eine zufällige Karnevals-Playlist. In einem mir bis dahin unbekannten Song zählen die Interpreten in den Strophen Wörter der kölschen Mundart samt hochdeutscher Übersetzung auf. Ich lerne: „Et kölsche Woot för Zwiebel es Öllisch“, einen Bürgersteig nennt man „Trottoir“ und einen Regenschirm „Paraplü“. So geht es Zeile um Zeile, bis es im Refrain heißt: „Op Kölsch jitt et för alles e Woot, nur för die Liebe nit. För alles han ich ’ne Plan B, nur för die Liebe nit.“ Nach diesen Zeilen war es um mich geschehen.

An „För die Liebe nit“ (Lupo) lässt sich prägnant zeigen, was ein Lied des Kölner Karnevals typischerweise ausmacht: eine simple, eingängige Melodie, ein zugänglicher Text zum Mitsingen inklusive „Nanana“-Element und eine große Schippe manchmal schwer zu ertragender Lokalpatriotismus. Zugleich strotzen die Lieder vor Herzlichkeit und Menschlichkeit, die sich in der Einfachheit der Texte unglaublich gut entfalten — und sie damit gefährlich nah an die zumutbare Kitschgrenze bringen. All das vorgetragen in einer Mundart, die beim Singen so weich und melodisch klingt, wie es das Hochdeutsche nie könnte. Nicht umsonst spricht man von der Mundart „Kölsch oder Kölnisch“ (eine Art des Ripuarischen bzw. rheinischen Regiolekts) auch vom „kölschen Singsang“. Der Karneval und die auf Kölsch verfassten Lieder tragen maßgeblich dazu bei, dass die Mundart lebendig bleibt und sich auch über Generationen weiterträgt.

Der Song „För die Liebe nit“ zeugt auch von der Unmöglichkeit, trennscharf zu bestimmen, was überhaupt als Karnevalslied gelten kann. Grob gesagt: Die Kölner:innen machen zum Karnevalslied, was sie zum Karnevalslied machen wollen. Viele Lieder, die im Kölner Karneval zu hören sind, haben lyrisch expliziten Karnevalsbezug, wie z. B. „Nie mehr Fastelovend“ (Querbeat) oder „Et Trömmelche“ (Räuber); andere beschreiben eher lose eine ausgelassene, karnevalistische Stimmung, wie „Superjeilezick“ (Brings) oder „Kumm, loss mer fiere“ (Höhner); manche zeichnen sich dadurch aus, dass sie die Stadt Köln und ihre Lebensqualität zelebrieren, wie z. B. „Tommi“ (AnnenMayKantereit) oder „Stadt mit K“ (Kasalla). Und die meisten Songs, die man im Kölner Karneval zu hören bekommt, sind ‚op kölsch‘ verfasst oder enthalten zumindest entsprechende Passagen.

Neben Liedern von Interpret:innen aus Köln und Umgebung hält der Malle-Party-Schlager immer größeren Einzug in die Musikrotationen des Kölner Karnevals — gerade bei jüngeren Generationen. Sichtbar vorangetrieben von einer Musikindustrie, die im (Kölner) Karneval den idealen zweiten Ausspielweg für die Hits von der Playa ausgemacht hat. Den kölschen Bands wiederum sichert die Ballermann-Liaison auch abseits der Karnevalszeit beständige Einnahmen.

Die beliebteste Karnevalsplaylist auf Spotify „[Karneval Party Hits 2026](https://open.spotify.com/playlist/7MCa6e9E3cPtVYyoCKz76C)“ — gespeichert von knapp 120.000 Nutzer:innen — wird verwaltet von dem Nutzer „Extreme Sound“. Hinter Extreme Sound steckt ein Kölner Duo, das unter anderem den Text für „20 Zentimeter“ (vielen lieben Dank dafür) geschrieben hat und das mit dem „Roten Pferd“ (Markus Becker), „Johnny Däpp“ (Lorenz Büffel) oder auch „Schatzi schenk mir ein Foto“ (Mickie Krause) einige der größten Malle-Hits überhaupt produziert hat. Die beliebteste Karnevalsplaylist auf dem größten Musik-Streamingdienst besteht daher neben Klassikern kölscher Bands zu über 50 Prozent aus der Crème de la Crème der Ballermann-Hits – von „Mama Laudaaa“ (Almklausi & Specktakel) über „Ich verkaufe meinen Körper“ (Peter Wackel) bis hin zu „Saufi Saufi“ (Tobee).

In der Playlist finden sich außerdem unzählige ‚Mallorca-Versionen‘ von kölschen Karnevalsliedern, häufig mit Malle-Star-Feature und gerne „Party-Edit“ genannt — als wäre der Karneval nicht schon Feierei genug.
Die Lieder passen sich dem Sound der Playa an und werden dabei schneller und elektronischer. Die ruhigeren, andächtigen, gar melancholischen Lieder, die fester Bestandteil des Karnevals sind, schaffen es dagegen selten bis nach Mallorca. Genauso wenig wie die kölsche Mundart: Bis auf vereinzelte Catchphrases verschwindet sie häufig aus den Songs, die für den Ballermann produziert werden. Anspielungen auf Köln werden teilweise zu Anspielungen auf Mallorca. Den relativ neuen Song „11 Jecken (bei 3 ist hier Karneval)“ (47_kö11sch) gibt es beispielsweise auch in veränderter Version als „Bei 3 ist hier Malle (11 Jecken)“.

Ballermann und kölscher Karneval vertragen sich schon sehr lange sehr gut. Seit über 50 Jahren gibt es jedes Jahr im September eine sogenannte [„Kölsche Woche“](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXH1emRXc18) auf Mallorca — inklusive Mini-Rosenmontagszug. In den 1980er Jahren lieferte die kölsche Band Paveier mit dem Lied „Buenos Dias Matthias“ eine der ersten Mallorca-Hymnen überhaupt; in kölscher Mundart wohlgemerkt. Und spätestens 1997 hat der Kölner Tom Gerhardt mit „Ballermann 6“ die inoffizielle Städtepartnerschaft zwischen Playa und Rheinmetropole besiegelt. Kommt mit der größeren Präsenz des Malle-Party-Schlagers im Karneval also nur zusammen, was ohnehin zusammengehört?

items.body:
photo cred: my dad

*Just a quick thing before this week’s post. If you’ve preordered* [THE STRANGEST IDEA IN THE WORLD](https://thestrangestideaintheworld.com/), I’d like to send you a little something extra in the mail. [Submit your preorder receipt and your mailing address here](https://sites.prh.com/strangestidea-preorder). This is only available to folks with US or UK addresses—apologies to those who live elsewhere! In the US, everyone with a valid entry will get one; in the UK they’ll pick winners randomly. The link will be open until December 11, and we’ll start mailing things out after that. I won’t spoil the surprise, but I will say that a) it’s very silly, and b) I can’t wait to get mine.

*(For the US: US Residents, 18+. Ends December 11, 2026. See terms at [https://sites.prh.com/strangestidea-preorder](https://sites.prh.com/strangestidea-preorder))*

*Anyway, onto the post!*

Before anybody enacts a major social policy or launches any philanthropic programs, they should sacrifice a goat. There ought to be an entire liturgy of grotesqueries, in fact—pricked fingers, names written in blood, robes, candles, chanting, obsidian blades, still-beating hearts, the whole shebang.

The point of this ritual is not to signal our obeisance to the gods (although if any of them want to stop by and help us out, that would be cool), but to remind ourselves that we know nothing. This is procedurally-induced humility, which is desperately necessary, because an alarming number of our best-intentioned interventions *do not work*.

For example:

- In 2009, Congress spent $3 billion on “School Improvement Grants” for the worst-performing schools in the country. As far as we can tell, [those grants did nothing](https://ies.ed.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/nces_pubs/ncee/pubs/20174013/pdf/20174012.pdf).
- Universities that hired a Chief Diversity Officer between 2001 and 2019 [did not end up with more diverse students, faculties, or administrators](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/soej.12584).
- The American government spent $280 million to help Afghan women get jobs, and now [they can’t really say whether any women got any jobs](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/09/13/world/asia/afghanistan-women-usaid.html).1
- Remember 20 years ago, when giving laptops to kids in developing countries seemed like the most important thing to do? Well, a 10-year RCT of 531 rural schools in Peru found [zero effects of “One Laptop Per Child” on academic performance](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272725002373).2
- Researchers developed four different messages that were supposed to convince parents to vaccinate their kids. None of the messages worked, and [one of them accidentally made parents more likely to believe that vaccines cause autism](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-abstract/133/4/e835/32713/Effective-Messages-in-Vaccine-Promotion-A?redirectedFrom=fulltext).

Most of those are left-coded failures, so here are some right-coded failures:

- When Arkansas added a work requirement to Medicaid, [the number of Arkansans with health insurance went down without any increase in employment](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12461122/).
- In 2002, the Bush administration launched the Building Strong Families Program, which provided counseling to low-income, unmarried parents with the goal of strengthening their relationships, keeping them both in their child’s life, and ultimately getting them married. Three years later, an independent evaluation found that [the program did none of those things](https://sci-hub.ru/10.1111/jomf.12094).
- And here is [the effect of four different abstinence-only sex ed programs](https://aspe.hhs.gov/reports/impacts-four-title-v-section-510-abstinence-education-programs-1) that run across the United States:

In the social sciences, [nothing ever dies; it merely becomes embarrassing](https://www.experimental-history.com/p/nothing-ever-dies-it-merely-becomes). We can’t say that it’s *impossible* for anything like these programs to ever succeed, given enough time, flimsy theorizing, and generous definitions of “success”. The point is that these effects should be large, and instead they are nonexistent. Seems to me like it’s time to get the goats in here.

## HEAVY METAL

It’s inevitable that some of our interventions are going to fail. (If they don’t, we should either be suspicious of the results, or we should be more ambitious with our programs.) What we really want to know is: when we try to improve the world through some policy or program, how often do we succeed?

We don’t have a good answer to this question, but we do have a good joke about it.

In 1987, the sociologist Peter Rossi wrote a tongue-in-cheek paper that accidentally became his intellectual legacy. He would later refer to it as “far from being one of my favorites” and “the source of considerable embarrassment”, and yet it’s the only thing of his that I’ve ever read or even heard of.3 It was called “[The Iron Law of Evaluation and Other Metallic Rules](https://gwern.net/doc/sociology/1987-rossi.pdf)“, and it went like this, lightly paraphrased:

- The Iron Law of Evaluation: The net expected impact of a large social program is zero.
- The Stainless Steel Law: Better-designed evaluations are more likely to find null effects.
- The Brass Law: The more a program is intended to change people, the more likely the impact of that program will be zero.
- The Zinc Law: The programs most likely to be evaluated are those most likely to fail.

Rossi [tried to walk back his laws shortly before he died in 2006](https://welfareacademy.umd.edu/rossi/Rossi_Remarks_Iron_Law_Reconsidered.pdf), insisting that there is now a “large number of well conducted impact assessments that yield statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”. Still, even after supposedly enduring 16 years of embarrassment from his one satirical paper, he concluded, “we really do not know whether programs over a wide variety of substantive areas are worth anything”.

items.body:
Thanksgiving is all about tradition, and one classic tradition is that after a big meal of turkey and associated carbs, the family gathers in the living room to watch professional football. This year, we have five straight days of football to keep the family entertained over the holiday weekend. How did that tradition begin?

Thanksgiving became a national holiday in 1863, when President Abraham Lincoln used it as a way of building unity during the Civil War. American football hadn't even been invented. But only six years later, the sport launched in colleges. Just a couple of weeks later, two Philadelphia cricket clubs staged a football game on Thanksgiving Day 1869! After all, the players didn't have to go to their regular jobs on a holiday, and spectators had free time to watch.

College football on Thanksgiving became a sensation and then petered out in the 1920s, but it wasn't forgotten. The holiday stunt that brought people out to watch football worked again for professional teams. Read [the history of Thanksgiving football](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/why-thanksgiving-football-emerged-as-an-american-tradition-in-the-aftermath-of-the-civil-war-180989897/) at Smithsonian.

(Image credit: [Frederic Remington](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Frederic_Remington_-_Touchdown,_Yale_vs._Princeton,_Thanksgiving_Day,_Nov._27,_1890,_Yale_32,_Princeton_0_-_1932.264_-_Yale_University_Art_Gallery.jpg))

items.body:
This is interesting — in 1904 the *Strand* sent a musician to Parliament to record the pitch and rhythm of the speakers’ voices on a musical staff. Some examples:

Sydney Buxton “speaks often and briefly, but into a short space of time he can cram a wonderful lot of words, being one of the most rapid speakers in the House. The dominant note is about C sharp, and the modulation seldom varies in character, the speech being broken up into short phrases, with a downward inflection at the end of each.”

Charles Fenwick “may lay claim to the lowest pitch. His strong, vigorous, ringing style is a good index to the character which has raised its owner from work in the collieries to a seat in Parliament.”

David Lloyd George “possesses a flexible voice of light, clear, and pleasant quality. … When in a practical mood he gets along on D and E, but at other times he bridges a considerable interval.”

Prime Minister Arthur Balfour’s voice “has that undefinable something in its timbre which one listens for in a first-class baritone’s singing. … The note on which he does most speaking is somewhere between D and E, but he frequently ranges the octave from G to G.”

[The whole article is here.](https://archive.org/details/the-strand/The%20Strand%20v27%201904/page/140/mode/2up)

items.body:
The [American Jewish Historical Society](https://ajhs.org/) shared [archival footage from the Kurt K. Field Film Collection](https://ajhs.org/macys-thanksgiving-day-parade-archival-footage-from-the-kurt-k-field-film-collection/) of the annual [Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade](https://laughingsquid.com/kermit-fozzie-1978-thanksgiving-parade/) in 1940, 1945, and 1946. There’s no footage from 1942 to 1944, the years the parade was canceled during [World War II](https://laughingsquid.com/?s=World+War+II).

> The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade footage found here is from 1940, 1945 and 1946. During World War II the parade was canceled due to war rationing for rubber and helium.

The 1945 footage opens with a title card calling it the “First Post-War Thanksgiving Day Parade”. The Kurt K. Field Film Collection documents one American Jewish family’s leisure activities from 1939 to 1966, including several trips to the parade.

items.body:
The surprising benefit of a common enemy

Sallust’s Theorem is that fear of an external enemy promotes internal social unity.

Perhaps more pertinent is the other side of Sallust’s Theorem: the absence or removal of an external enemy leads to internal moral decay and conflict.

Sallust, or more fully Gaius Sallustius Crispus, was a Roman historian and politician around the time of Julius Caesar. Remarkably, several of his works have remained intact to be read over 2000 years later.

Sallust describes unity in the face of common enemies and decline in their absence at several points in the history of Rome’s Republic. His strongest example is the fear of Carthage.

Here’s Sallust in his work The War with Jugurtha, chapter 41 (Latin terms included):

“…before the destruction of Carthage the people and senate of Rome together governed the republic peacefully and with moderation. There was no strife among the citizens either for glory or for power; fear of the enemy (metus hostilis) preserved the good morals of the state.

But when the minds of the people were relieved of that dread (formido), wantonness and arrogance naturally arose, vices which are fostered by prosperity. Thus the peace for which they had longed in time of adversity, after they had gained it proved to be more cruel and bitter than adversity itself.

For the nobles began to abuse their position (dignitas) and the people their liberty (libertas), and every man for himself robbed, pillaged and plundered. Thus the community was split into two parties, and between those the state (res publica) was torn to pieces.” (quoted from Neal Wood, see below)

Sallust sees Rome’s rise and decline as a psychological progression from liberty through glory and ambition to avarice (greed).

You may remember Carthage from the Colosseum scene in the film Gladiator, where Maximus is forced to represent the Carthaginians in Rome’s great victory at the “Battle of Carthage.” It doesn’t go to plan.

Tim Marshall introduced me to Sallust’s Theorem in his fascinating and relevant book Prisoners of Geography. He summarises Sallust’s idea in terms of alliances: “alliances are only strong with the fear of a common enemy.”

In some ways, Sallust’s Theorem is about the danger of getting what we want. We may resent a demanding boss, a fierce local rival, a struggle to build ourselves up from nothing, or a powerful business competitor, yet find that they gave us purpose and brought out the best in us as a group. We can miss them when they’re gone.

—

I believe the term Sallust’s Theorem was introduced by Neal Wood in Wood, N. (1995). Sallust’s Theorem: A Comment on “Fear” in Western Political Thought. History of Political Thought, 16(2), 174–189.

items.title: Two billion credentials publicly exposed, including everything needed for identity theft
items.subtitle: A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials.
items.feedText:
The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted. The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” …

items.body:
**Nach mehr als zwei Jahren Pause belebt Apple seine traditionsreiche (PRODUCT)RED-Reihe offenbar wieder. Wie der Bloomberg -Reporter Mark Gurman (via MacRumors ) berichtet, bereitet der Konzern für Anfang Dezember zwei neue Sondereditionen vor: den erst kürzlich erschienenen HomePod mini 2 sowie die AirPods Max 2.**

Die Ankündigung soll pünktlich zum Welt-AIDS-Tag am 1. Dezember 2026 erfolgen – passend zum 20-jährigen Jubiläum der Organisation (RED).

## Knallrot beim Lautsprecher, überraschend dezent beim Kopfhörer

Optisch geht Apple bei den beiden Audio-Produkten sehr unterschiedliche Wege: Der kompakte Smart-Speaker erhält dem Bericht [nach](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-23/apple-s-new-airpods-max-homepod-mini-2-to-get-product-red-release-for-holidays) ein durchgehend rotes Netzgewebe und ergänzt damit die fünf bisherigen Standardfarben (Weiß, Rosa, Grün, Blau und Mitternacht). Technisch bleibt alles unverändert.

Bei den Over-Ear-Kopfhörern verzichtet Apple demnach auf ein komplett rotes Gehäuse. Stattdessen feiern die Kopfhörer die Rückkehr der Farbe Silber kombiniert mit weißen Ohrpolstern und einem weißen Kopfbügel. Einziger roter Akzent ist die Digital Crown an der Oberseite.

## Erste (PRODUCT)RED-Hardware seit 2023

Aktuell führt Apple keinerlei (PRODUCT)RED-Hardware oder -Zubehör mehr im Sortiment. Die letzten roten Geräte waren das [iPhone 14 (2022)](https://www.apfelpage.de/news/iphone-15-vs-iphone-14-aktuelles-lineup-verkauft-sich-schwaecher-als-vorgaenger/) sowie die [Apple Watch Series 9 (2023)](https://www.apfelpage.de/news/rote-apple-watch-bringt-apple-bald-product-red-uhren/). Ein Teil der Erlöse aus dem Verkauf der Sondereditionen fließt traditionell an den Global Fund zur Bekämpfung von AIDS.

Neben den beiden Audio-Geräten arbeitet Apple laut Gurman zudem an weiterem rotem Zubehör, darunter ein neues Sportarmband für die Apple Watch sowie eine rote Trageschlaufe für AirPods. Offizielle Preise für die Sondereditionen sind noch nicht bekannt, dürften sich aber an den regulären Preisen (169 Euro für den HomePod mini 2 bzw. 579 Euro für die AirPods Max 2) orientieren.

items.body:
*Updated at 6:06 p.m. ET on November 23, 2026*

Americans learned several things over the past few days. The most recent news is that Jensen Huang, after a nanosecond of disgrace for an affair with a woman [allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/us/politics/alice-huang-china-spy-agency-nvidia.html), is back in control of Nvidia, the giant corporation that makes some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. Another is that China’s Communist regime has gotten its hands on the chips. The markets, as usual, have reconfirmed that they prefer profit to politics: Nvidia’s stock price jumped more than 30 percent on the news of Huang’s return.

But most important, Americans learned—yet again—that their president does not care about the national security of the United States. In fact, he is so aggressively resistant to any notion of security that his actions have become almost indistinguishable from those of a hostile foreign agent.

Step back for a moment and consider this sequence of events. The married Nvidia boss was caught in a sexual relationship with a woman named Alice Huang. (She is not related to Jensen, but I will use first names here to avoid confusion.) Alice, during this affair, worked for Megaspeed, a company in Singapore. Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips, and then [found ways](https://www.wsj.com/tech/li-ming-megaspeed-nvidia-chips-china-6260d836) to get them to China, despite U.S. export controls. She also reportedly maintained contacts with the Ministry of State Security, the Chinese intelligence agency, while carrying on with Jensen.

(Some reports call Alice an “agent” or a “spy,” others refer to her as an “asset.” The distinction makes little practical difference in Jensen’s case. Someone who is employed by an intelligence agency, has professional training, and may be acting under a false identity, is an *officer*. *Agents* and *assets* are people recruited from private life, outside of the organization, who have a cooperative relationship, in varying degrees, with such an agency but aren’t actually employed as spooks. Either way, Jensen was literally in bed with someone who was reportedly in bed with Chinese intelligence.)

*[[Josh Tyrangiel: Three theories of Jensen Huang’s resurrection](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/11/jensen-huang-nvidia-reinstated/689546/?utm_source=feed)]*

All of this certainly looks bad. It gets worse. The United States government, including President Trump, was [warned by American intelligence](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/politics/trump-china-trip-nvidia.html) that Alice was entangled with Beijing. In fact, Trump was warned *twice* in seven months, including once during a briefing by Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One in May as Trump was headed to China for a state visit. This must have been awkward, because shortly afterward, Jensen Huang boarded Air Force One and joined the U.S. delegation for the trip to China.

Trump ignored these warnings—or more accurately, in classic Trump style, he pretended not to know about these issues. “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people,” he [said,](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/us/politics/trump-jensen-huang-spy.html) just before his most recent visit to China. “They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”

Clearly not. Nor did these warnings move Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, whose former company, [Cantor Fitzgerald, has significant ties to Nvidia](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/howard-lutnick-nvidia-jensen-huang-china-cantor-fitzgerald.html), including financing some of the firms that were buying its chips.

The company is now run by Lutnick’s son.

Trump’s reaction to all this? When Jensen was discovered and had to leave his company, Trump got right to work [trying to put him back](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/20/trump-defends-jensen-huang-after-alleged-chinese-spy-affair/) in the big chair at Nvidia. “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.” [Nvidia wasn’t having it](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/16/trump-says-he-would-not-mind-jensen-huangs-return-nvidia/): Internal sources at the company made clear to reporters that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated.

So what changed in a matter of days? Nothing, except that the president apparently brought the American intelligence community into the fray to give Jensen a clean bill of health. At least that’s how it sounds from the Nvidia board’s public statement: “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

The national-security process is slow and deliberative for a reason; people with even modest clearances who have been accused of minor infractions have had to wait months, sometimes even going to court, before being allowed back to work. An executive working with some of America’s most exotic technology commits adultery with a foreign citizen who has ties to a hostile government, and is credibly accused of funneling highly restricted American technology to a hostile intelligence service—and the U.S. security mandarins give the guy a thumbs-up after a *week*?

Trump likes Jensen, he likes money, he likes the markets, and he likes Lutnick and his family. So perhaps he told the American spooks to sound the all-clear so that Jensen could get back to work. Trump indicated as much today when he told CNBC that he spoke with Nvidia’s board members. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them.”

In a [statement](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117666141823845971) on Truth Social, Trump said: “The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” That means exactly nothing. Saying that Todd Blanche does not “possess evidence” is an artful formulation meaning that Blanche does not have a file in front of him from the intelligence community detailing Jensen’s acts, some of which might have been dangerous even if they were not “unlawful.” (As any government employee can tell you, any number of “lawful” activities, including carrying lots of debt or having emotional problems, can sink a clearance and a job.) And because of Trump’s pressure to clear Jensen, it’s unlikely he ever will.

items.body: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. This agreement indicates that a strong developmental bias, reflecting the relative ease with which gene regulatory networks generate simple over complex leaves, has played a major role in shaping the evolution of leaf morphology. Our findings echo recent work showing that similar biases towards simplicity influence the evolution of molecular structures, including RNA secondary structures and protein quaternary assemblies. Together, these results suggest that a developmental bias favouring simplicity may be a widespread and general feature of evolutionary systems.

items.title: Uncorrelated perspectives
items.subtitle: After I sold my company, I had to learn about long-term investing.

items.body:
After I sold my company, I had to learn about long-term investing.
The best books all emphasized the importance of owning a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated assets that rise and fall independently.
If one crashes, the rest don’t.

Don’t put everything into stocks or real estate or commodities or any one market.
Don’t put it all into America or Europe or Asia or any one place.
Don’t over-invest in what’s popular or familiar.
Invest equally into the entire world economy.

I apply this metaphor to worldviews.

You start with the perspective of your parents and culture.

But you are over-invested in one or two worldviews.

You have to deliberately diversify - to intentionally invest in other perspectives.

When your government or media says some country is the enemy, it’s a good sign that place has an uncorrelated perspective.
The governments have conflicting interests, but the people there are not bad people.

When another culture feels completely foreign, weird, and wrong, it means you are under-invested in that worldview.

Even in your own country, right versus left or whatever.

When the “other side” seems crazy, you need to balance your portfolio.

Invest some understanding until you hold some of those perspectives.

If people can predict your opinion on something, based on your opinion on something else, then your worldview is too correlated.

To be an independent thinker, own a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated perspectives.

items.subtitle: Viele nutzen einen VPN, um sich gegen IP-Tracking zu schützen.

items.body:
Viele nutzen einen VPN, um sich gegen IP-Tracking zu schützen. Aber gerade Youtube, wo sehr umfangreichen Verhaltensdaten entstehen, funktioniert über VPNs oft nicht – vor allem, wenn man Videos über Drittanbieter-Apps, Downloadtools oder mit Werbeblocker schauen will. In diesem Artikel stelle ich einen einfachen und kostenlosen Trick vor, mit dem man statt VPN eine neue IP über das Smartphone bezieht. Über die recht neue App »[5G Proxy Pro](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.tokyoxpa3.androidproxy/)« kann man diese IP auch in einem einzelnen Browser oder per Kommandozeile am Desktopcomputer nutzen. Am Ende des Artikel liste ich dann noch Ideen auf, um dauerhaft einen 5G-Proxy für Youtube im Einsatz zu haben. Der Trick hilft natürlich auch bei anderen Schutzmaßnahmen, die einen VPN benötigten.

**Nicht für Einsteiger**: Dieser Artikel ist für Fortgeschrittene. Die Tipps sind Bastellösungen, die für manche Personen möglicherweise nützlich sind, um eine Alternative für einen IP-Wechsel zu kennen. Damit ist nicht immer automatisch mehr Datenschutz erreicht. Probleme wie DNS-Leaks oder unbemerkte IDs von Apps müssen beachtet werden.

Gut zu wissen

### Das Problem mit manchen alternative Frontends

Nicht alle alternativen Youtube-Frontends und Apps schützen vor IP-Tracking. Vor allem die bekannten Android-Apps NewPipe, PipePipe und LibreTube fragen die Daten direkt bei Youtube ab. Das kann man teilweise in den Einstellungen ändern, zum Beispiel bei LibreTube. Andere Projekte nutzen „Piped“-Instanzen, so dass die IP geschützt ist. Aber wenn Piped-Adressen über das Terminal genutzt werden, können sie ebenfalls direkte Youtube-Verbindungen herstellen. Das Setup also besser einmal mit PCAPdroid oder einem Netzwerk-Sniffer oder über die DNS-Abfragen prüfen.

## 1. Warum man sich gegen IP-Tracking schützen sollte

Viele Websites geben deine IP-Adresse an Werbefirmen weiter, die dann Verhaltensdaten für einen Haushalt ganz ohne Cookies speichern können. Ausführlich habe ich das 2024 in diesem Artikel beschrieben: [IP-Haushaltstracking bei Google und Drittanbietern](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/ip-haushaltstracking-bei-google-und-drittanbietern-was-es-ist-und-wie-man-sich-schuetzt/). Wenn du Glück hast, wird das IP-Tracking über eingebundene Drittanbieter ausgeführt, die man mit einem klassischen Werbeblocker deaktivieren kann. So ist das beispielsweise bei Spiegel Online mit Einwilligung. Bei großen Plattformen wie Youtube passiert das aber serverseitig und man kann es nicht blocken. Die Technik wurde bis 2024 von Google auch ohne Einwilligung eingesetzt. Daher ist grundsätzlich Misstrauen angebracht, ob Google sich beim Haushaltstracking an die DSGVO hält.

Gut zu wissen

### Grundidee: Google/Youtube und andere IP-Tracker nur über eine zweite IP nutzen

Im Idealfall eines perfekt geschützten Haushalts könnte man das IP-Tracking durch Google, Shops oder Nachrichtenseiten einfach ignorieren: Man bekäme über Nacht eine neue IP-Adresse, eventuell erzwungen mit einer Zeitschaltuhr am Router beziehungsweise dem Flugmodus über Nacht am Smartphone. Wenn man alles perfekt konfiguriert hat, kann Google die Aufrufe aus dem Haushalt nur für jeden Tag zusammenknüpfen, nicht aber für einen längeren Zeitraum. Voraussetzung dafür wäre:

- Kein Browser im Haushalt speichert Cookies von Google
- Keine Apps im Haushalt senden eindeutige Installations-IDs an Google Firebase
- Keine smarten Geräte wie Fernseher senden IDs an Google
- Im ganzen Haushalt werden keine Websites, Apps oder Geräte mit Drittanbieter-Logins betrieben, die Anmeldeinformationen an Identitätsprovider weitergeben, beispielsweise über Zalando oder einen Cloudanbieter.

Da dieses Szenario aber im Alltag und mit mehreren Haushaltsmitgliedern sehr schwer oder gar nicht zu erreichen ist, besteht die Grundidee von VPN oder Proxy als Trackingschutz darin, gezielt problematische Seiten – also vor allem werbefinanzierte Seiten mit spezifischen Interessensdaten wie Youtube, aber auch Nachrichtenseiten, bei denen man eine Einwilligung geben muss – über eine zweite IP zu leiten. So minimiert man zusätzlich zum Werbeblocker das Risiko, dass sehr viele problematische Verhaltens- und Interessensdaten langfristig in einem Haushaltsprofil gesammelt werden. Das IP-Tracking wird also nicht verhindert, sondern abgetrennt.

## 2. Spontane Variante: Flugmodus-Trick mit googlefreiem Smartphone

Wer GrapheneOS oder ein ähnliches googlefreies Android installiert hat, hat gegenüber Stock-Androids den Vorteil, dass weder ein Google-Login noch eine Werbe-ID mit dem Smartphone verknüpft ist. Wenn man nun Wifi deaktiviert und dann einmal den Flugmodus an- und wieder ausschaltet, bekommt das Smartphone vom Mobilfunkprovider üblicherweise eine neue IP-Adresse. Das muss nicht sein, daher sollte man es zunächst testen: Einfach vor und nach der Neuverbindung eine der vielen IP-Serviceseiten aufrufen – leicht zu merken ist [ip.me](https://ip.me/) von Proton, werbefrei dafür [stat.ripe.net](https://stat.ripe.net) von der europäischen Internetregistry). Wenn ein solcher IP-Wechsel stattfindet, hat Google ein wichtiges Merkmal weniger, um die Youtube-Nutzung mit den vorherigen Aufrufen auf dem Smartphone zusammenzuführen. Vor allem wenn man trackingfreie Drittanbieter-Apps wie Newpipe oder einen Privatsphäre-Browser auf dem Smartphone nutzt, ist man so gegenüber den wichtigsten branchenüblichen Trackingmethoden geschützt.

Wenn man für diesen Trick ein eigenes **Profil** anlegt, hat man zwar einen etwas besseren Schutz, weil andere Apps oder Websites nicht versehentlich gestartet werden können.

Aber was viele nicht wissen: Apps, die im Eigentümer-Profil im Hintergrund laufen dürfen oder die anderweitig vom System aktiviert werden können (beispielsweise Signals Verbindungen zu Amazon AWS), **laufen auch bei einem Profilwechsel im Hintergrund weiter**. Also auch wenn beispielsweise Signal nicht im Zweitprofil installiert ist, laufen die Verbindungen aus dem Eigentümerprofil weiter. Andersherum ist das nicht der Fall: Die Apps aus Nebenprofilen laufen nicht weiter, wenn man zum Eigentümerprofil zurückwechselt. Daher nutze ich für mein Setup RethinkDNS, um vor dem Wechsel alle Apps im Eigentümerprofil abzuschalten, bevor man wechselt.

Das will man verhindern: Diese Netzwerkverbindungen öffnet mein Android, obwohl ich ins Zweitprofil gewechselt bin, in dem diese Apps nicht installiert sind. Sichtbar wird das nur mit einem externen Sniffer, den ich auf meinem Router laufen lasse. Die Datenverbindungen zu Signal sind im Eigentümerprofil weiter aktiv. Außerdem stelle ich fest, dass die Gopro-App aus dem Eigentümerprofil aktiv ist, obwohl sie dort keine Hintergrundrechte hat. Google Firebase erhält hier vermutlich eindeutige Installations-IDs. Eben weil es so viele Möglichkeiten gibt, wie Google eine dauerhafte ID aus dem Haushalt erhält, empfehle ich das umständliche Vorgehen mit einer extra IP, einem Zweitprofil und RethinkDNS im Eigentümerprofil.

items.body:
Art history does not divide itself easily into decades, let alone into centuries or even eras, and that makes the 2020s so far a pretty unusual period of time. Not long into 2020, the world was shut down by the Covid pandemic. What followed from there was more chaos: wars in Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan, and elsewhere; two Trump administrations; culture wars around the world; and economic upheaval that has touched all corners of the world, including the art world.

And yet, not all has been bad. During [Art Week NYC](https://art-week.com/), a festival held earlier this month by *ARTnews*, *Art in America*, and *Artforum*, *ARTnews* convened art historian and curator Joseph L. Underwood along with *Art in America* deputy editor Emily Watlington to discuss the decade so far. Both agreed that some good has resulted, particularly when it comes to the art historical canon. But it remains unclear whether those changes will leave a permanent mark on the art world.

“We’ve recovered a lot of individual figures that have totally deserved [a spotlight], and I’m looking forward to how we can now use that research and rediscovery to tell different stories about art history,” Watlington said.

Underwood noted that this impulse was already underway pre-2020 and pointed to scholarship by historians such as Chika Okeke-Agulu, who published an influential book on Nigerian modernism in 2015. “There have been articles and books about single artists, but there hasn’t been that kind of interconnectivity,” he said. “That’s what was starting, and there is still some of it in art history. But museums and the market have cooled on it.”

That trend, he added, is evident when looking at the past few Venice Biennale editions. The 2022 edition, curated by Cecilia Alemani, contained many female Surrealists; the 2024 edition, organized by Adriano Pedrosa, presented a global view of modernism. “That cooled off in 2026,” he said, referring to Koyo Kouoh’s recently concluded exhibition, which had fewer dead and under-recognized artists.

“It’s certainly been a decade of two steps forward, one step back,” Watlington said. “Change the number of steps!”

items.body:
## Five Newly Born Cheetah Cubs Are Growing Up on Camera at the Smithsonian

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/smithsonian-cheetah-litter-of-five-healthy-cubs/)

Cheetah cubs inside the den of Zura, a 5-year-old cheetah. Her five cubs were born Oct. 5, 2026, at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute (SCBI) in Front Royal, VA. The cubs do not have names yet. Their gender is currently unknown. They are currently on the Cheetah Cub Cam hosted on the Zoo’s website.

Born October 5, 2026, at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute in Front Royal, Va., five cubs are growing up under the watchful eye of their mother, Zura. Although visitors can’t meet the newest arrivals in person just yet, they can watch the family bond, play, and nap together through the zoo’s live [Cheetah Cub Cam](https://nationalzoo.si.edu/webcams/cheetah-cub-cam).

Zura is a first-time mother at 5 years old, and her cubs are reported to be healthy, strong, and active. For now, animal care staff are keeping their distance to give the family time to bond, while monitoring their progress through the livestream. The first few weeks are especially important for young cheetahs as they develop a close relationship with their mother, who provides their food, warmth, and protection.

The new litter is also important for the Smithsonian’s conservation program. Zura’s five cubs represent the 21st litter born at the facility since 2007. This litter marks the fourth generation of the same cheetah family now living at the conservation institute. Zura was born there in 2021, her mother Rosalie arrived in 2015, and her grandmother Sanurra also lives at the facility.

Cheetahs are classified as vulnerable, with fewer than 7,000 estimated to remain in the wild due to habitat loss, declining prey populations, climate change, poaching, and conflict with humans. Breeding cheetahs in human care is not an easy task, either. Females have relatively short and unpredictable periods of fertility, and successful pairings can be difficult to achieve. Cheetahs also have limited genetic diversity because their ancestors experienced a severe population decline thousands of years ago.

The Smithsonian currently cares for approximately 30 cheetahs at its Front Royal conservation campus, where researchers and animal care specialists work to improve the species’ long-term prospects. They expect the cubs to remain visible on the livestream for approximately six to seven months, although they may occasionally disappear from view as Zura moves them around their habitat.

Eventually, the young cats will outgrow their shared den and move on to the next stage of their lives. They are expected to remain at the conservation institute for another year or two before potentially moving to partner facilities to support future breeding efforts.

## A cheetah named Zura gave birth to five healthy cubs on October 5 at the Smithsonian Institute in Virginia.

## This litter is the fourth generation of cheetahs born at the institute and is very important for conservation efforts, as cheetahs are deemed a vulnerable species.

items.body:
** The latest on Trump’s approval rating**

**Updated November 23, 2026**

After rebounding slightly to 38 percent, Donald Trump’s approval rating is back on the downswing. **Today, 37 percent of Americans approve of the job he’s doing, while 60 percent disapprove**.

Show more Show less

Just 18.9 percent of Americans *strongly* approve of Trump, dangerously close to the 18.3 percent who *weakly* approve. If the president continues to get less popular, those figures could flip in the not too distant future. **-EMD** **, 11/17/26**

**See also: [Iran War support dashboard](https://www.natesilver.net/p/iran-war-polls-popularity-approval).**

This is the landing page for Silver Bulletin presidential approval ratings. We’ll regularly update the charts below as new polls about Donald Trump’s approval rating come in.1 This page is designed to be [viewed on the web](https://tinyurl.com/3fzxm9wc) rather than in our email client or in the Substack app.

[Click here for more information on how the average works](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology). The Silver Bulletin average weights more reliable polls heavily — you can **[find our latest pollster ratings here](https://www.natesilver.net/p/pollster-ratings-silver-bulletin)**.

### The topline: So, just how popular is Trump?

Our default average reflects a combination of all polls, whether conducted among adults, registered voters or likely voters. If a pollster releases multiple versions of the same survey, we use the all-adult version of the poll before the registered voter version.2 This is because all Americans have a say in how popular the president is — whether or not they vote.

### The polls: What do the surveys say?

Each poll gets an “influence” score based on its pollster rating, its sample size, its recency, and how often a pollster is publishing numbers.3 Sometimes, surveys with mediocre pollster ratings have more weight in the model just because they were conducted very recently or polled more people.

items.feedText: Autistic people often meet criteria for anxiety, depression, and other psychiatric conditions; co-occurring psychiatric conditions are more prevalent in the autism population than in the general population.1 Psychotherapy is a first-line treatment for many psychiatric conditions, such as anxiety and depression, but appears to serve autistic adults less well than it does others: an analysis of the UK National Health Service Talking Therapies found a reduction of depression and anxiety symptoms among 8593 autistic adults, but lower odds of reliable improvement and recovery, and higher odds of deterioration, than in matched non-autistic peers.

Saturday Night Live [ran a skit](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-X9dxL17t1k) for an eldercare service that was simply calling your sister to take care of things. Many people related, because it is actually happening. [For Bloomberg, Lisa Jarvis has the numbers](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2026-11-18/snl-sister-skit-about-the-us-eldercare-crisis-is-too-relatable?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NTEyMTQ3MiwiZXhwIjoxNzk1NzI2MjcyLCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1A1Q0NLR1pBSk8wMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiIzRDhGMEEzMTc2MDc0NUM5OTg4NkFCNzA1NDk2RUNEQSJ9.8Rm4_qRQDNrQl5SG6qxNGsTkbi7DGmEbfQ1N588AByU):

> And the pressure is only mounting as America gets older and sicker. Time devoted to caregiving more than doubled between 2020 and 2025, rising from 9 to 23 hours a week, according to a recent survey of working Americans conducted by the insurance provider Guardian Life. The majority (57%) are caring for elderly relatives. The same survey found women were five times as likely as men to say they’d left the workforce to care for someone, whether that was an elderly parent, a spouse, a young child or a special needs child.

items.body:
# Facharzttermin gegen Aufpreis: Was Deutschland von Griechenland lernen kann

KBV-Chef Gassen fordert Extra-Bezahlung für schnellere Termine. In Griechenland wäre das strafbar – und das System dort ist trotz weniger Geld oft effizienter.

Schnellere Facharzttermine für gesetzlich Versicherte soll es, geht es nach KBV-Chef Dr. Andreas Gassen gegen Extra-Bezahlung geben. Der Ärztefunktionär meint, dass die Mediziner so auf die Honorarkürzungen der Gesundheitsreform reagieren müssen. Die Meldung wurde in Griechenland mit besonders großem Interesse gelesen.

Ein Vergleich Deutschlands mit Griechenland und den übrigen EU-Staaten zeigt zudem, dass das Problem der deutschen Gesundheitspolitik nicht unbedingt mit noch mehr Geld und weiteren Leistungskürzungen gelöst werden kann. Eher erscheint es, als wäre "Effektivität" das gesuchte Zauberwort.

### 2010 hätte so eine Nachricht blankes Entsetzten ausgelöst

Bevor im Mai 2010 Griechenland mit dem Gang zum Internationalen Währungsfonds (IWF) faktisch den Staatsbankrott erklären musste, wurde das staatswirtschaftlich taumelnde Land von der deutschen Presse besonders gründlich durchleuchtet. Man entdeckte das " Fakelaki ", das Fachwort für einen kleinen, mit Geldscheinen gefüllten Umschlag.

Damit kam man im Griechenland vor der Krise unter anderen schneller an einen Termin im Krankenhaus, auf dem Bauamt oder man konnte bei entsprechender Bargeldfüllung leichter eine Führerscheinprüfung bestehen. Dass so ein Usus für jede Volkswirtschaft Gift ist, darüber waren sich alle – auch die Griechen – einig.

Umso mehr wundern sie sich nun, dass es in Deutschland Facharzttermine nur gegen " Grigorosimo " geben soll. Über den griechischen Sprachdienst der Deutschen Welle kam diese Nachricht an die griechischen Medien, welche begeistert das Wording der Überschrift übernahmen.
