items.body:
Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin

Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images

Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected.

“It definitely looks promising,” says [Gayle Ross](https://www.thermh.org.au/our-people/gayle-ross) at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

[Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2491017-chronic-inflammation-messes-with-your-mind-heres-how-to-calm-it/)

Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13.

In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is [effective](https://www.dupixenthcp.com/atopicdermatitis/efficacy-safety/adult-real-world-results), it has had [limited uptake](https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S256209592300065X) in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage.

Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema.

Free newsletter

#### Sign up to Health Check

[Sign up to newsletter](https://www.newscientist.com/sign-up/health/)

In the [clinical trial](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07217015), 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks.

Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average [72 per cent reduction](https://investors.kymeratx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kymera-therapeutics-announces-positive-results-broaden2-phase-2b) in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial.

“These results exceeded our expectations,” said [Terence Rooney](https://www.kymeratx.com/about-us/leadership/terence-rooney-md/), the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a [webcast](https://investors.kymeratx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kymera-therapeutics-announces-positive-results-broaden2-phase-2b) on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end.

“It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross.

[Read more You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2507511-you-can-upgrade-your-immune-system-but-not-in-the-way-you-think/)

The medication also appeared safe. A small proportion of participants developed conjunctivitis as a side-effect, but it tended to be mild and didn’t cause anyone to discontinue treatment, said Rooney. In fact, since the trial, almost every participant has chosen to continue taking the daily pill as part of an ongoing study, he said.

People taking dupilumab can develop conjunctivitis too, so “we’re pretty used to dealing with that”, says Ross.

Kymera Therapeutics is now planning a larger trial of KT-621 for treating eczema that is scheduled to begin in mid-2027. The company is also currently running a [trial of KT-621 in people with asthma](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07323654), since the condition is caused by the same overactive immune pathway operating in the lungs. It hasn’t yet said how much the drug will cost if it eventually receives regulatory approval.

Wir haben uns die beiden Gitarren näher angesehen, ihre Möglichkeiten erkundet und herausgefunden, worin sie sich unterscheiden.**

## PRS Guitars Tekton Series – Das Wichtigste in Kürze

- Was ist die PRS Guitars Tekton Series? Die Gitarren aus der Tekton-Serie sind für den modernen Player konzipiert: schlanker Hals mit D-Shape, etwas flacheres Griffbrett und zwei Humbucker mit transparentem Ton auch bei High-Gain-Sounds.
- Welche Hölzer werden bei der PRS Guitars Tekton T für den Korpus verwendet? Die Tekton T hat einen Mahagoni-Korpus mit einer Mango-Decke und kommt wie alle Gitarren aus der Tekton-Serie mit einem Offset-Double-Cutaway-Korpus, der etwas dünner ist als bei den Standard PRS Modellen.
- Welche Hölzer wurden bei der PRS Guitars Tekton Floyd für den Korpus verwendet? Der Korpus der Tekton Floyd besteht aus Erle.
- Aus welchen Hölzern sind die Hälse der PRS Guitars Tekton Series-Gitarren gefertigt? Alle Instrumente aus der Tekton-Serie sind mit einem Ahornhals (Modern D-Shape) und einem Ebenholzgriffbrett bestückt.
- Welche Pickups sind bei den PRS Guitars Tekton Series Gitarren eingebaut? Die Gitarren sind mit den neu designten Stylus-Humbuckern ausgestattet – ein Stylus T am Steg und ein Stylus B an der Halsposition.
- Gibt es zusätzliche elektronische Optionen? Ja, die Tonabnehmer können per Push/Pull-Funktion des Tonreglers gesplittet werden.
- Welche Hardware ist bei der PRS Guitars Tekton T im Einsatz? Bei der Tekton T wird ein neu entwickeltes Tremolosystem verwendet, das mit Zweipunktbefestigung und Messingsätteln ausgestattet ist.
- Welches Tremolosystem hat die PRS Guitars Tekton Floyd? Bei der Tekton Floyd wird ein Original Floyd Rose 1000 Series Tremolo-System benutzt, mit Klemmsattel und Feinstimmern.
- Wird die Gitarre mit Koffer oder Gigbag ausgeliefert? Die Gitarren der Tekton Series werden alle mit einem Premium-Gigbag ausgeliefert.
- Das sagt der Test: Die PRS Tekton-Modelle verbinden moderne Bespielbarkeit mit klanglicher Vielseitigkeit. Sie überzeugen durch erstklassige Verarbeitung, perfekte Werkseinstellung und transparente Stylus-Pickups, die ihre Stärken besonders bei High-Gain-Sounds ausspielen.

## Was sind die besonderen Eigenschaften der PRS Guitars Tekton Series?

Diverse Kundenwünsche nach einem Gitarrenmodell mit modernen Spezifikationen bildeten den Ausgangspunkt für das Team von PRS Guitars, das auf dieser Basis die Tekton-Serie umsetzte.

Aktuell gibt es vier unterschiedliche Modelle: Tekton (Fixed Bridge), Tekton T (Tremolo), Tekton Floyd (Floyd-Rose-Tremolo), Tekton SVN (Seven String mit 26,5″ Mensur). Alle Gitarren kommen mit einem Doublecut-Korpus, bei dem die Cutaway-Hörner etwas länger sind als beim Standard-PRS-Shaping. Außerdem ist der Korpus minimal dünner, was sich im geringeren Gewicht positiv bemerkbar macht. Der Hals-Korpus-Übergang ist ergonomisch geformt, sodass die hohen Lagen sehr gut erreichbar sind. Stichwort Hals: Der schlanke D-Shape-Hals aus Ahorn ist mit einem Ebenholz-Griffbrett mit 16″-Radius und 24 Edelstahl-Jumbo-Bünden bestückt. Für die Tekton-Modelle wurden auch die neuen Stylus-Pickups entwickelt, deren Fokus auf High-Gain-Sounds liegt, mit klarem Ton und sauberer Saitentrennung.

## In welcher Qualität sind die verwendeten Bauteile?

Die PRS Guitars Tekton T und Tekton Floyd sind hervorragend verarbeitet – genau so, wie man es von PRS-USA-Modellen gewohnt ist. Stimmmechaniken und beide Tremolosysteme arbeiten einwandfrei, lediglich den einen oder anderen könnten die mitschwingenden Federn bei harten High-Gain-Einsätzen etwas stören.

Die Pickups übertragen erstklassig, allerdings auch kleine Nebengeräusche. Die fallen bei mittleren Zerrgraden zwar nicht wirklich auf, aber wenn der Gain-Regler weit oben steht, treten sie ans Tageslicht. Aber dafür gibt es ja einfache Abhilfe in Form von Gummiringen (String Dampener).

## Wie ist die Einstellung der PRS Guitars Tekton Series ab Werk?

An der Einstellung von Hals und Saitenlage gibt es nichts zu kritisieren. Die Halsneigung sowie das Abrichten und Polieren der Bünde sind akkurat erledigt. Beide Gitarren kommen mit moderater, nicht allzu flacher Saitenlage, die schnarrfreies Spielen erlaubt.

## Entspricht das Angebot dem Preis?

Beide Gitarren liegen preislich in der Oberklasse um 3000 Euro und die Lieferung entspricht den Erwartungen: Hervorragende Verarbeitung, Holz-Abstimmung und dadurch resultierendes Schwingungsverhalten, erstklassige Bespielbarkeit und die Sounds, die von den Stylus-Pickups übertragen werden, rechtfertigen den Preis.

Unter den zahlreichen Black-Friday-Angeboten für Autofahrer fällt vor allem die deutliche Preisreduzierung des TomTom-Verkehrsassistenten Tom auf. Statt der unverbindlichen Preisempfehlung von 79,99 Euro verlangt Amazon für den [TomTom-Fahrbegleiter aktuell nur 38 Euro](https://www.ifun.de/amzn/B0FMXSTSMR). Das entspricht einem Preisnachlass von 52 Prozent.

#### Die Tomtom-App steht kostenlos bereit

Den kleinen Verkehrswarner haben wir seit seiner Einführung redaktionell begleitet. Tom arbeitet ohne eigenes Display, verbindet sich mit der TomTom-App und informiert auch ohne aktive Navigation über Gefahrenstellen und Verkehrsbehinderungen.

Seit dem Marktstart hat der Hersteller [mehrere Software-Aktualisierungen](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/tom-tomtom-erweitert-seinen-bildschirmfreien-fahrbegleiter-278428/) veröffentlicht, die unter anderem die Zuverlässigkeit der Verbindung und die Ausgabe der Warnhinweise verbessern. Ein Abonnement ist nicht erforderlich.

Produkthinweis

[TomTom Verkehrsalarm Blitzerwarner für Auto| ohne ABO | CarPlay | Tom by TomTom - Made in Europe](https://www.amazon.de/dp/B0FMXSTSMR?tag=musicweb02&linkCode=ogi&th=1&psc=1)
38,00 EUR
79,99 EUR

Ebenfalls deutlich reduziert sind die beiden Verkehrswarner des dänischen Anbieters Needit. Der [Drive One Pro kostet aktuell 49 Euro](https://www.ifun.de/amzn/B0H7K3WG8J) statt regulär knapp 90 Euro. Das Gerät verfügt über ein eigenes Farbdisplay, unterstützt Apple CarPlay und greift auf die Daten von Blitzer.de zurück. Auf die Ausstattung sind wir [hier ausführlicher eingegangen](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/neuer-drive-one-pro-kein-abo-aber-display-carplay-und-blitzer-de-288912/).

Produkthinweis

[Needit Drive One Pro Verkehrsassistent I Bis zu 160 Stunden Akkulaufzeit | Offizieller Partner von Blitzer.de I Für...](https://www.amazon.de/dp/B0H7K3WG8J?tag=musicweb02&linkCode=ogi&th=1&psc=1)
49,99 EUR
89,95 EUR

Der erst Anfang November [vorgestellte Drive One 3](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/needit-drive-one-3-neuer-ooono-konkurrent-mit-blitzer-de-290165/) kommt ohne eigenes Display aus, bietet aber ebenfalls eine CarPlay-Anbindung und einen wiederaufladbaren Akku mit bis zu drei Monaten Laufzeit. Statt knapp 80 Euro kostet das Gerät [derzeit nur 39 Euro](https://www.ifun.de/amzn/B0HNKL4W38). Beide Needit-Modelle verzichten auf laufende Gebühren.

39,99 EUR
49,95 EUR

## Dashcams und drahtlose CarPlay-Adapter

Auch der Dashcam-Anbieter 70mai hat seine Preise zur Black-Friday-Woche gesenkt. Die einfache aber beliebte [70mai A800 ist für 49 statt 79 Euro](https://www.ifun.de/amzn/B0HF87RXJX) erhältlich.

[70mai Dashcam Auto Vorne A800 Nano, 4K Dashcam mit Smart HDR, APP & WiFi 6 | F1,55, Super-Nachtsicht...](https://www.amazon.de/dp/B0HF87RXJX?tag=musicweb02&linkCode=ogi&th=1&psc=1)
49,99 EUR
79,99 EUR

Interessanter für Anwender, die das Verkehrsgeschehen vor und hinter dem Fahrzeug in hoher Auflösung dokumentieren möchten, ist die [70mai A900 für 139 statt 199 Euro](https://www.ifun.de/amzn/B0HDTFLKND). Das [Ende September vorgestellte Modell](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/a900-neue-4k-dual-dashcam-mit-wi-fi-6-gps-app-und-4g-286984/) zeichnet mit beiden Kameras in 4K auf und bietet GPS, Wi-Fi 6, App-Anbindung und gepufferte Notfallaufnahmen.

items.title: When A Farewell to Arms Was Censored For Foul Language
items.subtitle: The young novelist Ernest Hemingway was angry and frustrated.

items.body:
The young novelist Ernest Hemingway was angry and frustrated. *Scribner’s Magazine* had decided to cut “shit,” “fuck,” “balls,” “cocksucker,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” and “Jesus Christ” from his new book, [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839), when it began serializing it in May 1929. The semi-autobiographical novel followed the experiences of an American ambulance driver on the Italian Front in World War I. For publication as a book, Maxwell Perkins, Hemingway’s editor at Charles Scribner’s Sons, managed to get the last three phrases restored, in sentences such as “I shot the son of a bitch with my rifle,” “they were loading the girls from the soldiers’ whorehouse into a truck,” and “Jesus Christ what I could do with two hundred and fifty dollars.” Hemingway and Perkins negotiated, the editor conceding “scrotum” instead of “balls,” but refusing “c—s r” as an alternative to “cocksucker” (which became, instead, “‘I killed that – of a sergeant’ ”). The author had to turn his other “four-letter words” into phrases like “Go something yourself.” Hemingway protested that “emasculation was a minor operation to perform on men, animals, and books, but its effect was great.” He was waging a fight for “full use of the language.” But he gave in.

Hemingway had won part of his fight. But predictably, “scrotum,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” “Jesus Christ” (as an exclamation), and the premarital love affair at the novel’s core were themselves too much for the Word Police, at least in some jurisdictions. In Boston—a city already known for its gusto in banning any work of literature or art deemed indecent by officials—Police Superintendent Michael Crowley announced that the June issue of *Scribner’s* was being barred from sale because of its “salacious” material, even before the book version restored some of the offensive words. Scribner’s jumped to Hemingway’s defense, issuing a press release defending him as “one of the finest and most highly regarded of the modern writers,” and promised that it would continue serializing [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)in coming issues. But Scribner’s also felt called upon to underscore the novel’s “distinctly moral” nature. “It is the story of a fine and faithful love, born, it is true, out of physical desire,” the release continued. “If white is to be contrasted with black, thereby emphasizing its whiteness, the picture cannot be all white.”

Spare, truthful words—honest names and honest profanities—had dignity and humanity. It was grand phrases that were obscene in their evasion of hard truths.[/pullquotes]

This defense sidestepped the fact that Hemingway himself, an admirer of Mark Twain, would have rejected any notion of a simplistic “black” and “white” moral in his novel as a shabby evasion serving outmoded and dishonest values. But the press release went forth, and Scribner’s investment paid off. [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)sold 31,000 copies in its first print run and helped make its author financially independent. As book industry executives expected, being “banned in Boston” probably boosted sales—even among Bostonians, who could cross the city line to buy copies elsewhere. One of the passages in *[A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)* rang as a clarion call for turning ideas about what was “obscene” on their heads. In it, an Italian soldier, reflecting on the staggering death toll of a recent offensive, remarks that the sacrifice cannot have been “in vain.” In response, Hemingway’s protagonist, the American Frederic Henry, muses on the power and deceit of words:

I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious, and sacrifice and the expression in vain…I had seen nothing sacred, and the things that were glorious had no glory and the sacrifices were like the stockyards of Chicago if nothing was done with the meat except to bury it…Abstract words such as glory, honor, courage, or hallow were obscene beside the concrete names of villages, the numbers of roads, the names of rivers, the numbers of regiments and the dates.

Spare, truthful words—honest names and honest profanities—had dignity and humanity. It was grand phrases that were obscene in their evasion of hard truths. One form of language lied. The other, if used to register authentic emotional experience, didn’t. “Fuck,” “shit,” and “cocksucker” expressed real feelings in real speech. “Glory,” “honor,” and “courage” deluded.

Yet the miniature Culture War that [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)unleashed was also fought out behind closed doors in the Manhattan offices of Charles Scribner’s Sons. After all, Scribner’s and other prestige presses were themselves Word Police, upholding nineteenth-century aesthetic and moral ideals that company elders brought to their self-appointed roles as gatekeepers of American taste and cultivation, all while selling books and magazines to make money. Perkins had already run this gauntlet more than once. His elders at the house had objected loudly in 1922 when another of his young stars, F. Scott Fitzgerald, wanted to title a short story collection [Tales of the Jazz Age](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780307476371). The word “jazz” was the problem: they felt, Perkins explained, “that the word whatever implication it actually has, will itself injure the book.” But the title stayed, and, as Fitzgerald correctly predicted, “it will be bought by *my own personal public*, that is, by the countless flappers and college kids who think I am a sort of oracle.” Many of those flappers and collegians knew that jazz’s “implications” included semen, orgasm, and sex.

Hemingway’s first novel, [The Sun Also Rises](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780743297332), had almost been rejected by Scribner’s in 1926, despite Perkins’s advocacy. That novel’s spare account of emotionally rootless young Americans in post-World War I Europe bewildered the house’s older editors, and Hemingway and Perkins fought hard to retain the word “bitch” to describe the heroine, Lady Brett Ashley. As another writer observed, old “Charles Scribner would no sooner allow profanity in one of his books than he would invite friends to use his parlor as a toilet room.” The company had agreed to publication with great reluctance, resigning itself to the inevitable Boston banning. But *The Sun Also Rises* sold quickly; by the time of Hemingway’s death in 1961, an estimated million copies had circulated. Writing of the 1920s, the critic Edmund Wilson mused on the novel’s impact: “The great watchword was ‘Have a drink’; and in the bars of New York and Paris the young people were getting to talk like Hemingway.” As John Updike reflected decades later, “an entire generation of American men learned to speak in the accents of [his] stoicism.”

items.body:
# Parlamentswahlen in Spanien: Wählen mit dem Taschenrechner

## Parlamentswahlen in Spanien : Wählen mit dem Taschenrechner

Spaniens sozialistischer Premier Pedro Sánchez setzt seine letzte Hoffnung in die kleineren linken Parteien. Auch taktisches Wählen kann ausschlaggebend sein.

24.11.2026

7:12 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Will die Hoffnung nicht aufgeben: Pedro Sánchez (links) nach einer TV-Debatte mit seinem konvervativen Herausforderer Alberto Núñez Feijoo Foto: Manu Fernandez/ap

Aus Madrid

Am 29. November wählt Spanien ein neues Parlament. Fast alle Umfragen gehen von einem klaren Sieg der Rechten aus. Die konservative Partido Popular (PP) von Alberto Núñez Feijóo wird demnach gemeinsam mit der rechtsextremen Vox von Santiago Abascal eine absolute Mehrheit erzielen. Eine Brandmauer gibt es in Spanien nicht.

Doch der seit acht Jahren regierende sozialistische Ministerpräsident Pedro Sánchez will die Hoffnung auf eine erneute Regierungsbildung nicht aufgeben. Dafür braucht er die Unterstützung der linken Parteien, links von Sánchez PSOE.

Doch gerade die schwächelt. Nicht zuletzt deshalb, weil die Sozialisten viele der Errungenschaften, wie etwa die Arbeitsmarktreform, die auf Druck der Linken zustande kamen, für sich vermarkten konnte. Nach der Wahl 2013 kam das Bündnis Sumar, der Juniorpartner in der bisherigen in Minderheit regierenden Koalition, auf 31 Abgeordnete. Die Umfragen sehen die Nachfolgeorganisation Frente Amplio (Breite Front), unter der einstigen Bürgermeisterin von Barcelona Ada Colau, nur noch bei 10.

Obwohl Frente Amplio 11 Parteien vereint, tritt die linke gespalten zu den Wahlen an. Die linksalternative Podemos, deren Angeordnete einst aus Sumar ausgetreten waren, nach dem sie keine Ministerposten erhielten, stellt sich alleine zur Wahl und wird aller Voraussicht nach, keine Vertreter ins neue Parlament entsenden. Es könnten somit wertvolle Stimmen verloren gehen. Dass Podemos und Frente Amplio nicht zusammenkamen, liegt weniger an inhaltlichen Punkten als an persönlichen Animositäten.

Von den drei linken Kräften vertritt Podemos, bei Wohnungs-, Verteidigungs- und Wirtschaftspolitik die radikalsten Positionen, während die PSOE am moderatesten auftritt. Beim Thema Migration sind sich die Parteien weitgehend einig.

## Auch mit Regionalparteien wird es eng

Darüber hinaus gibt es in mehreren Regionen, wie dem Baskenland, Galizien, Katalonien und Andalusien, eigene linke Kräfte. Diese vertreten neben sozialen Forderungen mehr oder weniger nationalistische oder regionalistische Bestrebungen. Sie werden wohl besser Abschneiden, als 2023. So sehen die Umfragen EH Bildu aus dem Baskenland etwa mit einem starken Zuwachs, ebenso die Republikanische Linke Kataloniens (ERC). Beide haben in den letzten acht Jahren Sánchez unterstützt.

Hinzu kommt das spanische Wahlsystem, in dem nach dem sogenannten D'Hondt-Verfahren ausgezählt wird, das großen Parteien Vorteile verschafft. Während die Methode bei großen Mengen zu vergebener Sitze relativ gerecht ist, kann es bei einer kleinen Zahl das Ergebnis stark verzerren. Und das ist in Spanien der Fall. Denn die Sitze werden auf Provinzebene vergeben. Manche Provinzen haben nur drei oder fünf Abgeordnete. Selbst Parteien mit über zehn Prozent der Stimmen können so einfach außen vor bleiben.

Angesicht der Befürchtung, die rechtsextreme Vox könnte schon bald in der Regierung sitzen, macht sich im linken Teil der Gesellschaft ein Gefühl breit, dass es so noch nie gab. Es geht vielen darum, das die Linke als Block gewinnt. Ob sie dafür letztendlich Frente Amplio, PSOE oder eine regionale Option wählen ist zweitrangig. Die Rede vom „taktischen Wählen“ macht die Runde.

In den sozialen Netzwerken und in einigen Zeitungen wird Provinz für Provinz analysiert, welche Parteien die besten Chancen haben, im Auszählungssystem der Rechten einen Sitz zu entreißen. Das bietet breiten Raum für Spekulation.

In vielen kleineren Provinzen etwa ist eine Stimme für Frente Amplio eine verlorene Stimme. So mancher vergisst darüber seine langjährige Ablehnung der Sozialdemokratie und wird wohl zum Stimmzettel der PSOE greifen. In Galizien ist es angebracht die linksnationalistische BNG zu wählen, im Baskenland die PSOE oder die linksnationalistische EH Bildu, in Andalusien je nach Provinz PSOE oder auch die linke Regionalpartei Adelante Andalucia.

Nur eine Option ist wackelig: Podemos. Diese Partei könnte knapp draußen bleiben und zu Folge haben, dass der letzte Sitz eben nicht an Frente Amplio oder PSOE, sondern an Vox geht.

Laut der O nlinezeitung eldiario.es sind 48 der 350 Parlamentssitze offen und hängen oft nur von einigen Hundert Stimmen ab. Taktisches Wählen kann so bei einem engen Wahlausgang ausschlaggebend sein.

items.body:
At the September 2026 Republican convention in Dallas, and then from  MAGA rally to  MAGA rally, Donald Trump announced that everyone should vote as if he were on the midterm ballots. Well, the votes are in. By any measure, by any geographic survey, whether looking at federal or state elections, whether looking at  the west coast or the east coast, or the midwest, or the north or the south, or the states outside the continental United States, or red states or blue states, the midterm election results proved to be a devastating national rebuke of Trump far exceeding the expectations of any pundit or prediction market.

On November 5, two days after election day, I visited online trumpstore.com, the retail outlet of The Trump Organization. This is where you can buy Trump branded merchandise.  The site declared there was an early Black Friday sale—50 % off. Trump martini glasses. Trump bras. Trump sportswear. Trump sneakers. Trump hats. Trump candles. Trump honey. Trump coffee.

But missing were such things as Trump steaks, Trump $100,000 watches, Trump  gold colored cell phones and Trump wine. Even missing was the Trump God Bless the USA Bible (King James version, printed in China, tariff exempt, costing $3 to print and retailing for $59.99).

All these items, wherever they can be found, remain a  haunting reminder that before Donald Trump was a politician, he was always a salesman. And the product to be sold was always the same. The product was Donald J. Trump.

Trump will always be selling that product. But now there will be far fewer customers. The midterm elections may mark the end to the best of Trump’s salesmanship days.

Polls show that Trump is perceived, by even those in the MAGA camp, to have lost power within the GOP. His attempt a few days after the election to suggest on Truth Social that the elections were rigged  was widely ignored but even semi-fellow traveler Megyn Kelley dismissed this sales pitch with undisguised contempt. (On November 19, Trump acknowledged that Democrats won the House and the Senate.)

JD Vance also got in the act. He pronounced the reason why so many Republicans were swept out to oblivion in a blue wave was because of Iran, affordability, and Israel, a not too subtle dig at the Trump administration’s agenda and record. To rub it in, Vance said about  the decision to go to war with Iran: “If you like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so.” Surprisingly, almost shockingly, Trump at first did not slap Vance down; he even implied he went along with the diagnosis.

Not surprisingly Trump later distanced himself from the midterms Republican disaster. The problem, he said in an interview on Sixty Minutes and elsewhere, was that his name was not on the ballot. What is laughable is almost pathetic in its justice. There is no Trump the triumphant. Instead we have Trump the lame duck who ducks blame.

Alarmingly, what is also becoming more obvious to more people, there is something wrong with him. His rambling speech on the eve of the November 3rd election before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was noted for its bizarreness. The major portion of the speech was on the pool itself, and its purported history of disrepair and decay. It could almost be taken as a soliloquy that symbolizes the state of his administration and, for that matter, of himself.

Some have noticed discolorations and apparent needle marks on his hands covered up ineffectively with make-up. Others have commented on how he falls asleep in public. It has been reported that in his second term, he has fallen asleep in public at least 29 times, and  most recently he fell asleep in public in a meeting with Putin and Xi. Some claim it appears he has even  briefly nodded off while standing when others were speaking. His disjointed public comments on how he aesthetically appreciated the shape of a male senator’s ass raised eyebrows. None of this is a good look for a salesman.

There are parallels  between Trump and Arthur Miller’s  salesman, Willie Loman, in the play “Death of a Salesman”:  the tawdriness, the narcissism, the amorality,  the self-delusion, the decline. But ultimately Trump is no Willie Loman. Loman ended up broke and buried in obscurity. Instead, Trump has demonstrated an astounding phoenix like resilience in rising out of the ashes of his own making.  Whether its six bankruptcies, failed casinos and airlines enterprises, a taped admission on how he likes to grab women by their private parts, a payout of hush money to a porn star, a jury finding him liable for sexual assault, a jury handing out 34 felony convictions for fraud, or a failed  attempt to overthrow the election of a president by lies and mob violence, he emerges somehow intact. And  each time he rises we all end up talking about him. He even gets re-elected president.

Maybe this time it’s different. This time Trump smells of decay and corruption. The one  who promised  to drain the swamp is now seen bathing in it. Formerly vociferous MAGA supporters have turned on Trump over Epstein. Polling has shown that topping even issues of affordability and an unpopular war with Iran, is the issue of corruption. In less than in two years in his second term, Trump’s net worth has gone up by three billion. Millions may be paid out to his crypto enterprise with presidential pardons to follow. Family and friends get wealthier too. Billionaires curry favor by paying out millions to his causes, such as for a ballroom to replace a wing of the White House wiped out by his wrecking ball.

In the midterm elections Trump gave his sales pitch that he should be considered to be on the ballot. Now he faces  rock bottom approval ratings  and a Congress dominated by Democrats voter instructed to turn things around and stand firm against his failed agendas. With an  election outcome paralleling Vicktor Orban’s  overwhelming election defeat last April, it is likely Trump as salesman has transitioned to involuntary retirement. Who will listen to his pitches?  Not a Congress that was elected to oppose him. Not the great majority of voters that rebuked him. His last pitch in the midterms will prove to be precisely that, his last sales pitch.

So Trump may now have to turn to his other master role, the role of a bully. Trump remains president and holds immense power. Instead of backing down, his appointment of Stephen Miller as his chief of staff signals Trump may be spoiling for a fight. Miller has endorsed threats from Trump administration lawyers that they may criminally prosecute members of Congress for investigating  or threatening to investigate the administration. But such legally ludicrous threats display desperation, not strength.

…

items.body:
While my husband kept his eye on the light plastic kickball wavering indecisively in the air above, his arms upraised to catch it for the out, his feet scuttled side-to-side on the bumpy field, as he tried to position him perfectly. It was his birthday, and we were playing a celebratory game with our extended family at his parents’ house an hour away from ours. After triumphantly catching the ball, he collapsed abruptly to the ground and, when we rushed over, he immediately told me to take him to the ER because he knew a bone had broken. I hate to admit that one of the first things I looked at—silently, selfishly—was which leg was hurt.

Right leg. Driving leg. At that moment, I knew that I was in for what my therapist friend would later call a “growth opportunity.”

Up until that point, my husband had done all of the driving for our family of four, us and our 13-year-old twins; I pinch-hit only when he went out of town. Living previously in Beijing, Brooklyn, and then downtown Boston had obviated most any need to drive, and my skills were basic anyhow, as my immigrant parents had severely limited my mobility as a suburban teenager. In the decade since moving to Cambridge and buying a car, my slight fear of being behind the wheel had deepened into a full-on phobia. The road seemed increasingly like a slippery sheet of ice, unpredictable and dangerous, and I clung to public transit, which is better in Boston than in most American cities though far from comprehensive.

I had always maintained that being terrified to drive in greater Boston was a rational response. Based on accident statistics, Allstate has ranked Boston as America’s worst city for drivers for eleven straight years. There is the running of red lights, the “banging” of “ueys,” the weaving through former-cow-path streets, the traffic jams, the rush hour daredevilry, the cutting off, the honking, the flicking off, the jaywalking, the lawless bicycling, the urgency, the rage, the tailgating. Indeed, it was this last behavior that set me off more than any other. I can picture it now: the heat in my rearview mirror, the voice inside my head that said, *You’re going too fuckin’ slow, you’re a pathetic driver, you need to get out of my way and off the road, you don’t deserve to be here—oh look, an Asian woman, of course.*

Unfortunately, the porous emotional boundaries that had served me well to date as a writer were terrible for a driver. Every time I got behind the wheel, I felt squeezed by the time-is-money capitalist python and crushed down by the country’s sexism and racism; the entire experience of being seen, judged, and honked at was psychologically harrowing. My cringing fear translated into a self-abasing timidity, and I let every single person who wanted to cut in front of me cut. Flash, flash; flash, flash.

After the ER trip that put my husband’s broken fibula in a temporary cast, I managed to pilot the car the hour home on the highway. After his surgery, he was ordered to keep weight off the foot for at least a month, and I prepared to take over the driving. Weekend drum and tennis lessons, weeknight capoeira lessons. I was finally going to learn to drive in Boston.

My instinct on my first drive was to flick loving-kindness at all the other drivers around me as I drove. *May you be happy—and you—and you—and you—and you.* This was a practice I’ve had on and off for the past two decades, ever since I sat my first weeklong silent retreat at the Insight Meditation Society, a loving-kindness focused program led by vipassana teacher Michele McDonald, who counseled us to take a light approach. If you’re sitting on the subway, you can just flick [metta](https://tricycle.org/magazine/metta-practice/) quickly at people, one by one, she said. You don’t have to make it something big and serious. I was living in New York at the time, and it was easy to feel barricaded or hostile or shrunken, especially when crammed into the tin can of the subway with strangers, and flicking loving-kindness at fellow riders shifted something in me—it expanded me, softened me, softened the space between me and others, woke me to the present. When I did the same while driving, it worked similarly, creating a radiant force field through which all the cars moved and related to one another. I could impute positive intentions to drivers I’d read earlier as only erratic, selfish, or terrifying. Even when confronted with impatience and rage, through the practice I learned that those feelings did not have to become mine. Each time I drove, my mind grew quieter.

Of all of the categories of people one can send loving-kindness to (self, benefactor, friend, neutral, difficult), I’ve always found the self the hardest, or at least I’ve found it hard to receive my own good intentions, but in this time of forced growth, I had to try. I returned to the [Metta Bhavana](https://dharmaseed.org/talks/3512/): *May I be safe, may I be peaceful.* In this mindset, when I had to make a turn, I realized that I didn’t have to peel out in front of oncoming traffic in a death-defying manner, no matter what the person behind me insisted. I could simply wait until there was a gap in traffic or someone let me go. And they did. There’s actually a lot of kindness out on the roads, in moments people do seem to understand that we’re suffering through this abominable system together and a little kindness can shift the whole system. These kindnesses, and my own, enabled me to enter the slipstream of humanity as an equal. Before, I used to flash my lights, urging others to turn out of terror, but slowly and through practice, I began to do it mainly to be part of the web of the road. I’ve become more confident about driving exactly how I want; after all, these roads are my roads too. And I admit that on some days I do hit the gas instead of flashing my lights because there are places I need to get to on time too.

…

items.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
items.subtitle: A legendary philosopher calls out Anthropic: Thomas Nagel, whose 1974 bat essay helped define consciousness studies, criticized openness to AI sent…

items.body:
*This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,* [sign up here](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/ai-demystified-the-algorithm/) *.*

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility [more seriously](https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploring-model-welfare) than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of [respected philosophers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986) in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent [poll](https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/AI_poll_results_20260402.pdf), 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 [survey](https://survey2020.philpeople.org/survey/results/5106) of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness *is*, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an [interview](https://www.wired.com/story/just-ridiculous-a-famed-philosopher-takes-on-ai-consciousness/) with *Wired* last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain *does* is equivalent to reproducing what a brain *experiences*.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “[terrible” and “bizarre](https://x.com/PAHoyeck/status/2123277310740808190).” Others came to Nagel’s [defense](https://x.com/dmdebruijn/status/2123423391176630390) to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. [He](https://x.com/bengrossbg/status/2123263674944991252) asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously [hard](https://www.technologyreview.com/2023/10/16/1081149/ai-consciousness-conundrum/) problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical [machines](https://www.technologyreview.com/2023/10/17/1081818/why-itll-be-hard-to-tell-if-ai-ever-becomes-conscious/). If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while [racing](https://misanthropicstatement.com/) ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

items.body:
Timothy Williamson will be the inaugural speaker in a new lecture series accompanying a new journal: *[The Chinese Journal of Philosophy](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?)* (CJP).

Published by Oxford University Press, the CJP is an open-access (including no cost to authors) general philosophy journal.

It is edited by Roger T. Ames (Hawaii), Wei Cheng (Peking), Nicolas De Warren (Penn State), Sebastian Sunday Grève (Peking), and You Zhao (Peking).

The journal is open to submissions “from anyone working in philosophy and on all philosophical topics.” According to its [website](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?),

> the journal aims to represent the multitude of topics and approaches that may fall under the heading of ‘philosophy’ in the world today, with a special focus on philosophical research that has the potential to make different traditions of thought more fruitful for one another.

That is to say, it is not a journal primarily about Chinese philosophy, anymore than the *Canadian Journal of Philosophy* is a journal about Canadian philosophy, or the *Australasian Journal of Philosophy* is about Australasian philosophy. The [note](https://phil.pku.edu.cn/xzqk/cjp/intro.htm), “like these other journals, the *Chinese Journal of Philosophy* originates in a particular region whilst editing and publishing as an international collective, operating in English, and promoting work from around the world.”

CJP is currently open for submissions and plans to begin publishing articles in April.

The launch of the journal includes the start of a new lecture series from the [Department of Philosophy and Religious Studies at Peking University](https://phil.pku.edu.cn/index.htm). Williamson’s inaugural lecture is this Wednesday, and will be delivered in person and [online](https://us06web.zoom.us/j/86727223234).

Learn more about the journal [↗ academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?).

items.body:
Love time travel movies? You're not alone and, as a sci-fi staple, cinema has no shortage of timey-wimey greats. It's [Black Friday week](https://www.space.com/best-black-friday-deals-sales) and many of these titles are now deeply discounted. So, I picked out the ten time travel movies you need to own, from classic blockbusters like Back to the Future, through to modern gems such as Needle in a Timestack, where the only obstacle to time travel is your bank balance.

We do mean own, too. All too often, we've sat down to rewatch a film to find it's vanished from our streaming service. At best, it's rematerialized on a different streaming service; at worst, it's been exterminated as some media conglomerate's tax write-off. Even 'buying' a movie, you're just getting a license that can be revoked at any time.

The solution? By buying these time travel movies on Blu-ray or 4K UHD Blu-ray, they'll still be sitting on your shelf ready to watch and rewatch for years, even decades, from now.

Frequency

Needle in a Timestack

12 Monkeys

Predestination

Primer

The Girl Who Leapt Through Time

The Final Countdown

A Wrinkle in Time

items.title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.

items.body:
Richie Jones at Stone Mountain Park in Georgia this month. Jones and his doctor repeatedly tried to get his insurer, Ambetter, to cover his cancer treatment. Jones often visits the park for quiet reflection. Matt Odom for ProPublica

Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.

A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”

“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.

Kevin Counihan, who was CEO of Ambetter and had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, conceded that a customer’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” Brooks Kraft/Getty Images

A veteran health insurance executive who had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, Counihan conceded on the call that Felicia’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” But he assured her that “we really want to get you what you” and your doctor “think is the most appropriate medication for you.”

“I’m working on it as fast as possible,” said Counihan.

Counihan’s call was a rare acknowledgment from the company’s top brass of a pervasive problem. Ambetter, the most popular plan on the ACA marketplace, has one of the worst track records of delaying or denying medical coverage by refusing to cover the costs.

ProPublica has found that Ambetter last year denied these kinds of requests — known as prior authorization — at a higher rate than any other large insurer on the ACA marketplace. Our analysis of Ambetter’s own data, along with interviews with more than two dozen recent customers, sheds new light on the vast and sometimes illogical nature of how the company can block access to care.

Each dot below is a marketplace plan in Texas, sized according to the number of prior authorization requests it reported in 2025. Plans further to the right deny those requests at higher rates. Ambetter plans are shown in red.

In Texas, where Ambetter’s denial rates were above 32%, the company initially refused to pay for a medical scan for a patient with Stage 4 colon cancer because the doctor hadn’t ordered a cheaper, less precise scan first.

In Iowa, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 31%, it approved a patient’s colonoscopy but denied a request for the bowel prep that all patients must drink in advance of the procedure.

In Kansas, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 26%, it stopped covering an anti-inflammatory treatment for a patient with Crohn’s disease because it wanted the patient to try a different drug.

A ProPublica analysis of nearly 200 federal marketplace plans across the country found that Ambetter had the highest denial rates in most states where it provided data.

Ambetter plans had an average denial rate of 25% in states where the company reported data for last year. That’s substantially higher than the 16% average denial rate for all marketplace plans.

Our analysis is based on data that federal regulators required marketplace plans to report and publish for the first time this year. The requirement is intended to offer greater transparency into how often insurers restrict care by denying prior authorization for treatment.

Since the ACA marketplace launched in 2013, there has been little transparency around how often insurers request — and deny — prior authorization. Insurers use prior authorization to limit spending on treatment, equipment and prescriptions. They say it is also intended to ensure that doctors try less expensive and less invasive treatments before pricier ones. Health insurance experts said that the process of how or when prior authorization gets used is largely a black box.

U.S. Rep. Craig Goldman, a Republican from Texas, sponsored a bipartisan bill that would require marketplace plans to disclose more information about their use of prior authorization. “These companies represent these individuals — and yet denying them coverage and not being transparent with what they will be able to cover,” he said. “They’re just not there for the best interest of the people.”

Four former heads of state insurance departments who reviewed ProPublica’s findings said that Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that current regulators should examine further.

“This is stunning — and not in a good way,” Mila Kofman, a former insurance superintendent in Maine who now oversees the District of Columbia’s ACA marketplace, said of Ambetter’s denial rate. “This is something insurance regulators need to understand. There’s a huge opportunity for regulators to address the improper use of prior authorization.”

## We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your Health Insurance Denial.

[↗ Primärquelle: propublica.org](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/propublica-health-insurance-prior-authorization-reporting)

ProPublica is looking into the ways health insurers’ use of prior authorization impacts patients. We need your help to figure out if the process is still leading to delayed or missed treatments, tests, medical equipment or medication.

[Share Your Experience](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/propublica-health-insurance-prior-authorization-reporting)

Sarah London, CEO of Ambetter’s parent company, Centene, recently said in a statement on its website that it was “[creating a more predictable and transparent experience](https://www.centene.com/news/ahip-partnerships-prior-authorization_progress.html)” for its customers. That statement followed growing backlash against the industry and a push to limit the practice of prior authorization.

items.feedText: Immigration and Customs Enforcement records obtained exclusively by The Intercept. The chasm between GEO’s March 2026 asset appraisal and the sale price just eight months later represents a “massive increase,” according to Michael Wriston, co-founder of the government watchdog Project Salt Box, which tracks ICE spending and contracts. “ICE should explain h…
items.body:
As it eyed a sale of a jail in Tacoma, Washington, this spring, the private prison giant GEO Group valued the facility at $67 million, according to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement records obtained exclusively by The Intercept.

This month, the federal government just paid GEO almost seven times that — [$453 million](https://www.projectsaltbox.com/p/geo-group-sells-tacoma-detention) — when it purchased the facility, the Northwest ICE Processing Center.

The chasm between GEO’s March 2026 asset appraisal and the sale price just eight months later represents a “massive increase,” according to Michael Wriston, co-founder of the government watchdog Project Salt Box, which tracks ICE spending and contracts.

“ICE should explain how it arrived at $453 million and release the appraisal behind that price,” Wriston told The Intercept.

“I think this is what happens when you move too fast without sufficient internal controls,” John Roth, the former inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, told The Intercept. “You’re going to waste a lot of money. And that assumes everyone has the best intentions and hasn’t got some sort of side deal or corrupt motive.”

Neither ICE nor GEO responded to requests for comment about the sale. Without answering questions about the sale price, the Department of Homeland Security told The Intercept the purchase was “to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations.”

A screen capture of a March 2026 ICE spreadsheet showing GEO Group’s valuation of Northwest ICE Processing Center. Screenshot: Jacqueline Stevens/The Intercept

With Democrats set to [take control](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midterms-democrats-agenda-congress-iran-ai/) of Congress, ICE’s real estate purchases are already coming under intense scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

> “These deals raise serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and corruption at DHS.”

“This new report is worthy of serious investigation and is part of a pattern of Department of Homeland Security purchases of detention facilities for hundreds of millions of dollars more than they seem to be worth,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, told The Intercept in a statement. “These deals raise serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and corruption at DHS.”

Hassan opened a [probe](https://www.hassan.senate.gov/news/press-releases/amid-corruption-allegations-senator-hassan-opens-investigation-into-purchase-of-ice-detention-facility-for-420-million-above-previous-asking-price) earlier this month into ICE’s $495 million purchase of a detention center the private prison giant CoreCivic previously offered to the state of Minnesota [for $75 million](https://www.kare11.com/article/news/investigations/senate-democrats-to-investigate-dhs-purchase-of-appleton-prison/89-b7ee1b9a-790e-4e79-ac47-5d5df30196d6) — a sale the state’s corrections commissioner told the news site [Punch Up](https://thepunchup.substack.com/p/6aa2d459-7864-40ba-b5d1-a106389ca439) was being discussed for $3 million.

[Related Private Prison Falsified Records in Detainee’s Death in ICE Custody](https://theintercept.com/2026/02/26/ice-geo-group-moshannon-death-falsify/)

GEO Group’s March 2026 valuation for Northwest ICE Processing Center, which the company purchased in 2005 as part of its acquisition of another private prison firm, was submitted to the Department of Homeland Security in accordance with its contract with ICE.

According to a [chart in the document](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28930958-ice-doc-showing-geo-group-valuation-of-nwipc-jail/), GEO calculated the current $67 million value of the detention facility, which is not the same as its market value, by subtracting annual depreciation figures from its original value of $109 million.

Roth, the former Homeland Security inspector general, expects scrutiny into the nearly half-billion-dollar sale’s paper trail.

“I’d be curious to know,” he said, “what sort of due diligence they did before they put that number down.”

## Cost of Avoiding Regulations

ICE officials told Government Accountability Office investigators that their robust plans for purchasing existing immigration detention facilities was not to save money, but to avoid issues with local governments.

“Officials noted that while they do not expect this effort to result in cost savings, it will help ICE fulfill its mission in locations where state governments may resist expanded detention efforts,” said a Government Accountability Office [report](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-27-108665/index.html) released this month.

[Related How a Small Kansas City Became a Critical Hub for Trump’s Deportation Regime Against Its Will](https://theintercept.com/2026/09/22/leavenworth-kansas-corecivic-ice-mass-detention-deportation/)

Like [other private prison firms](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/arizona-ice-camp-mtc-sexual-abuse/) across the country, GEO’s efforts to build and operate facilities it owns have met obstacles in local rules and regulations.

In some cases, state-level regulators have gone after GEO for violations of labor laws like minimum wage and occupational safety regulations. Earlier this year in California, the company [paid a $100,000 fine](https://www.ccijustice.org/post/geo-group-calosha-settlement-fine) and agreed to extend worker protections to immigrant laborers over alleged violations of California worker safety standards.

One of the cases focused on the Northwest ICE Processing Center, the Tacoma facility that GEO just sold to ICE. In 2021, a judge ordered GEO to pay [$26 million](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/geo-group-must-pay-minimum-wage-immigrant-detainees-court-rules-2023-12-22/) to former detainees and the state of Washington for, among other allegations, state minimum wage violations. (Andrew Free, one of the authors of this article, was an attorney for the ICE detainees in the lawsuit.)

The verdict was [upheld](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/geo-group-cant-nix-23-mln-verdict-over-immigrant-detainee-pay-2025-01-16/) by a federal appeals court in 2025 after GEO sought the same immunity from state minimum wage laws enjoyed by the federal government. The Supreme Court is currently deciding whether it will hear GEO’s appeal.

In a May earnings call, GEO chair George Zoley noted the problem in areas with Democrats in charge of regulation.

“I think the logical solution to much of that is federal ownership of the facilities,” Zoley told the earnings call, according to the [Philadelphia Inquirer](https://www.inquirer.com/news/nation-world/moshannon-valley-detention-center-ice-trump-deportation-contract-20260923.html).

…

items.body:
*A trained car mechanic who plays 150 BPM trance in a shirt and tie, and checks his tracks by dancing around his room. Meet Davyboi*.

In recent years, trance and its faster, more euphoric relatives have found a new generation of dancers across Europe. Among the DJs who have built a following on the back of that revival is Davyboi, a Munich-based DJ and producer with Polish roots. His sets usually sit between 148 and 155 BPM and draw on trance, eurodance, and hard house in equal measure.

Going out in a city where hard techno dominated, he wanted more melody and uplift than most nights offered, so he began playing the records he wanted to hear himself. That approach, delivered in his trademark shirt and tie, has since taken him to Gotec, Rotterdam Rave, and Into The Woods Festival.

We asked him to introduce himself for Introducing, our series on up-and-coming producers and DJs, many of whom have gone on to much bigger things.

## Who are you?

I’m Davyboi, a DJ and producer. I love fast music, big melodies and dancing just as much as the people in front of me. You’ll usually find me behind the decks wearing a shirt and tie.

## Where are you from?

I’m from Munich, Germany, with Polish roots.

## What do you sound like?

Mostly trance and eurodance, but I also love groove, gabber and makina. It’s fast and energetic, with plenty of melodies and vocals. I want people to dance, sing along and have a good time together.

"Your problems are someone else’s dreams"

## Why should we follow what you’re doing?

If you love dancing and getting a bit carried away with your friends, I think we’ll get along. That’s what I enjoy most about a night out, and it’s the feeling I want to share when I play. I’ve also got plenty of new music on the way that I’m excited for people to hear.

## Which of your tracks sums you up? Why?

“Discotheque,” my collaboration with Mika Heggemann. It’s a good introduction to the energy I like bringing to my sets. When I make music, I always ask myself whether I’d enjoy dancing to it if someone else played it. That’s a big part of why I chose this one.

## What have you got coming out in the near future?

My remix of BUNT.’s “I Need You” is coming, and I’ve been busy working on more tracks. There are a lot of ideas I’m excited about, but I want to give each release a little time before moving on to the next.

[quote align=right text="I don’t really feel like I’ve had to give anything up completely."]

## Who or what is your biggest influence, and why?

A lot of it comes from being on the dancefloor myself. Some nights really stay with you, especially when a DJ plays something you weren’t expecting, and it completely changes your mood. I still think about those experiences when I’m choosing music. I know how much a good night can mean to someone.

## How did you get into DJing OR producing to begin with?

I was going out a lot in Munich, where hard techno was very present. I enjoyed the energy, but I wanted to hear more melodies and uplifting tracks too. Eventually, I started putting together the kind of music I wanted to hear on a night out. Coming from the crowd still influences how I play today.

## What are three things on your studio shopping list?

A monitor, a height-adjustable desk and [Nexus](https://refx.com/nexus/) to use in [Ableton](https://www.ableton.com/shop/live/?affiliate=F4nlA735). A few things to make working on music a bit more comfortable and give me some new sounds to play with.

### Who or what have you sacrificed for your art?

I don’t really feel like I’ve had to give anything up completely. It’s more that fitting everything in has become harder. Seeing my friends in Munich takes more planning now that I’m away so often. I still want to make time for them, even when things get busy.

## What’s been your favourite place to play so far?

[Thuishaven](https://thuishaven.nl/) is a favourite. I really love playing for Dutch crowds, and that’s a place I’m always happy to come back to.

## Where can we hear your music?

Mostly on [SoundCloud](https://soundcloud.com/davyboii), where you can find my tracks and mixes. My releases are also on Spotify, Apple Music and the other usual platforms.

## What one song would feature on the soundtrack to your life?

“Tokyo Drift” by Teriyaki Boyz. I trained as a car mechanic and got into tuning cars quite early. That song reminds me of that time, which I look back on really fondly. It always puts me in a good mood.

## What motivates you?

Knowing that people have made an effort to come and see me. Some bring their friends, some travel quite far, and some have been looking forward to that night for a while. I really appreciate that. Seeing them enjoy themselves makes me want to keep improving and give them a reason to come back.

## Tell us an interesting fact about yourself.

I get up and dance to my tracks after working on them. It helps me hear things differently. Sometimes a section seems fine while I’m sitting at the laptop, but when I’m moving to it, I realise it goes on too long. So dancing around my room is actually part of the process.

## Complete this sentence: At heart I’m just a…

…raver who ended up behind the decks.

## What’s the best bit of advice you’ve received?

“Your problems are someone else’s dreams.” I take it as a reminder to appreciate what I get to do. It helps me keep some perspective.

## Where will you be in five years’ time?

I’d love to reach more people with my music and make something that means something to them, whether it helps them through a difficult day or becomes a song they share with their friends. Knowing that something I made could become a small part of someone’s life would mean a lot to me.

**Davyboi and DJ Cringey "Naughty" is out now. [Listen on Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/track/67MB3IlBzSxG6Q9SGh7qXF?si=3fcc2aea3dfb4851). Buy on Bandcamp.**

**Find Davyboi on [Instagram.](https://www.instagram.com/iamdavyboi/?hl=en)**

**Don’t have Ableton Live? Buy it [↗ ableton.com](https://www.ableton.com/shop/live/?affiliate=F4nlA735). Heads up, it’s an affiliate link. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission (it doesn’t affect the price).**

items.body:
# 2035 came early

> tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire , GL gears , xeyes , a voice , the weather over curl , or Firefox .

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

> Atwood’s Law Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev .

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev .

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package , over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix .

> Aside What is unkernel ? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm , 1 1 With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload. 2 2 The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland , and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl , git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay. 3 3 Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is Firefox in trynix , and it loading trynix.dev , and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 4 4 Do not be too overjoyed. It took more than an hour for this to render.

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

2035 came early.

items.feedText: Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. items.body:
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science [Margaret Rossiter](https://sts.cornell.edu/margaret-rossiter) coined[the term “The Matilda Effect”](https://www.openculture.com/2025/12/matilda-effect.html) to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film *[Hidden Figures](https://amzn.to/2HTG1jS) * have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, [in footnotes](https://www.openculture.com/2019/02/womens-hidden-contributions-to-modern-science-get-revealed-by-new-study.html).

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “[Floating University](https://www.openculture.com/2016/07/marie-curie-attended-a-secret-underground-flying-university-when-poland-blocked-her-other-women-from-advancing-their-education.html)” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the[Nobel Prize](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/) [in Physics](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/) with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the [Sorbonne](https://www.sorbonne-universite.fr/en/university/history-and-heritage/history), the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site [Famous Scientists](https://www.famousscientists.org/marie-curie/), “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the [French Academy of Sciences](https://www.academie-sciences.fr/en/). It would take another 51 years before the first woman, [Marguerite Perey,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Perey) a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more [influential scientists](https://www.openculture.com/2017/12/read-the-dont-let-the-bastards-get-you-down-letter-that-albert-einstein-sent-to-marie-curie-during-a-time-of-personal-crisis-1911.html) and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Incidentally, in the following year, the Curies’ daughter Irène Joliot-Curie and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Since then, only seven other women have claimed that honor, and [only five women, including Marie Curie, have won the Prize in physics](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/are-the-nobel-prizes-missing-female-scientists/?redirect=1), out of 230 winners total.

There may be nothing yet like gender parity in the sciences, but those who know where to look can find the names of dozens of women scientists running women-owned companies, women-founded research institutes and academic departments, and, like the famous Curies, making [major contributions to chemistry](https://www.thoughtco.com/famous-women-in-chemistry-609453). Perhaps not long from now, many of those exceptional scientists will be as well-known and widely celebrated as Marie Curie.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2019.
