As [MusicTech wrote](https://musictech.com/reviews/plug-ins/baby-audio-transit-2-review-andrew-huang/) when Baby Audio’s Transit 2 multi-effects unit came out in 2024, “this plugin is actually awesome.” Now producers can get this top tier addition to their arsenal for the insanely low price of £49. That’s 50% off the original price of £99.

[deals ids=”3487195c-50c6-4e4d-a063-25acd15047ae”]

But what’s in the box (pun intended) when you buy this revered product? To start there are 28 effects modules that can be operated with six different motion modes. Its bread and butter is its huge capability for creating interesting transitions between different moments in a song. Instead of obsessing over automation, use one single knob on the Transit 2 to add effects sweeps spanning everything from digital chorus to tremolo to noise to flanger.

Moreover, there over 400 presets from primary designer Andrew Huang to use for yourself or to act as a foundation for your own exploration. Another approach is Transit 2’s randomisation engine. Create something completely new with the click of a button or define the process with different random ranges to affect certain parameters with the function.

Transit 1 only had 18 effects. With 10 new ones, there is simply no limits to the combinations of effects users can create and how those can interact with the music. Other than that there are four new motion modes to control how the knob will action the effects chains. To maximise how the motion and the effects work together, every element of each effect and can be added or removed from the motion parameters as well.

items.body:
President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has [ordered the US military to halt plans](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117667060434959655) to [detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide](https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/outrage-questions-swirl-as-army-delays-blowing-up-stockpile-of-toxic-lead-azide/) at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January.

The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).

Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in [an emergency court filing](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ca8.116088/gov.uscourts.ca8.116088.00805660322.1_1.pdf) that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.

## Lisa Hanawalt's "I Can't Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex" (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/20/intrusive-horse-thoughts/#lisa-hanawalt)

The title of animator Lisa Hanawalt's new graphic memoir *I Can't Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex* is a perfect encapsulation of the book's contents: a frank, self-aware, funny, horny, horsey exploration of Hanawalt's life, relationships, gender, and digestive issues:

[https://drawnandquarterly.com/books/i-cant-stop-thinking-about-horses-and-sex/](https://drawnandquarterly.com/books/i-cant-stop-thinking-about-horses-and-sex/)

Hanawalt is probably best known as the character designer for *Bojack Horseman*, but is also much loved in animation circles for her all-too-short-lived show *Tuca & Bertie*:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuca_%26_Bertie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuca_%26_Bertie)

She lived with the comedian/podcaster/showrunner Adam "Ruins Everything" Conover for 14 years, and the memoir revolves around the couple's breakup.

As the title promises, Hanawalt is also a lifelong horse-lover, who spent her childhood developing scars on her knees and calluses on the tops of her feet from endless all-fours sessions of pretending to be a horse. As an adult, she rides at the Los Angeles Equestrian Center, where she meets other horse people, who are beautifully depicted as the mix of posh sociopaths, obsessive animal-lovers, and lovable misfits (my daughter's middle school was around the corner from the LAEC and she grew up shoveling manure and tacking up at a teaching barn there; I can vouch for Hanawalt's faithful portrayal of the vibe).

Horses are Hanawalt's touchstone, the thing that brings her thoughts and emotions back into equilibrium, no matter what life throws at her. Eventually – inevitably – she acquires a horse, and just as inevitably, that horse proves to be her savior and her heartbreak. Horses are massive, majestic, impossibly powerful animals that are nevertheless forever on the verge of death, one weird disease or inexplicable fall from being maimed for life or keeling over.

The story of Hanawalt's pony Juni is intertwined with the story of her and Conover's breakup and her post-breakup relationships. Both threads of the tale are developed through beautiful, *extremely* funny, deeply personal vignettes that are brought to life by Hanawalt's art, which depicts bodies (animal, human, and animalistic human avatars) as hilarious, weird, and sexy all at once.

These two motifs criss-cross as we journey through Hanawalt's dating life, her childhood sexual trauma, her IBS, and her fears and hopes about her fertility (two of the major subplots involve Hanawalt's experiences with egg-freezing and bowel problems, and the way that the medical system treats women).

Hanawalt has a gift for compact, revealing character studies that leave the reader feeling both warm affection and exasperation with everyone in her life (including Hanawalt herself). It's a world without heroes and villains, where flaws and virtues are almost always flip-sides of the same coin. Everyone is crazy sometimes, including Hanawalt, and Hanawalt is self-aware enough to know when she's getting in her own way, and even why that happens, and also (just like all of us) can't always stop herself from tripping herself up.

Hanawalt's written and drawn a wise, funny, horny book that wrings comedy *and* insight out of trauma and melancholy. It's a gorgeous read that lingers.

Hanawalt isn't the only person who made smart, funny media out of her and Conover's breakup. Conover's comedy special about the breakup and its aftermath is called "Big Divorce Energy" and it was released the same week that *Can't Stop Thinking* hit the shelves:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CVB-SUX7zgk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CVB-SUX7zgk)

I saw Conover perform this set live and it was terrific – and it got even better by the time he recorded it for the special. It makes for a perfect bookend for Hanawalt's memoir, a fact that both Conover and Hanawalt affirm in a lovely, warm conversation they recorded for Conover's *Factually* podcast. It's an interview that raises the bar for the kind of affection and even love a mature couple can salvage from a breakup:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BUXEDUiICM4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BUXEDUiICM4)

The book itself is from Montreal's Drawn and Quarterly, who have a well-deserved reputation for publishing quality graphic novels, especially memoirs. D&Q always puts together a beautiful physical artifact, and *Can't Stop Thinking* is no exception: a handsome hardcover with luxurious, thick semi-matte pages and a bookmark ribbon sewn into the binding. It's the perfect gift for any friend going through a breakup (or thinking about buying a horse).

items.body:
# How to Win Big Betting on Jensen Huang? Listen to Trump

Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior , Nvidia’s board insisted it had no plans to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge.

The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The New York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not.

On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped six percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president said he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy.

According to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket’s markets largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to returning, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when President Trump threw his support behind the former CEO. But there were several large trades that could not be tied to public developments.

Betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode identified clusters of trades on Huang’s return that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return.

Despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and longshot buyers,” he says.

For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump.

Isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and professional sports bettor, says he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief said on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says that he figured that the board would consider Huang’s return if it looked likely to improve the company’s stock performance. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “ pee in your brain .”) “It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman says. “Should’ve bet more.”

A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he says his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED.

Other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” says Kalshi trader Caleb Davies.

Aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, says he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials said over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says.

items.body:
*τρία* is the third instalment in **Aeson Zervas’** ongoing sequence for Heat Crimes, continuing the numbering of his untitled pieces from the self-titled debut (1–8), through *Hazlom* (9–17), and now from “Χωρίς τίτλο 18” to “Χωρίς τίτλο 29”. That continuity matters. Zervas’ reclusiveness, the absence of explanatory titles and the progressive numbering make the three albums feel like fragments of one unresolved archive. On *τρία*, Greek folk memory, rebetika, damaged soundtrack music and dubby electronics repeatedly surface and disappear. “Χωρίς τίτλο 20” slips into filmic suspense; “Χωρίς τίτλο 21” gives itself over to rebetika; the almost unbearably melancholic “Χωρίς τίτλο 22” is followed by the repeated scream of “Χωρίς τίτλο 23”; later, “Χωρίς τίτλο 25” places traditional material over an electronic dub framework. The album keeps circling between fairground unease, glitchy tapes, folk citation and invented memory. Is this, as Mark Fisher would have it, a harrowing investigation of memory disorder?

Mark Fisher’s hauntology is an obvious reference point: damaged repetition, obsolete media and sounds that appear to belong to futures that never arrived. [Matt Bluemink](https://shop.becoming.press/products/the-future-is-not-lost-music-technology-and-the-creation-of-worlds-2026-by-matt-bluemink) takes that diagnosis and pushes against its pessimism, arguing that anti-hauntology can use the past as material for new cultural forms rather than remaining trapped in mourning. But the work of Egyptian-born producer [Abadir](https://acloserlisten.com/2026/09/18/abadir-the-primitivist/), whom we interviewed recently, complicates the argument further. Abadir rejects the assumption that “newness” must be tied to an abstract future at all, especially when that future is defined through a Western critical vocabulary. For him, the more interesting question is how the past can be used creatively “without mourning it” while remaining grounded in the present; he is equally suspicious of escaping backwards through nostalgia and forwards through futurism. That position feels particularly useful for *τρία*. Zervas is clearly, but also self-consciously, nostalgic, yet nostalgia here is unstable and frequently unpleasant. Rebetika is not restored as heritage; it is scratched, looped, interrupted, displaced and contaminated by technologies and musical languages from elsewhere.

This also makes the Mediterranean dimension of the record more important than a simple Fisherian reading might allow. Zervas’ Greece is not an isolated national memory but a sedimented space in which Greek, Anatolian, Ottoman, North African and contemporary electronic histories overlap. The idea of Mediterranean music as a form of historical recomposition—taking materials already in circulation and assembling them into new cultural possibilities—fits *τρία* closely. Its imagined past may never have existed, but that does not make it escapist; it can also be a way of refusing a museumised, Eurocentric version of Greek antiquity as suggested by the label notes.

Marc Armand’s cover captures this beautifully. A broken archaeological piece lies on the floor of what appears to be a museum, caught in a shaft of light, while intact artefacts remain displayed on the walls. *τρία* behaves similarly: it removes cultural memory from the wall, breaks chronology and leaves the fragments where they can interfere with the present. The question, then, may not be whether Zervas is producing the music of the future. Abadir is right to make that category suspect. Perhaps the more urgent music now comes from artists for whom neither past nor future offers an easy refuge—artists forced to work inside an unstable present and to make something from whatever histories, technologies and damaged materials remain available.

The album raises many questions that deserve further elaboration. For what it is worth, I personally believe that those making the music of the future today—whatever that might mean—are often those for whom the future is not a given: artists in Ukraine and elsewhere confronting imperialism, war and genocide, and those faced with the very impossibility of the present. ( **Gianmarco Del Re** )

items.subtitle: Die Rückkehr des Nvidia-Chefs hat den deutschen Leitindex wieder deutlich über die Marke von 25.000 Punkten getrieben.
items.feedText: Kurstafel der Frankfurter Börse. Foto: Handelsblatt Düsseldorf. Die Rückkehr von Nvidia-Chef Jensen Huang hat nach dem jüngsten Ausverkauf die Stimmung am deutschen Aktienmarkt aufgehellt. Das überraschende Comeback hat am Montag die Investoren in Begeisterung versetzt. Angetrieben vor allem durch Profiteure von Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) war der deutsche Leitindex am Montag um 2,2 Prozent angestiegen und schloss den Handel bei 25.337 Punkten . Die Erholung folgte auf die Ankündigung vom Chipkonzern Nvidia , den wegen einer Affäre mit einer mutmaßlichen chinesischen Agentin zurückgetretenen Huang mit sofortiger Wirkung wieder als Vorstandschef einzusetzen.
items.body:
# Dax und Börse aktuell: Sechs Punkte, die für Anleger heute wichtig sind

Kurstafel der Frankfurter Börse. Foto: Handelsblatt Düsseldorf. Die Rückkehr von Nvidia-Chef Jensen Huang hat nach dem jüngsten Ausverkauf die Stimmung am deutschen Aktienmarkt aufgehellt. Das überraschende Comeback hat am Montag die Investoren in Begeisterung versetzt. Angetrieben vor allem durch Profiteure von Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) war der deutsche Leitindex am Montag um 2,2 Prozent angestiegen und schloss den Handel bei 25.337 Punkten .

Die Erholung folgte auf die Ankündigung vom Chipkonzern Nvidia , den wegen einer Affäre mit einer mutmaßlichen chinesischen Agentin zurückgetretenen Huang mit sofortiger Wirkung wieder als Vorstandschef einzusetzen.

Ob aus dem Freudentanz eine nachhaltige Trendwende entstehe, müssten die kommenden Handelstage erst noch zeigen, sagte Stratege Salah-Eddine Bouhmidi vom Broker IG. „Die Rückkehr des Konzernchefs allein beantwortet noch keine Fragen nach Bewertungen und der Rentabilität milliardenschwerer KI-Investitionen“.

Am frühen Dienstagmorgen setzt sich der Trend zunächst nicht fort. Auf außerbörslichen Handelsplattformen notiert der Dax vorbörslich unverändert.

Anlegerinnen und Anleger richten ihre Aufmerksamkeit neben Nvidia heute auch auf diverse Konjunkturdaten. In Deutschland steht die Veröffentlichung des Ifo-Geschäftsklimaindex an. In den USA werden gleich mehrere Daten veröffentlicht.

items.body:
# Jensen Huang und Trumps Männerkult

Erst erklärte Donald Trump den wieder eingesetzten Nvidia-Chef Jensen Huang zum „national treasure”, einer Art Nationalheiligtum. Zu Huangs Rückkehr beglückwünschte der Präsident nicht nur die Amerikaner, sondern gleich die ganze Welt. Und dann verbreitete er über Truth Social eine Fotomontage, auf der Huang einen roten BH am ausgestreckten Arm wie eine Trophäe in die Luft hält; Trump griff dafür auf das legendäre Foto zurück, das ihn selbst mit gereckter Faust nach dem Attentat in Butler zeigt. Neben dem blutverschmierten, aber triumphierenden Helden Huang prangt statt der amerikanischen Flagge eine Fahne mit Nvidia-Logo. Erst die Heiligsprechung, dann der Herrenwitz.

Und falls noch jemand an der Deutung zweifelte, bekräftige Trump gegenüber dem Sender CNBC, Huangs Affären mit einer mutmaßlichen chinesischen Spionin und einer Kollegin bei Nvidia könnten für den CEO am Ende sogar ein „net positive“ sein, unter dem Strich also ein Gewinn. „Sex sells, fellas“, formulierte es der Präsident. Die Leute wüssten, was Huang „durchgemacht“ habe. Aus einer Affäre mit möglichen sicherheitspolitischen Konsequenzen soll so im Handumdrehen eine Geschichte männlicher Bewährung werden.

### Hauptsache mannhaft

Dieses Männerbild mag durch die MAGA-Schlappe bei den Midterms zwar beschädigt sein, es ist aber noch immer attraktiv für viele Menschen. Auch in Huangs öffentlicher Reue blieb der zum Genie stilisierte „große Mann“ in den letzten Tagen der Mittelpunkt des Geschehens. Der gestrauchelte CEO beschrieb sich als Mann, der Unglück über seine Familie und seinen Konzern gebracht habe. Dass Huang womöglich nicht nur Akteur, sondern auch Gegenstand fremder Interessen war und vielleicht sogar von einer Frau benutzt und vorgeführt wurde, soll nebensächlich sein. Auch in Trumps Fotomontage war von der handelnden Frau nur noch ein Stück Unterwäsche übrig.

Die amerikanischen Medien loten derweil die Größe des Schadens aus. Im Magazin „Foreign Policy“ ist vom „größten nationalen Sicherheitsskandal der amerikanischen Geschichte“ die Rede. Das „New York Magazine“ titelt angesichts der moralischen Implikationen lakonisch: „Nothing Matters“, nun sei wohl alles egal. In der Wirtschafts- und Technologiepresse geht es unterdessen um die Erleichterung der Anleger nach Huangs Rückkehr und um Amerikas Wettbewerbsfähigkeit. Die Unentbehrlichkeit des Nvidia-CEOs ist demnach keine reine Erfindung seiner Bewunderer.

Wie Medien berichten, schuf der Mann, der sich in Lederjacke als Rockstar der Technologiebranche inszenierte, durch persönlich ausgehandelte Finanzierungs- und Liefergeschäfte weitreichende wirtschaftliche Abhängigkeiten. An der KI-Euphorie hängen mittlerweile auch Wirtschaftswachstum, Altersvorsorge und private Vermögen. Und wie das Magazin „The Atlantic” betonte, war Huang in der Zeit nach seinem Abgang und ohne Job „die gefährlichste Art Zeuge, die es gibt”, hätte Ermittlern also viele Geheimnisse verraten können.

Huang, der Hardware und Software für eine Technologie verkauft, die Menschen eines Tages angeblich überflüssig machen könnte, soll selbst nun also unersetzlich sein. Elf Tage lagen zwischen seinem Abgang und der Rückkehr an die Spitze von Nvidia: Auch, wenn die Ermittlungen andauern, ist das eine ziemlich kurze Zeit für eine Gesellschaft, die immer mal wieder über die angeblich vernichtenden Folgen einer „Cancel Culture” streitet.

items.body:
**Geburtstag, Jahrestag, Weihnachten, Namenstag… Das Jahr steckt voller Gelegenheiten, ein geliebtes Gesicht zum strahlen zu bringen! Dein bester Kumpel macht sich als Musikproduzent selbständig und hofft auf deine Unterstützung? Die Lebensgefährtin träumt vom eigenen, professionell produzierten Podcast? Keinen Bock mehr auf Omas Häkeldecken-Pakete zu jedem Anlass? Diese Producer-Geschenktipps verschönern jeden Wunschzettel!**

Inhalte

- Warm Audio WA-47jr SE
- Tegeler Audio Crème
- Wavebone Headquarter Wood Studio Desk
- Warm Audio Bus-Comp
- Wavebone Viking Foam Chair
- Warm Audio WA-87jr (SE)
- Warm Audio Jude-MP2

## Warm Audio WA-47jr SE

„Warm und charaktervoll“, so [klingt das WA-47jr SE](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/warm-audio-wa-47jr-se-test/)! Wenige Zahlen machen Musikproduzenten den Mund so wässrig wie die 47, denn sie verweist in der Audiotechnik auf das legendäre Neumann U47. Das [WA-47jr ‘Studio Essentials’](https://www.thomann.de/de/warm_audio_wa_47jr_se.htm?offid=1&affid=84)bringt dir einen ähnlichen Vintage-Sound wie das vergriffene Original zu einem Bruchteil des Preises. Das Studiomikro ist schnörkellos auf’s Wesentliche reduziert: Es hat die wohl am meisten genutzte Richtcharakteristik (Niere), kommt ohne Röhren und Übertrager aus und verzichtet auf Extras wie Pad, Filter und Spinne. Dafür bekommst du für kleine Maus ein charaktervolles Werkzeug für deine Gesangs- und Instrumental-Produktionen oder die deiner Liebsten! Zwei Finishes stehen zur Auswahl.

## Tegeler Audio Crème

Was nützt das beste Signal ohne die passende Bearbeitung? [Tegeler Audios Stereo-Prozessor Crème](https://www.thomann.de/de/tegeler_creme_green.htm?offid=1&affid=84) sitzt perfekt auf der Summe, veredelt aber schon beim Recording deine Einzelspuren: Der VCA-Kompressor mit Sidechain-Filter beherrscht sanfte Verdichtung ebenso wie Punch und Limiting, die Chicken Head-Potis und das VU-Meter versprühen Vintage-Charm in der Bedienung und die [Filterbänder der EQ-Sektion im Pultec-Stil arbeiten äußerst musikalisch](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/tegeler-audio-manufaktur-creme-test/)! Klar, zweikanalig und Made in Germany hat das seinen Preis. Vielleicht sagst du den Arbeitskollegen, sie sollen bei deinem Dienstaustritt auf die goldene Uhr zugunsten des Crème verzichten?

## Wavebone Headquarter Wood Studio Desk

Schwebendes Streicherarrangement in deinem Popsong? Klavier-Intro und Rhodes-Sound für die Power-Ballade? Ja gerne, am einfachsten als virtuelle Instrumente. Nur, wohin mit dem 88-tastigen Masterkeyboard? Die elegante Lösung: [Wavebones Headquarter Wood Studio Desk](https://www.thomann.de/de/wavebone_headquarter_wood.htm?offid=1&affid=84) mit höhenverstellbarer Keyboardablage auf Rollen! Für die Keys hast du sechs Positionen zur Auswahl, der stabile Tisch aus Stahl und MDF bietet eine erhöhte Ablage für deine Monitore und eine optionale Kabelhalterung gibt’s auch. Tipp: Schenk dir den Wavebone einfach selbst, ohne, dass es jemand merkt. „Scha-haaatz, wolltest du nicht schon lange einen neuen Wohnzimmertisch? Ich hab da ein total stylishes Modell in Walnussholz-Optik gefunden…“

## Warm Audio Bus-Comp

u träumst vom perfekten Mix-Glue, deine Oma sagt aber, mehr als 800 Euro gibt’s dieses Jahr nicht zu Weihnachten? Dann kannst du den [SSL Bus-Kompressor](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/ssl-bus-comp-classic-test/) wohl vergessen, seinen Sound aber nicht! Denn der [zweikanalige Warm Audio Bus-Comp](https://www.thomann.de/de/warm_audio_bus_comp.htm?offid=1&affid=84) macht seine Sache außerordentlich gut und bietet gegenüber dem Original sogar eine [„erweiterte Threshold-Range“ und einen „höher angesetzten Gain-Umfang“](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/warm-audio-bus-comp-test/). Die Cinemag-Transformer im Signalweg sind schaltbar und die Rückseite bietet zusätzlich zu den XLRs Klinken-Ins und Outs. Frohes Fest!

Studiostandards: Kompressoren und Limiter

Manche Kompressoren, wie den LA-3A, den 1176 oder einen API 2500 findet man in der Mehrzahl der Studios – oder Varianten davon. Wieso bloß?

12.01.2016

4,5 / 5

2

Zum Test

## Wavebone Viking Foam Chair

Mal eben vom Mischpult wegdrehen, die Klampfe greifen und die Idee festhalten, die im Kopf rumschwirrt: Mit dem Wavebone Viking Foam Chair kinderleicht! Denn der ergonomische Stuhl ist auf das schnelle Navigieren im Studio zwischen Spielen, Mischen und Editieren abgestimmt. Seine Armlehnen klappst du weg, er gleitet auf leisen, Parkett-schonenden PU-Rollen und du stellst den Wikinger mit wenigen Handgriffen optimal auf deine Rückenlänge und Sitzposition ein. Doch das Beste kommt noch: Mama und Papa werden glauben, ihr Kind sei endlich vernünftig und mache doch noch etwas Anständiges aus seinem Leben, weil du dir zum Geburtstag einen ergonomischen ‘Bürostuhl’ wünschst!

## Warm Audio WA-87jr (SE)

Die 87 ist noch so eine magische Zahl unter Audioingenieuren, denn das Neumann U87 ist aufgrund seiner Allrounder-Qualitäten ein Desert Island Mic. Wenn du die Million Euro noch nicht geknackt hast, verschenkst du zum Fest besser erst einmal ein dem Original nachempfundenes [Warm Audio WA-87](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/warm-audio-wa87-test/), das es in verschiedenen klanglich überzeugenden Varianten gibt. ‘Junior’ ist die übertragerlose FET-Version. Dank Doppelmembrankapsel schaltest du die Richtcharakteristik (Niere, Acht, Kugel) wie beim WA-87 und bekommt eine Spinne und ein Ledertäschchen als Zubehör. Das [Warm Audio WA-87jr](https://www.thomann.de/de/warm_audio_wa_87jr.htm?offid=1&affid=84) kommt in silber und schwarz. Gesang, Sprache, Drum-Overhead, Mikrofonierung der akustischen Gitarre, das WA-87jr macht an vielen Schallquellen eine gute Figur. Die SE-Version hat die feste Richtcharakteristik Niere, dafür legst du auf dem Weg zur ersten Million mehr bei Seite.

Studiostandards: Vocal-Mikrofone

Oh ja, es gibt sie, die klassischen Mikrofone, die für Gesangsaufnahmen in Tonstudios gerne benutzt werden. Und, oh ja: Sie sind teuer bis unbezahlbar. Wir zeigen hier die Klassiker – und preiswerte Alternativen.

5 / 5

## Warm Audio Jude-MP2

Hey Jude! Legendären Studio-Sound aus der Beatles, Stones und Doors-Ära gefällig? Dann wünsch dir den Warm Audio Jude-MP2! Denn die Technik dieses Preamps fand sich ursprünglich in der Sound Techniques ‘A-Range’-Konsole und verhalf Künstlern wie David Bowie und Led Zeppelin, ihren charismatischen Sound im Studio voll zu entfalten. [Die Impedanz passt du in neun Positionen an das angeschlossene Mikro und die Schallquelle an](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/warm-audio-sound-techniques-jude-mp2-test/) und die Custom-Cinemag-Übertrager sorgen für ordentlich Mojo.

items.body:
Wer auf dem iPhone regelmäßig interessante Artikel, Nachrichten oder andere Webseiten mit Freunden und Familienmitgliedern teilt, sollte die unterschiedlichen Darstellungsoptionen kennen, die Apple in der Nachrichten-App anbietet.

#### Die Standardansicht beim Teilen aus Safari heraus an die Nachrichten-App

Beim Versand per iMessage oder RCS lässt sich beeinflussen, wie viel Platz ein Link im Gesprächsverlauf einnimmt und welche Informationen der Empfänger bereits vor dem Öffnen der Webseite zu sehen bekommt.

Die entsprechenden Einstellungen sind direkt beim Verfassen einer Nachricht verfügbar, dürften vielen iPhone-Anwendern aber bislang entgangen sein. Insgesamt stehen drei Varianten zur Auswahl, zwischen denen ihr vor dem Abschicken einer Nachricht wechseln könnt.

## Link-Vorschau kompakter gestalten

Ruft ihr in Safari eine Webseite auf, betätigt anschließend den Teilen-Pfeil in der unteren Symbolleiste und wählt die Nachrichten-App aus, erstellt das iPhone zunächst eine Link-Vorschau. Diese enthält den Titel der Webseite, deren Domain und, sofern vom Webseitenbetreiber bereitgestellt, ein passendes Vorschaubild.

#### „Anpassen“ erlaubt das Wählen einer kompakten Darstellung

Tippt ihr nun einmal auf die Vorschau und anschließend im eingeblendeten Kontextmenü auf den Menüpunkt „Anpassen“, bietet euch das iPhone eine kompaktere Darstellung an. Diese verzichtet auf das großformatige Bild und beschränkt sich auf den Seitentitel, die Domain und das kleine Symbol der Webseite.

Das ist vor allem dann praktisch, wenn ihr einen Link zusammen mit einer längeren Nachricht verschicken oder mehrere Webseiten innerhalb eines Gesprächs empfehlen möchtet. Die kompakte Darstellung hält den Nachrichtenverlauf übersichtlich und rückt den begleitenden Text stärker in den Vordergrund.

## Ausgewählte Textpassagen als Zitat verschicken

Eine dritte Darstellungsvariante steht zur Verfügung, wenn ihr vor dem Teilen einer Webseite zunächst einen Textabschnitt in Safari markiert. Wählt dazu die gewünschte Passage aus und betätigt erst anschließend den Teilen-Pfeil in der unteren Symbolleiste.

#### Auch Textzitate lassen sich mit Link teilen

Entscheidet ihr euch jetzt für die Nachrichten-App, übernimmt das iPhone den ausgewählten Text als Zitat in die Link-Vorschau. Darunter erscheinen der Titel des Artikels, die Domain und ein kleines Vorschaubild. So könnt ihr den Empfänger gezielt auf eine interessante Aussage innerhalb eines längeren Artikels aufmerksam machen, ohne die betreffende Passage zusätzlich in die Nachricht kopieren zu müssen.

Auch bei dieser Variante könnt ihr die Vorschau antippen und über den Menüpunkt „Anpassen“ nachträglich verändern. Da ihr diesmal bereits einen Textabschnitt ausgewählt habt, stehen euch alle drei Darstellungsformen zur Verfügung: die Zitatkarte, die reguläre Vorschau mit großem Bild und die platzsparende Textvariante.

items.title: How Important Were Medieval Viking Drinking Games?

items.body:
It’s clear from mythology that alcohol was ritually significant in Norse culture, and none more so than mead, which was considered a godly drink and one that imbued the drinker with poetic skill.

In the ancient sagas the origin story of mead comes from a daring series of thefts, with the drink first created through the spit-based peace negotiations of two warring god-families. Their congealing spit, naturally, birthed a mystic with the highest intelligence called Kvasir whose blood was in fact all mead, and through this blood flowed poetry itself.

Unfortunately, Kvasir was not intelligent enough to avoid murder by dwarves for his blood-mead, and then this precious liquid was stolen again by a giant. Odin, king of the gods, wanted his own share of this bloody-mega-mead and so disguised himself as an eagle and stole the mead from the giant, allegedly seducing the giant’s daughter in the process. As Odin escaped from the giant’s lair, some of the mead was spilled from his eagle’s beak and fell to earth. It was said that the great Norse saga poets were those folk who by luck were struck by drops of falling mead from Odin’s beak.

Booze was a bind which helped keep Norse society together, with shared drinking a way of professing loyalty.

Beyond the wild and winding escapades of the gods in pursuit of blood-mead, we know a lot of drinking also happened in the mortal Norse realms. Booze was a bind which helped keep Norse society together, with shared drinking a way of professing loyalty and signing contracts, from marriage to inheritance. This drinking, along with most other gatherings (and anything else, for that matter), would take place in the hall, the only place to be in Norse society, what with the winter weather and limited fuel for fires. It was in these halls that the very important business of feast-throwing and drinking in honor of a lord or warrior would take place.

The feast, a sometimes days- or weeks-long exhibition of power and hospitality by the host, was a common (if extraordinarily expensive) way of gift-giving and demon-strating respect among the elites of Norse society. A big bouquet for your sister’s birthday or a nice dessert to take to your aunt’s weekend lunch seems more reasonable now. Great halls designed for this purpose would ring with music, played on bone flutes, bells, stringed instruments and rattles, as well as shields, which were beaten as drums. Such music would be accompanied by other entertainment, including dramatic performances of the old sagas. Drinking was such an integral part of these feasting celebrations that some later sagas show those who did not drink being ostracized from the retinue of their host with some hostility, their lack of involvement seen as an affront.

This binding together of drinkers was done through a (perhaps unhygienic) custom of *sumbl*, a ritual ceremony also known as “oath cup,” where a woman, often related to the host, would share out a ritual drink among the gathering, one sip at a time and from the same glass. It’s possible women undertook this as a nod to their perceived magical power, and their role as brewers too. The order of those served would help establish the hierarchy of the gathering, a diplomatic tightrope no doubt decided carefully by the hosting household. In the sagas, this drinking ritual was often accompanied by an oath or vow.

In *Beowulf*, an Anglo-Saxon poem recounting a saga, Queen Wealhtheow is the cupbearer at a *sumbl*, greeting her husband and king, Horthgar, with drink first before serving others in turn. Beowulf the warrior takes an oath through this ceremony of the *bragafull* after being challenged by the Queen to rid her hall, the hall of Heorot, of the evil beast that stalks it. Oath-making and -keeping, though, could be lower stakes than defending a hall from its dragon enemies; marriages, alliances and other agreements were kept as oaths, and bound often with communal drinking as a shared witness.

For those not rich, battle-famous or influential enough to be invited to the great feasts in the chieftain’s hall, they too found a way to enjoy a glass or two after a tough day on the fjords. This took place in the *Skytningar*, a more informal refectory, essentially a pub, where individuals paid their own dues, rather than the quite expensive business of throwing a feast and footing the bill for everyone. As a result, these drinking places attracted the less wealthy looking for a fix, like farmers, merchants and townsfolk. These everyday dives tended to have a pretty bad reputation, the mark of a good time no doubt.

Foreign merchants were often blamed for the noisy impact of these drinking houses on their surroundings, with Snorri’s *Olaf’s saga* recording how between 1067 and 1093 King Óláfr Haraldsson Kyrri was displeased with the “drinking bouts in marketplaces about the land as a consequence of the large number of merchants.” Later Norwegian kings also continued to rail against the drunkenness of the common man, with King Sverrir in 1300 making a speech against the drunkenness of both his people and the troublesome Germans, who had proved such effective merchants that the stronger wine they traded could now be bought at a price equivalent to local ales, causing outrageous drunkenness among townsfolk.

From gods stealing blood-mead from their giant enemies, to warrior chieftains feasting, toasting and oath making in their great halls, Norse society was intertwined with alcohol.

From gods stealing blood-mead from their giant enemies, to warrior chieftains feasting, toasting and oath making in their great halls, Norse society was intertwined with alcohol, often with a rich societal meaning. Yet this seriousness wasn’t the only way drinking was done; in fact, a range of less formal and honourable drinking methods exist in the form of Norse drinking games.

Many sagas tell of drinking competitions, including those taking place between guests at feasts in the game of *mannjafnaor*. The game was essentially a bragging match in which men and sometimes women pitted their wits against each other to rank themselves against the rest. Often tasked with debating who was the greater warrior, based on their athleticism or attractiveness or their preeminence in a given district or hall, debates were quarrelsome and raucous. Such preening could quickly turn sour and descend into another drinking game called *senna,* a form of one-on-one competitive insulting before a crowd, often done in exaggerated poetic verse, with horns of ale drunk between verses which turned this rap battle into a drinking match, as the wit of insult and the strength of stomach were tested before the halls. items.body:
# Reform der Geheimdienste: Darf das Gespräch beim Psychotherapeuten abgehört werden?

## Reform der Nachrichtendienste : Dürfen Geheimdienste Therapiegespräche abhören?

Nachrichtendienste bekommen mehr Befugnisse: Das betrifft auch Jour­na­lis­t:in­nen und Psychotherapeut:innen. Was sich für diese jetzt ändern könnte.

23.11.2026

7:04 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Die Nachrichtendienste können bald große Datenmengen speichern, Hackerangriffe starten und auf IT-Systeme zugreifen Foto: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa

Von

Nachrichtendienste in Deutschland dürfen bald viel mehr. Das ist das Ergebnis der Reform des Nachrichtendienstrechts und besorgt insbesondere Berufe, deren Arbeit auf Vertraulichkeit beruht. Jour­na­lis­t:in­nen und Psy­cho­the­ra­peu­t:in­nen sorgen sich um den Schutz ihrer In­for­man­t:in­nen und Klient:innen.

Der Bundestag hat die Reform am 13. November beschlossen. Demnach sollen der Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) im Ausland und der Bundesverfassungsschutz (BfV) im Inland mehr Befugnisse erhalten. So dürfen sie im digitalen Raum künftig nicht mehr nur Daten sammeln, sondern auch Informationen speichern und aktiv in IT-Systeme eingreifen. CDU/CSU und SPD stimmten für die Reform, AfD und Linke dagegen. Die Grünen enthielten sich. Am 18. Dezember wird über die Reform abschließend im Bundesrat beraten.

Jour­na­lis­t:in­nen sehen ihre In­for­man­t:in­nen durch die erweiterten Befugnisse von BND und BfV nicht mehr ausreichend geschützt. Bereits im Oktober forderte ein Bündnis unter anderem aus ZDF, ARD und Reporter ohne Grenzen, dass deutsche Sicherheitsinteressen gegenüber dem Redaktionsgeheimnis und dem Quellenschutz nicht pauschal überwiegen dürften. An der Kritik habe sich auch nach der beschlossenen Reform nichts geändert, sagte der Deutsche Journalisten-Verband der taz. Weiter könnten durch die geplante automatisierte Datenanalyse potenzielle Whistleblower als gefährlich eingestuft werden. Ein mangelnder Rechtsschutz bei Hackerangriffen der Nachrichtendienste auf Jour­na­lis­t:in­nen sowie die Datenmasse, die der BND monatelang speichern dürfe, gefährdeten außerdem die Pressefreiheit.

Es sei zusätzlich unklar, wann der Verfassungsschutz Jour­na­lis­t:in­nen und ihre Kontakte beobachten dürfe. Der Geschäftsführer von Reporter ohne Grenzen, Christian Mihr, teilte mit, dass man sich eine Klage vor dem Bundesverfassungsgericht vorbehalte. Zwar müssen die Maßnahmen gegen Jour­na­lis­t:in­nen und ihre Quellen durch BND und BfV vorab durch den Unabhängigen Kontrollrat genehmigt werden. Es fehle aber an Durchsetzungsfähigkeit, damit seien Jour­na­lis­t:in­nen und ihre Quellen bei sensiblen Recherchen nicht ausreichend geschützt, sagte Mihr. Für den BfV gilt die Vorabkontrolle einiger Maßnahmen zudem erst ab Ende 2027.

## Keine Wanze im Behandlungszimmer

Weniger dramatisch als zuvor angenommen sieht es bei den Psy­cho­the­ra­peu­t:in­nen aus . Anfangs war die Sorge unter Pa­ti­en­t:in­nen groß, Geheimdienste könnten therapeutische Gespräche abhören. Das dürfen sie nach der beschlossenen Reform nicht. Das therapeutische Gespräch ist so besonders geschützt. Notwendige Änderungen seien nach den parlamentarischen Debatten größtenteils umgesetzt, schreibt die Bundespsychotherapeutenkammer in einer Pressemitteilung.

Etwas unklarer ist der Fall für Telefonate zur Terminvereinbarung oder wie mit Inhalten aus der elektronischen Patientenakte umgegangen wird. Während im BND-Gesetz auch diese Bereiche geschützt sind, fehlt ein vollumfänglicher Schutz dazu im Bundesverfassungsschutzgesetz. Der Verfassungsschutz darf hier zum Beispiel Daten abgreifen, allerdings nur in Ausnahmefällen. Ein solcher wäre gegeben, wenn Psy­cho­the­ra­peu­t:in­nen selbst im Fokus der Ermittlungen stehen oder der Verfassungsschutz von einer Bedrohungslage ausgeht. Dem muss jedoch – und das ist neu – der Unabhängige Kontrollrat zustimmen.

Trotzdem bleibt offen, wie zum Beispiel mit dokumentierten Behandlungsinhalten umgegangen wird, sollte der Nachrichtendienst im Rahmen seiner Ermittlungen Zugriff auf sie erlangen. Eigentlich fallen auch diese unter die Vertraulichkeitsbeziehung zwischen The­ra­peu­t:in­nen und Pa­ti­en­t:in­nen und sie dürften theoretisch nicht verwendet werden.

Die Bundespsychotherapeutenkammer fordert, den Schutzstatus bei beiden Nachrichtendiensten anzugleichen. „Es ist nicht nachvollziehbar, warum das Vertrauensverhältnis zwischen Psy­cho­the­ra­peu­t:in­nen und ihren Pa­ti­en­t:in­nen beim Bundesnachrichtendienst stärker geschützt wird als beim Verfassungsschutz“, sagte Andrea Benecke, die Präsidentin der Kammer.

items.title: People who just won tough races should try to win again — and hold Trump accountable
items.subtitle: Josh Turek campaigns in Iowa on November 1, 2026.

items.body:
The sheer scale of the 2026 blue wave — an anti-MAGA swing large enough to carry Democrats in places like Mississippi and South Carolina — poses a question of democratic theory that I think is a lot more interesting than the tired empirical debates about moderation. What should a person who won somewhere they “shouldn’t” have do with their term (or terms) in office, knowing that it’s objectively unlikely that the terrain will be as favorable in future cycles?

My perception is that most mainstream Democrats adhere to an ethic I would call Pragmatic Progmaxxing.

They understand that [Ayanna Pressley tweeting about reparations](https://x.com/RepPressley/status/2122109986306195477) is bad politics, that politicians like Josh Turek and James Talarico are going to have to stay away from 100-proof left-wing politics, and that even Abdul El-Sayed needs to do some picayune localism related to the auto industry. But their basic orientation is as [intense policy demanders](https://read.dukeupress.edu/jhppl/article/43/2/271/133583/How-Intense-Policy-Demanders-Shape-Postreform) who are trying to maximize the amount of progressive change by pushing elected officials to be as left-wing as they can possibly get away with.

Pragmatic Progmaxxing has especially interesting implications for the people who won the real reach seats. From a Progmaxxing point of view, you accept a certain amount of moderation from Sherrod Brown and Roy Cooper so they can win re-election. But Scott Colom needed a D+13 national political climate *and* an amateur hour opponent to barely win, so he should just give up and vote like Ed Markey. It’s basically a free Senate seat for six years.

I want to push back against this.

I think American democracy has been in a really dangerous place for the past 10 years. That’s proximately due to Donald Trump and the MAGA movement. But the intense policy demanders have been creating an underlying structural weakness by framing thumbing your nose at your constituents as noble and trying to be a loyal servant of the people as cowardly.

I would like to see Colom and Annie Andrews and the couple dozen House Democrats who won deep red seats make a good-faith effort to represent their constituents. That doesn’t mean they answer every policy question with a poll of public opinion in Mississippi. But it does mean they have to take seriously the question of whether a particular piece of legislation aligns with what their constituents are asking for. Because it’s not “brave” or “fearless” to ignore the public will in order to curry favor with your side’s interest groups. That pattern of behavior has made voters cynical about the democratic process, eroded faith in party politics, and given us the bad phenomenon of “safe seats” where the incumbents barely even care what’s happening.

To the extent that newly elected members run big political risks, I hope they look into their own hearts about what motivated them to run for office as Democrats at a time when large swaths of the business community were deciding to bandwagon with the MAGA movement. My guess is that in most cases, the Democrats who ran in 2026 were both aware that the “save our democracy” messaging of 2024 was not persuasive and also (rightly) believed in the merits of that messaging.

If I’m right about that, I think the best way to behave consistent with that ethic is to:

- Fight for democracy by being willing to take risks to hold Trump and his cronies accountable for violations of the law.
- Practice democracy by acting as if you care more about the policy views and interests of the voters in your constituency than the views and interests of ideological donors and the groups.

My fear is that in practice the opposite combination is more likely. The Democratic base is in some sense very fired up about the issues in bucket (1). But in terms of [concrete political power](https://www.slowboring.com/p/from-the-veal-pen-to-the-groups) — campaign dollars and the endorsements that can win you primaries — it’s all about the greens and the labor unions and the civil rights orgs and the child care advocates and the immigration lawyers.

If you feel that you need to break with party leadership on something, the thing you’re most likely to get latitude on is Trump accountability. This is more or less “how things work” in the modern era of American political parties — they demand a lot of party loyalty on votes about policy ideas — but it’s terrible for the country.

#### The nobility of winning

In his [classic 1974 book “Congress: The Electoral Connection,”](https://politicalscience.yale.edu/publications/congress-electoral-connection) David Mayhew says we should understand members of Congress as single-minded seekers of re-election.

In a world where that’s broadly true, it’s also true that when a member of Congress deviates from the rule, that’s usually driven by courage and prescience. All of your colleagues are looking at the Voting Rights Act through the narrow lens of re-election, but you decide that the most important thing is whether you can tell your granddaughter that you did the right thing, so you vote yes. Maybe you lose in 1966, maybe you don’t. But either way, it’s the right thing to do.

It’s important to understand, though, that a lot has changed since then. American political parties used to be basically patronage operations whose business model was winning elections so they could hand out jobs and contracts. Around the time that Mayhew wrote his book, these old patronage parties were dissolving in the face of amateur political activists who were rapidly forming professionalized issue-advocacy groups.

Those groups have now formed into quasi-stable coalitions that are aligned with and finance the political parties. The business model now is to deliver wins for intense policy demanders. And to accomplish that, you do need to win power sometimes — it’s Pragmatic Progmaxxing, not doctrinaire left-wing politics — but that’s quite different from Mayhew’s singular focus on winning.

Similarly, just being a member of Congress has become a significantly less elite job even as high-end income inequality has exploded. I wouldn’t say anyone is deliberately losing elections just for the pay raise, but it’s objectively true that going down in defeat and then becoming a media personality or a senior fellow at the Center for Pragmatic Progmaxxing is going to mean your living standards go up rather than down.

In this post-Mayhew universe, it’s of course still possible for a member to risk their re-election prospects for the sake of a transcendent moral cause.

But we don’t actually have any issues that are as titanically significant as civil rights. And I would say a much more typical case is a situation like the 2025 Congressional Review Act vote to disallow the state of California from imposing a de facto ban on internal combustion engine cars.

…

items.body:
Olivia Gavoyannis at *Engelsberg Ideas*:

Alfred and Alma Hitchcock. Credit: Allstar Picture Library Limited

In November 1938, [The Lady Vanishes](https://theartsstl.com/criterion-backlist-the-lady-vanishes-1938-nr/) was released in America to critical acclaim. The film, which centres on the mystery of a woman who seemingly disappears into thin air during a train ride through Europe, cemented Alfred Hitchcock’s status as the master of suspense.

As the critic Peter Bradshaw noted in [a five-star review](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2008/jan/11/romance.thriller) when the film was re-released to mark its 70th anniversary: ‘Master chef Alfred Hitchcock brought together the ingredients of mystery, comedy and suspense with sublime ease in this prewar classic. In fact, he invented the dish.’ But if Hitchcock invented it, his wife Alma Reville was the sous chef.

Alma Lucy Reville was born on 14 August 1899, just one day after Hitchcock, but she started her film career some time in advance of her future husband. Aged 16, Reville secured a ‘cutting’ position at Twickenham Studios in London where her father worked in the costume department, and she honed her craft splicing together film by hand. This process of re-ordering large quantities of footage was seen as a manual task akin to sewing, so it was largely given to young women like Reville with little or no experience.

More [↗ engelsbergideas.com](https://engelsbergideas.com/notebook/hitchcocks-secret-weapon-alma-reville/).

items.body:
For poet Chase Twichell, Zen practice and writing have long been deeply intertwined. “Zen is said to be a ‘mind-to-mind transmission,’” she told the [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/chase-twichell). “The best poems are exactly that: They leap from one mind to another without stopping to explain exactly how they did it.... In our culture, out of necessity, we’re used to living in a mostly literal mind, and poetry demands that we enter it with another kind of mind.”

Her latest collection, [The World It Was](https://www.coppercanyonpress.org/books/the-world-it-was-by-chase-twichell/), offers one such opportunity to access another kind of mind—one carefully attuned to grief, transience, and environmental destruction. Composed in the wake of the Covid pandemic, the collection consists of restrained, nearly skeletal elegies—for her late husband, for her aging body, and for the Earth itself—that look directly at suffering and ask how to live in the face of seemingly all-pervasive loss (or, as the book’s description states, “being fully alive inside the brief body and the dying world”).

Though this question is of course unanswerable, the poetic worlds that Twichell builds suggest that [attention](https://tricycle.org/magazine/attention-means-attention/) plays a key role in figuring out a way forward. “Zen and poetry have both taught me that the quality of attention we pay to the world is crucial,” Twichell[said in a 2016 interview](https://ashberyland.com/2016/11/19/poetry-and-life-an-interview-with-chase-twitchell/). “Of course there are many ways to make people see the damage we’ve done, and poetry is only one of them. But to me, it’s the arrow that most deeply pierces my consciousness.” *The World It Was* presents sixty-seven such arrows: invitations to embody a different kind of mind, and, in the process, relearn what it means to exist fully in a world defined by impermanence.

*–Sarah Fleming, senior editor*

## The World It Was

I was a kid transfixed by

the endlessly mutating

gloomy rooms among the trees,

and I wandered far.

At seventeen, I married thunder

and wind and snow. I took vows.

I pledged to be only half human,

so only half guilty of our crimes

against Earth and all its beings.

Wherever I am, I visit Earth’s memorial.

Sometimes I leave a few words

in the dirt on a car.

The memorial surrounds us.

Earth’s body is also its grave.

## Death’s Hors d’Oeuvres

A school of dead gray fish drifts

across my vision—floaters.

No names come when I call.

Is this what old age will be like?

No, this is old age now.

I like to take little sips of the horror,

morsels of poisoned meat,

each taste a foretaste.

I’m preparing for future pain,

not this pain.

That’s the lie I tell myself.

## I Can’t Make Sense of It

In one of these many centuries,

my words fell briefly through the air.

A flurry, among many flurries.

I can’t make sense of it:

the word-bearing trees

grew older, bore less and less fruit.

Birds carrying the twigs of poems

still fly in from time to time

but they don’t nest here anymore.

## Flower of False Starts

It’s a strange flower,

the flower of false starts.

I dress in its withered petals.

Each knob on the stem

is the scar of a flower

that never fully bloomed.

Or it bloomed, but the flower

was not the flower I dreamed.

It’s almost all stem now.

Withered petals—pretty dress.

The flower is nearing

the end of its life.

Each poem leaves a scar.

## Solitaire

When Russell was dying

I sat beside his bed

playing solitaire on my phone,

practicing his not being there.

I liked the way the cards came

in quick cold cascades of numbers,

clusters of luck,

and I could visit that bright flow

day or night.

I liked the way the game was

always starting over, always

not quite daybreak on the screen,

the longest time until dark.

♦

*“The World It Was,” “Death’s Hors d’Oeuvres,” “I Can’t Make Sense of It,” “Flower of False Starts,” and “Solitaire” from* [The World It Was](https://www.coppercanyonpress.org/books/the-world-it-was-by-chase-twichell/) *, copyright 2026 by Chase Twichell, used by permission of Copper Canyon Press.*

items.body:
*This is today’s edition of* [The Download](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/briefing-the-download/?_ga=2.179569122.736533416.1649661040-405833893.1649413289), *our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.*

### The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some capabilities are improving exponentially—but models aren’t as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report updates METR’s [widely shared time horizon plot](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/02/05/1132254/this-is-the-most-misunderstood-graph-in-ai/), which tested models on a large suite of tasks. The new version adds more open-ended tasks, such as designing AI evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments.

Models struggled with these tasks, which could prove crucial to automating research and development.

[Find out where AI progress is running into tougher challenges](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/20/1149399/the-most-misunderstood-graph-in-ai-just-got-a-major-update/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*).

*—Grace Huckins*

### Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

Google, Microsoft, and others are investing hundreds of millions of dollars in startups spreading crushed rock across farms to capture carbon from the air.

The approach, known as enhanced rock weathering, could also improve soil quality and boost crop yields.

But new research raises serious questions about how much material can be added to farmland before it starts reducing yields, *MIT Technology Review* can exclusively report. The findings suggest the carbon removal potential could be far smaller than previously estimated.

[Here’s why major concerns are emerging about enhanced rock weathering](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/23/1149392/why-using-rocks-for-carbon-removal-could-eventually-reduce-crop-growth/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*).

*—James Temple*

**The must-reads**

*I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.*

**1 AI may have cracked math’s greatest unsolved problem** Anthropic’s Claude was used to prove the Riemann hypothesis. ([WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/anthropic-mathematician-says-claude-has-solved-the-most-famous-problem-in-math-9361920b) $)
*+ Two groups have independently verified the proof.* ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/21/anthropic-riemann-hypothesis-solved-claude-ai))
*+ It could be the biggest math breakthrough in decades.* ([New Scientist](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2600235-mathematicians-are-amazed-by-holy-grail-proof-of-riemann-hypothesis/?utm_campaign=RSS%7CNSNS&utm_content=home&utm_medium=RSS&utm_source=NSNS) $)
*+ AI may be changing who gets to do math.* ([MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/09/08/1143747/what-openais-latest-controversy-tells-us-about-the-future-of-math/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*))

**2 The COP31 climate talks have collapsed after a fossil fuels row**
The EU rejected a deal it called “greenwashing.” ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/science/climate-change/cop31-climate-talks-break-angry-dispute-fossil-fuels-rcna610656))
*+ Saudi Arabia, Russia, and India opposed mentioning fossil fuels.* ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cqwy06zrd26lo))
*+ Calls are growing for “net negative” instead of just net zero.* ([Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03789-3))
*+ Last year’s talks avoided fossil fuels.* ([MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2025/11/27/1128443/climate-talks-fossil-fuels/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*))

**3 The woman at the center of Nvidia’s scandal has ties to China’s military** Firms in her family’s network work with Chinese defense contractors. ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/us/politics/nvidia-alice-huang-chips-china.html) $)
*+ Her associate allegedly ran the chip smuggling behind the scenes. (* [WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/tech/li-ming-megaspeed-nvidia-chips-china-6260d836?mod=rss_Technology) $)
*+ US intelligence says she was in touch with a Chinese spy official.* ([ABC](https://abcnews.com/US/woman-center-nvidia-scandal-touch-chinas-top-spy/story?id=138369034))
*+ Republicans are pushing a new AI strategy to counter Beijing.* ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/after-trumps-china-trip-us-house-republicans-push-ai-strategy-counter-beijing-2026-11-20/) $)

**4 Hackers have breached the FBI’s criminal information database**
It contains information used by law enforcement at all levels. ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/fbi-database-ncic-hack-d066cff87a64a564db0a00172c124972))
*+ Hackers also breached an Agriculture Department system.* ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/national-security/agriculture-department-breached-hackers-sources-say-rcna610497))
*+ And the Austrian foreign ministry’s website.* ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/technology/austrian-foreign-ministry-says-its-website-was-hacked-staff-details-viewed-2026-11-20/) $)

**5 Russia, the US, and Israel have stalled global rules on “killer robots”**
The UK, Japan, South Korea, and Turkey also resisted binding rules. ([Politico](https://www.politico.eu/article/effort-regulate-killer-robots-delayed-until-2028-ai-un/))
*+ Around 100 nations backed regulations, but arms producers balked. (* [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/21/countries-agree-to-un-talks-aiming-to-regulate-killer-robots-by-2028.html))
*+ Talks will continue through 2028.* ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/un-drones-robots-un-lethal-ai-weapons-ebe057d2a47cde53100970c8f648e7fa))

**6 Trump says he’ll ban US companies from building data centers abroad** He threatened them with a “tremendous tax.” ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/20/trump-data-centers-ai-companies-tax.html))
*+ Electricity is fuelling the data center backlash.* ([MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/09/1148194/the-backlash-about-data-centers-might-really-just-be-about-electricity/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*))

**7 US lawmakers are nearing a deal to ban Chinese cars** They plan to prohibit sales of Chinese vehicles in the US. ([Quartz](https://qz.com/us-lawmakers-deal-ban-chinese-cars-mercedes-112026))

items.body:
It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon.

To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in [simulated moon dust](https://www.space.com/the-universe/moon/moon-dust-may-help-astronauts-power-sustainable-lunar-cities-heres-how) with promising results. The researchers [published](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41526-026-00668-z) their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal.

"We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in [a statement](https://news.oregonstate.edu/news/study-finds-potatoes-grown-simulated-lunar-soil-match-earth-grown-performance). "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon."

To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to [regolith](https://www.space.com/19582-moon-composition.html), the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. [The moon](https://www.space.com/55-earths-moon-formation-composition-and-orbit.html) contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions.

The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil.

Oregon State University researchers David Handy and Aymeric Goyer studying potatoes grown in lunar regolith. (Image credit: Aymeric Goyer/David Handy/OSU)

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement.

The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth.

NASA funding supported this research.

items.body:
A commuter riding the Metro in Washington, D.C., snapped photos of a man working on a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” Obtained by ProPublica

Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

### Do You Have a Tip for ProPublica?

If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.

Send Us a Tip

The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s departure as head of the Smithsonian, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

Three Smithsonian museums, dedicated to African American history, American history, and natural history, seen from the Washington Monument Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

As [recounted by ProPublica in September](https://www.propublica.org/article/how-smithsonian-museum-american-history-became-target-trump-culture-war), the American history museum has faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in 2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-reckoning.

The White House report emphasized that the museum should not whitewash blights on the nation’s history such as slavery and Jim Crow, but argued that it was failing to give visitors any sense of how it developed into the country that it is. “It should tell the whole story of a nation,” the report stated, “including the good and the bad, so Museum visitors can understand the development that led our nation to where it is today.”

…

items.body:
The place where the village of Nunapitchuk remembers its dead is disappearing.

Vincent Wassilie remembers pointing it out to his adult nephew while bringing memorial flowers to their relatives’ graves, which sit on a cemetery hill overlooking the Indigenous Alaskan village.

“Look at that,” he recalled saying. “We used to play on it.”

Wassilie’s nephew looked over and did a double take. The hill beneath the graves, which the two men remembered towering over the surrounding tundra, had sunk by what they estimated to be nearly 10 feet since they were children.

In fact, almost all of Nunapitchuk’s [roughly 7 square miles](https://data.census.gov/profile/Nunapitchuk_city,_Alaska?g=160XX00US0256680) of land is sinking. ** ** Government records and scientific assessments obtained by The Intercept via a Freedom of Information Act request reveal sinking homes, damaged infrastructure, thawing permafrost, and growing flood risks across the village of approximately 620 Alaska Native Yup’ik people. One federal analysis found that almost the entire village could be inundated during a 100-year flood under projections for 2030 to 2050.

The federal government has been aware of this for almost a decade. The documents show that tribal leaders have spent years navigating proposed studies, unimplemented scopes of work, and funding constraints. They aren’t asking the government to somehow fortify their land or stop the thaw of permafrost. They just want its help to pick up the village and move it about a mile uphill, where higher ground would keep residents safer from increased risks of flooding and erosion.

“Every spring, my parents’ house turns into an island,” said Tia Tobeluk, who grew up in the village and has since moved to Utah. Tobeluk, now 25, started noticing the devastating effects of climate change when she was 14 or 15, and she remembers moving her parents’ fish racks, traditionally used to smoke and preserve wild-caught fish, up to higher ground.

Left/Top: Homes line the banks of the Johnson River in August 2025. Right/Bottom: Nunapitchuk’s public safety building sinks into the Johnson River as sandbags are used to hold back the water, seen in August 2025.
Photos: Sheryl Musgrove

Nunapitchuk tribal leaders formally warned the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers that the community was “highly vulnerable to environmental hazards” and “may not be habitable in the future” in 2018. They asked the Corps to help identify a safer place for the village and determine whether it could withstand future flooding, erosion, and thawing permafrost. But the village faced an obstacle from the beginning: Nunapitchuk was considered economically distressed, and the Army Corps imposes cost-sharing requirements that the village could not afford.

The Corps produced no records showing it conducted any relocation planning in response to the tribe’s 2018 request, suggesting that the federal entity did nothing. The request was the start of a maddening multi-agency pursuit that has forced tribal leaders to repeatedly ask for help, search for funding, and wait on federal studies and proposed plans, even after selecting where they want to move and documenting why the new site is safer.

Part of the problem is that there’s no single agency responsible for relocating a threatened village like Nunapitchuk. For all its issues, the Federal Emergency Management Agency at least has a clear mandate to help communities rebuild after disaster strikes. In the case of climate relocation, there’s a patchwork of more than 20 federal agencies that could have some role, according to previous reporting by [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/nov/03/alaska-nunapitchuk-climate-melting-permafrost), including the Army Corps, FEMA, Bureau of Indian Affairs, Department of Housing and Urban Development, and Denali Commission. The Government Accountability Office has repeatedly recommended that the federal government establish clearer leadership for communities facing climate-driven relocation.

“It’s up to the tribe to kind of bring together all these different resources to try and get relocated,” said Sheryl Musgrove, until recently the climate justice director at the Alaska Institute for Justice. “There’s no central funding source.”

Nunapitchuk’s isolation compounds those challenges. The village is inaccessible by road, and reaching it requires air travel into remote western Alaska. There are days when changing conditions make travel difficult even within the village, keeping children from safely crossing the Johnson River to school and complicating residents’ access to the airport during medical emergencies. Hundreds of miles away, in Alaska’s larger tourist destinations, museums and souvenir shops market the state’s proud Alaska Native culture.

“You’re talking about Alaska Native tribes that have subsisted on these lands for thousands of years,” Musgrove said. “To say that we can’t afford to help them is wrong. The federal government has a trust responsibility to them to protect them and their lands. And the federal government isn’t doing that.”

[Related Trump Sacrifices Alaska Wilderness to Help AI Companies](https://theintercept.com/2025/10/08/trump-ai-alaska-national-park-ambler-road/)

Nunapitchuk is not alone. The Guardian, citing a 2020 Bureau of Indian Affairs report, noted that [144 Alaska Native villages face potential relocation](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/nov/03/alaska-nunapitchuk-climate-melting-permafrost) because of infrastructure damage associated with the changing climate. Estimates placed the cost of relocating Nunapitchuk alone at approximately $230 million.

Wassilie wonders whether the federal government will act before the village experiences the kind of disaster residents are trying to avoid.

“Maybe they’re waiting for something catastrophic to happen before they do anything,” Wassilie said.

The Johnson River splits Nunapitchuk between its west side and its east, or “main,” side, where the village’s school and businesses are located. Historically, winter transformed the river into a route between the two sides once the ice became thick enough to bear a person’s weight.

Older generations, including his mother, remember it freezing quickly every winter, Wassilie said. Sometimes, a single cold Arctic night was enough for the river to become safe to walk across.

“Nowadays, it takes a week or more, depending on how the weather is going,” Wassilie said. Often, the river thaws again quickly after the freeze. “During spring and fall, kids miss school due to unsafe river conditions when it’s freezing up.”

In one instance, a resident needed urgent medical attention while the Johnson River was unsafe to cross. The village’s airport sits beyond the river on the west side, leaving residents to improvise a way to get the patient across.

…
