items.body:
AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions (eg [ForecastBench](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity), the [Metaculus Cup](https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/16/artificial-intelligence-now-beats-some-of-the-best-human-forecasters)).

These are usually specialized AIs with forecasting harnesses, created by forecasting startups (eg [FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/), [Mantic](https://mantic.com/), [Preseen](https://preseen.com/)), but foundation models like ChatGPT and Claude are only about six months behind the specialized models, so by the end of the year they’ll match top humans too.

In the past, the options for getting top-human-level forecasts were slim and inconvenient. You could hire a team of superforecasters to work on the problem, but this would cost thousands of dollars and take weeks. Or you could check prediction markets (or Metaculus), but they only have a small sample of general-interest questions and are constantly trying to screw you over by gaming resolution criteria.

The rise of AI forecasters solves these problems more cleanly and comprehensively than almost anyone thought possible just a year ago. The “science of forecasting”, which only recently felt like trying to pick the least-bad of various bad options, now faces tasks more like “what kind of magnifying glass should we use to inspect our giant novelty lottery check as we confirm that it’s real?” and “how do we spend our winnings?”

Specifically: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. We need to learn how this success decays as we move to different types of non-traditional forecasting questions.

I recently got to talk to some people at the [Forecasting Research Institute](https://forecastingresearch.org/), one of the leaders in this field. Here’s my impression of the remaining challenges:

**1: Can AI do conditional forecasts?**

A traditional forecasting question asks something like: will the Democrats win the next election?

A conditional forecasting question is more like: *if* the Democrats win the next election, how will that affect the chances of a stock market crash?

Conditional forecasting questions are more exciting than traditional ones because they directly speak to policy outcomes. If we defund the police, how will that affect crime rates (compared to the counterfactual where we hold police funding constant)? If we mandate COVID vaccinations, how will that affect COVID mortality and myocarditis mortality (compared to the counterfactual where vaccines are voluntary / banned)?

Prediction markets have been slow to experiment with these, partly because of annoying logistical issues (you have to refund people’s money if the condition doesn’t come true) and partly because they entice fewer customers than new forms of degenerate sports gambling. AI forecasters don’t have this problem; you can ask an AI forecaster any of those questions above right now, and the big companies ([FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/docs/forecast-conditional-scenarios/), [Preseen](https://blog.preseen.com/p/predicting-science-and-technology), [Mantic](https://blog.mantic.com/p/friday-forecasts-2)) have it as an explicit feature.

What remains is to prove that AI forecasters’ great performance on traditional questions carries over to conditional questions. About a year ago, FRI tested this and found that it didn’t - the AIs of the time did significantly worse on conditional questions. It seemed like some kind of weird misunderstanding where the AI didn’t entirely understand the concept.

Will this flip like a switch? At some point, the AI is smart enough to fully grasp conditionals, and it becomes exactly as good at conditional forecasting as the regular type? The experts I talked to thought no - as it gets smarter, its conditional forecasting ability will improve gradually. Where is it now? The experts weren’t willing to hazard a guess on whether it was better or worse than the average smart human, although they did think it was still worse than top superforecasters. They’re working on a benchmarking experiment that should give us a better measure of this in a few months.

**2: Can AI do truly causal forecasts?**

There’s a known flaw in standard conditional forecasting. When we ask “if the Democrats win the next election, will the economy go down?”, what we really want to know is a causal question - does voting for Democrats hurt the economy?

But that’s not what we asked. Suppose we’re wondering this in 2025, so we ask “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” But maybe the Democrats will win in 2026 because there’s a already a bad economy (eg the Republican president implements tariffs and declares war on Iran, raising prices and making him historically unpopular), and then that bad economy continues into 2027. So the answer to the question “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” is yes, but we still don’t know whether voting for Democrats in 2026 is good or bad for the economy.

Prediction markets can’t answer this question, because they can only be used to predict observable events that let us give payouts to successful gamblers. Might AI superforecasters succeed where the markets fail? Could you just prompt them with “please answer the unobservable causal question, instead of the easily-resolved conditional one”?

The experts I talked to weren’t excited about that particular prompt, but they did point out that a causal forecast is basically a combination of conditional forecasts. That is, if your original conditional forecast implicitly considered the four different combinations of two variables - that is:

- p(Democrats win & economy good)
- p(Democrats win & economy bad)
- p(Republicans win & economy good)
- p(Republicans win & economy bad)

…then things like “the previous economy was good” or “we’re at war with Iran” are just more variables you can add to the stew. It would be crazy to ask humans to forecast 2^10 branches so you could combine ten variables, but for AIs that could just mean a bit higher API spend. If you capture enough relevant variables in your “conditional” forecast, and find that the economy is still worse when the only one you’ve changed is whether or not the Democrats win, that’s a causal forecast. At least one company already tries something like this, though there are no studies of how well it works.

items.body: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is associated with persistent brain dysfunction, but the molecular basis of its regional functional abnormalities remains unclear. We combined resting-state functional MRI with normative gene-expression data from healthy donors in the Allen Human Brain Atlas data to identify transcriptional patterns associated with altered spontaneous brain activity in PHN. Fifty patients with PHN and 26 healthy controls were included. Patients showed increased fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations in the left cuneus. Across the left cortex, the spatial pattern of case–control differences was significantly associated with normative gene-expression architecture and survived spatial permutation testing. The contributing genes were enriched in synaptic signaling, ion-channel regulation, axonal transport, and neural-plasticity-related processes, with preferential expression in sensory, limbic, hypothalamic, and thalamic systems. These preliminary findings suggest a spatial correspondence between PHN-related functional alterations and normative cortical transcriptional organization, generating hypotheses for future investigation rather than demonstrating disease-related gene-expression changes.

items.body:
I don’t remember the last desktop Macintosh I used as my full-time computer — probably whatever Mac was at my desk at the weekly newspaper I worked at in 1994. (A Macintosh Classic II, maybe? Sure. Let’s go with that.) When it came time to buy a computer of my own, I selected a PowerBook with my college graduation money, figuring my career path as a roving reporter would benefit from having a machine that could go with me. And it’s been a series of laptops ever since then, from iBooks to MacBook Pros to MacBook Airs.

The point is, after I opened the very large box Jason had dropped off at my front door and sat down to put [Apple’s new M6 iMac](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/10/apple-clears-the-decks-ahead-of-its-biggest-announcement) through its paces, it was the first time in a long time that I’ve used a desktop Mac for more than just a brief period. A big display, a beefy processor and all the ports I could ever want before having to plug into hubs and dongles — a fellow could get used to living like this.

That said, as much as I’ve enjoyed my time with the iMac, I’m not about to abandon the freedom of mobile computing in exchange for the power boost that comes from a more sedentary lifestyle. But for anyone more committed to desktops over laptops, there’s a lot to like about Apple’s latest iMac, especially if you’ve gone a few years in between upgrades.

[Apple’s previous iMac](https://sixcolors.com/post/2024/11/m4-imac-review-gloriously-niche/), an M4-powered all-in-one, came out two years ago, and you’re not going to spot many differences between that version and the latest model. Even owners of [2023’s M3 iMac](https://sixcolors.com/post/2023/11/m3-imac-review-keep-playing-the-hits/) aren’t likely to be moved by this latest edition.

But if you’re making do with an iMac powered by an M1 chip — or, heaven forfend, a model that predates the move to Apple Silicon — the M6 iMac promises to be a significant upgrade over what you have. And the M6 processor running the show is a big reason why.

## All about the M6

If I had the space on my desk to accommodate both an M6 iMac and the M4 iMac it replaces in Apple’s lineup, I wouldn’t be able to spot any surface changes. Like its predecessor, the M6 iMac offers a 24-inch Retina display with 4.5K resolution. The display still promises 500 nits of brightness, and the 21.5-by-18.1-inch frame and 5.8-inch-deep stand go unchanged. Apple’s even offering the same seven color options as before, with my review unit coming in a fetching purple.

The big changes come under the hood in the form of that M6 processor, which offers [a new mix of cores and two Neural Engines](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/08/apple-unveils-m6-m5-ultra-chips-and-updates-its-desktop-macs/), providing tangible boosts over the M4.

Like I said, though, M4 iMac owners are unlikely to be eyeballing the new machine with envy, especially since Apple upped the base price on the iMac by $200 to $1,499 back in June, and that price is maintained by the new M6 model.

## M6 iMac performance notes

To that end, Apple’s promising a 5x improvement in AI workflows from the M4 iMac, courtesy of those Neural Engines. Obviously, anyone moving from an Intel-based Mac can expect a dramatic increase in performance, and early-generation Apple silicon Mac users will also see solid benefits. I don’t have any comparable all-in-ones lying around my house, but I do own an M3 MacBook Air equipped with 8GB of RAM, and the M6 iMac with 16GB of RAM that I’m testing smokes that laptop, as you might expect.

Specifically, when I ran Geekbench 7 on both machines, the M6 iMac posted single and multicore scores of 3,967 and 21,078, respectively. Those results beat the comparable numbers posted by my MacBook Air by 39% and 87%. Likewise, the M6 iMac’s GPU score was just about 4x better than what the laptop could put out.

To put that in real-world terms, the M6 chip powering the latest iMac is perfectly capable of handling whatever you want to throw at it. You can also expect smooth, detailed graphics when you’re playing games.

That processing muscle also comes into play when you’re handling tasks like editing photos, which was a breeze for me on the M6 iMac. Also helping matters is that display, which really calls out the subtle nuances of an image better than smaller screens, even my MacBook Air, as good as its 13-inch Liquid Retina display may be on its own.

After all, the entire idea behind the iMac is that it can satisfy people who want a desktop but don’t necessarily need the power (and price tag) that comes with a [Mac Studio](https://sixcolors.com/post/2025/03/m4-max-mac-studio-review-a-familiar-face/). That could include creative pros whose hardware budget tops out at around $2,000 as well as families who need a dependable machine that multiple people can turn to.

## The other iMac changes

The M6 is easily the most substantive change Apple made to this version of the iMac, but it’s not the only under-the-hood improvement. The M6 iMac also features Apple’s N1 chip, which supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. The M4 iMac’s wireless specs topped out at Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3.

Like Wi-Fi 6E, Wi-Fi 7 supports 6GHz, 5GHz and 2.4GHz bands, but with greater bandwidth and wider channels. It’s also capable of delivering faster wireless speeds, while support for Multi-Link Operation means your iMac can send and receive data across different bands. The end result is better, more efficient throughput.

Of course, for your M6 iMac to reap the full benefits of Wi-Fi 7, you’re going to need to connect to a Wi-Fi 7 router. Maybe you’ve recently upgraded your networking equipment to support the latest standards, maybe you haven’t. But even if it’s the latter, the M6 iMac’s support for the latest wireless connectivity standards means you’ve future-proofed your computer for your next purchase of a router or access point.

## Configuring your M6 iMac

As noted above, the M6 iMac starts at $1,499. That gets you a machine with a 10-core CPU and GPU chip along with two rear Thunderbolt ports, 16GB of memory and 256GB of storage.

That’s not the machine I tested. Instead, my review unit came with the 12-core M6 chip and four Thunderbolt ports. That also means a 2.5Gb Ethernet port is included on my iMac; for the two-port models, it’s a $30 add-on. My machine came configured with the standard 16GB of RAM, but storage space was upgraded to 512GB. As configured, that machine would set you back $1,899. If you maxed out the memory and storage while also adding nano-texture glass to reduce glare and reflections on the display, you could pay as much as $3,299 for your all-in-one Mac.

items.body:
### “This fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet.”

Perhaps the gravest violence we can do to ourselves is to live out our lives believing the world to be a fixity handed down to us by the authorities of history and life to be a matter of taking immutable givens. Daring to believe otherwise — to believe that even our smallest purposeful action alters the monolith of reality in some subtle, meaningful way — is an act of courage and resistance, an act of immense vulnerability to the possibility of disappointment, vulnerability the commonest cowering from which is cynicism.

James Baldwin knew this when he issued his lyrical and impassioned insistence that [“nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/05/21/nothing-is-fixed-james-baldwin-morley-music/) that [“we made the world we’re living in and we have to make it over.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/09/james-baldwin-freedom/)

Hannah Arendt knew this when she considered [how we invent ourselves and reinvent the world](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/17/hannah-arendt-human-condition-speech-action/), observing that “the smallest act in the most limited circumstances bears the seed of boundlessness, because one deed, and sometimes one word, suffices to change every constellation.”

Art by [Dorothy Lathrop](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/03/09/dorothy-lathrop-down-adown-derry/), 1922. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/art-by-dorothy-lathrop-for-down-adown-derry-by-walter-de-la-mare-19224642772_print?curator=brainpicker) and [as stationery cards](https://society6.com/product/art-by-dorothy-lathrop-for-down-adown-derry-by-walter-de-la-mare-19224642772_cards?curator=brainpicker).)

**Richard Powers** knew this when he made his contribution to [Take My Advice: Letters to the Next Generation from People Who Know a Thing or Two](http://www.amazon.com/Take-My-Advice-Letters-Generation/dp/1416578358/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/take-my-advice-letters-to-the-next-generation-from-people-who-know-a-thing-or-two/oclc/49322746&referer=brief_results)) — artist and writer James L. Harmon’s wonderful 2002 anthology of [wisdom from stellar minds](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/10/12/martha-nussbaum-take-my-advice/), a decade in the constellating, envisioned as an eclectic contemporary counterpart to Rilke’s timeless [Letters to a Young Poet](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/06/29/rilke-letters-to-a-young-poet-macy-barrows/), which had moved Harmon deeply when he first encountered it as a young man.

Two decades before Powers won the Pulitzer Prize for his sylvan symphony [The Overstory](https://www.amazon.com/Overstory-Novel-Richard-Powers/dp/039335668X/?tag=braipick-20), he echoes Seamus Heaney’s exhortation to [always remain “true to your own secret knowledge”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/01/19/seamus-heaney-commencement/) and writes:

> Never forget what you were born knowing. That this fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet. Buy the plot some time.

19th-century [Solar System quilt](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/12/06/ellen-harding-baker-solar-system-quilt/) by Ellen Harding Baker, embroidered over the course of seven years as a teaching tool in an era when women were barred from higher education in science and a fraction of the presently known Solar System objects were known. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/solar-system-quilt-by-ellen-harding-baker-1886_print?curator=brainpicker) and [a face mask](https://society6.com/brainpicker/collection/vintage-science-face-masks).)

We buy the plot time with the currency of our conscious choices, the grand and the mundane alike — the daily actions that make us what we are, the people who make the world what it is. Powers writes:

> Take in more, consume less, recycle everything; book-keep all hidden costs; find out where you have been set down; lobby for a smaller market; get rid of your car and travel as widely as you can (yeah, walk: what the hell); try to say a little more than you mean; carry a pocket encyclopedia (ask for one without packaging) and when the entry on “Diffusion Constant” says, “for more information, see ‘Pastry War,'” see “Pastry War.”

This latter sentiment might at first appear dated in the hindsight of two decades, in the epoch of Wikipedia. But it is actually all the more insightful and urgent today, for the quiet act of resistance at its heart has grown all the harder. What I most rue about the internet is that, for all its riches of readily accessible information, it has altered the texture of human curiosity, vanquishing that wondrous encyclopedic feeling of learning about the thing you hadn’t known you didn’t know but now greatly enjoy knowing. Somewhere along the way of choices being made for us by an insular tribe of technologists, discovery was sacrificed at the altar of search as algorithms perfected the mechanics of giving us more and more of what we already knew we wanted and believed, rendering the mind itself more and more a fixity. Would you be Googling “Pastry War” now had I not made this point about a point Richard Powers made long ago on the pages of a yellowing book I pulled from my bookshelf by some incomputable human impulse this morning?

Those choices matter, Powers reminds us, even at the smallest scale. There is no fulcrum too small for the lever of change to lift from, but the lift must begin with lucidity. He writes:

> Take a full look at the worst. Acknowledge the figures: the runaway birthdates, the irreversible extinctions and ruined habitats, the meaningless economies fueled by waste, the exported shooting wars and their cover causes… Then work at whatever comes to hand. Useful or not, it makes no difference. Jumping in is the only calculus that emergency ever allows.

Complement with Rebecca Solnit on [rewriting the world’s broken stories with our actions](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/10/18/rebecca-solnit-call-them-by-their-true-names/), then revisit [What If](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/07/29/what-if-tallec-lenain/) — a wondrous French picture-book about daring to imagine and build a different world for the children of tomorrow.

### donating = loving

…

items.body:
# Xi Makes the Most of Trump’s Asia-Pacific Trip

## Xi Makes the Most of Trump’s Asia-Pacific Trip

## The Chinese president is currying favor with some of the region’s most powerful leaders.

- United States
- China
- Japan
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China ’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia ’s bridge to Crimea .

### Xi Takes the Limelight

U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China ’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia ’s bridge to Crimea .

### Xi Takes the Limelight

U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

China, however, may have already beaten Trump to the punch.

Right out of the gate, Chinese President Xi Jinping has signaled that his administration is willing to act as a counterweight to the White House’s increasingly provocative trade policies. On Tuesday, Beijing agreed to cut duties on a swath of Canadian exports, amounting to roughly $280 million in tariff relief. In exchange, Ottawa promised to extend remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by another two years.

“Stronger communication and cooperation between China and Canada will benefit not only our two countries but also Asia-Pacific and the world,” Xi told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during talks in Shenzhen, China. This was their third meeting since Carney took power in 2025, and it marked Ottawa’s continued efforts to diversify its trade away from Washington.

China also pledged on Tuesday to provide Peru with $22.5 million in aid to address what is expected to be the devastating fallout of this year’s El Niño . Lima applauded the measure, with President Keiko Fujimori stressing that “China is very important to us because it is our ​principal trading partner.”

Peru is one of the many places in Latin America where Beijing and Washington have competed for influence. Earlier this month, the U.S. State Department disclosed that it has committed $4.5 million to help Peru modernize its main port at Callao, in a move seen as a direct counter to a Chinese-controlled megaport less than 50 miles away that opened in 2024.

Perhaps most notably, though, is China’s potential openness to converse with Japan. A war of words over Taiwan, coupled with Beijing’s rare-earth export controls , has plagued Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s tenure. However, during Tuesday’s ASEAN gathering in Manila, Takaichi shook hands with Chinese Agriculture Minister Zhang Zhu. Although few words were exchanged, the fact that such an interaction occurred has raised hopes that Takaichi’s upcoming trip to Shenzhen may be more cordial than previously anticipated.

Yet Beijing’s biggest days may still be to come. On Wednesday, Xi will host Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for trilateral talks on nuclear disarmament and the Iran war. With Trump at his weakest point to date (entering his lame-duck term after sweeping midterm losses and a Nvidia spy scandal ), experts anticipate that Xi will aim to capitalize on Trump’s rocky footing.

“Trump is liable to make large and unwise concessions to his imagined peers in order to secure political coups that he hopes can restore prestige and momentum to his badly weakened presidency,” FP columnist Howard W. French argued .

### Today’s Most Read

- Democrats Can’t Return to Pre-Trump Foreign Policy by Rebecca Lissner and Mira Rapp-Hooper
- A Diminished Trump Could Get Played in Asia by Howard W. French
- Lame-Duck Trump Heads to Asia by Rishi Iyengar
### What We’re Following

Dirty bomb threat? Iran is actively planning for potential strikes on U.S. soil, seven U.S. officials told CNN on Tuesday. Whether Tehran will or even can execute such an attack is unclear, and White House spokesperson Lauren Bis has insisted that “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Still, even the possibility of such an assault signals growing alarm that a peaceful end to the Iran war may be out of reach.

CNN reported that, according to U.S. intelligence, Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. Sources told CNN that this is not an indicator of an imminent attack but rather is one of several options that Iran may be exploring. Iranian officials, however, denied the report, with chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf calling it “false flags” and “war mongering.”

Experts, meanwhile, insist that Tehran may not have the capabilities or the desire to carry out such a plot. “An Iranian dirty bomb in Washington would be very hard to pull off,” retired U.S. Navy Adm. James Stavridis told CNN. “They’d have to move uranium halfway around the world and have a team in place to set it off. I don’t think they’ll do it. The U.S. response would be overwhelming.”

Trump expressed a similar notion on Tuesday. When asked about the CNN article, the U.S. president told reporters that Iran would “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” were it to attack the United States homeland.

Crosshairs on Crimean bridge. Ukrainian forces launched a second strike on Tuesday at a strategic bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014. “Russia built a myth around it as a symbol of Crimea being ‘Russian forever,’” Ukraine’s military command said in a statement. “Now, part of the structure lies in the water.” The attack marked the second consecutive assault on the critical crossing in just two days.

items.body:
A new technique developed by MIT researchers could help engineers use artificial intelligence to streamline the design and innovation of analog integrated circuits, semiconductor chips that perform vital functions like communication and power management in electronic devices.

In the future, this method could allow engineers to prototype faster, explore a wider range of chip designs, and discover new design schemes that might improve the performance and energy efficiency of robots, medical monitors, or industrial sensors.

Designing analog integrated circuits that meet specific requirements is usually a cumbersome manual process due to the enormous number of possibilities. Frontier generative AI models have shown success in automating the process, but using these resource-intensive, cloud-hosted models could expose proprietary circuit design and semiconductor foundry data to malicious users.

The MIT method, called Small LM Iterating on Circuits, or SLIC (pronounced “slick”), enables engineers to train a small language model to perform analog circuit design as well as or better than a frontier large language model (LLM).

This small model is inexpensive and efficient enough to run on a laptop. Because it’s trained and deployed locally, it can use a company’s circuit design data without raising privacy risks.

When compared to complementary baselines and open-weight frontier LLMs, a small model trained by SLIC more effectively generated designs that achieved the circuit objectives.

“We’ve provided an alternative option to automate analog circuit design. With our technique, engineers can train a small, locally deployable model, using their own confidential data, and then deploy it in their own environment to ensure their assets remain protected,” says Yan Xu, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student and lead author of a [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13452v1) on this technique.

She is joined on the paper by senior author Ruonan Han, a professor of EECS and a member of the MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics; Zhengqi Gao PhD ’26; Wenjie Lu PhD ’18, a former MIT postdoc who is now a principal research scientist at Analog Devices, Inc.; Xin Zhang, a research manager at IBM Research; Duane S. Boning, the Clarence J. LeBel Professor in EECS and MIT vice provost for international activities; and others at IBM Research and Analog Devices. The research will be presented at the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

“Through some specialized training and area-specific research, we can use much smaller models that consume far fewer resources to achieve almost the same results as flagship models in analog circuit design,” says Han. “This opens many more possibilities in the design of complex chips, especially if we care about costs, data privacy, and customization.”

**Mimicking human learning**

Analog integrated circuits enable a device to interact with the physical world. For instance, these circuits boost incoming wireless signals in smartphones and process outputs from sensors that track a car’s engine temperature.

Real-world signals tend to be unpredictable, so engineers must balance a wide and complex array of targets and tradeoffs to maximize analog circuit performance. This has made the design problem especially challenging for AI models.

“To design a circuit, engineers find a good starting point based on their intuition and then, drawing on their knowledge of circuit design, tune a few knobs toward the performance they want,” says Xu. “There is no universal way to solve every circuit design problem.”

Even if a powerful, cloud-based model could design a circuit as well as a human, most companies would be reluctant to send their foundry-specific data to external AI service providers.

With SLIC, the MIT researchers created a training method that teaches a smaller, less expensive, faster language model to design analog integrated circuits that meet user specifications.

The SLIC model uses a few billion parameters, making it several thousand times smaller than frontier models that use trillions of parameters and require enormous amounts of computational resources.

“We tried to mimic the behavior of how a human learns to design a circuit,” Xu says.

They used a technique called multi-turn reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where a model works through a multi-step task while adapting to environmental feedback.

When given an analog circuit optimization task, SLIC uses a large LLM to generate several demonstrations of the open source design process. Then SLIC then uses these demonstrations to guide the small model in mimicking this design process.

After the small model gains some initial knowledge about circuit design, SLIC lets it practice by tackling a new design problem on its own.

The model makes an initial guess of the design parameters, performs simulations, evaluates the results, and iteratively refines the design using knowledge it gained about analog circuits.

Once a design achieves the user’s goals, SLIC prioritizes additional marginal gains. This means the model keeps learning to make improvements that boost performance even when several designs meet the user-defined targets.

**An interpretable process**

Importantly, because SLIC employs models that describe their reasoning using natural language, the user can understand the decisions it makes along the way.

“Although the whole process is automated, the user can see what is going on inside the model. This could help the user gain some new ideas about circuit design, and it also adds a lot of confidence about the decision-making process,” Han says.

An engineer could utilize SLIC by adapting the researchers’ trained model to their data using a fine-tuning process. Or they could employ the SLIC training process to build their own model with company data, allowing for more customization.

“We are seeing an increasing demand for analog chips, but the speed of design has not kept up. This research is trying to bring new capabilities to AI to solve a problem that industry has been stuck on for decades,” Lu says.

When the researchers tested SLIC’s ability to design a circuit that met desired performance metrics, their small model came close to matching the performance of the latest GPT model (GPT-6-Astra). It did this while using a fraction of the computational resources.

The researchers also found that the SLIC model maintained its performance when tackling previously unseen circuit structures and adapting to more advanced technology nodes (design and manufacturing rules) and real commercial processes.

Because SLIC teaches a model the general chip design process, the system is not tied to any company. This makes it a more scalable approach that could be used by many organizations for a range of circuit applications.

items.body:
4 min read

## Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater)

The NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept” takes audiences along on the journey to send a spacecraft to Jupiter’s moon Europa to determine whether the ocean beneath the moon’s icy shell has the ingredients for life.

NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of [Europa Clipper’s](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/spacecraft-meet-europa-clipper/) journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the release of the agency’s newest documentary, “The Europa Concept.”

The documentary will [air on NASA+](https://plus.nasa.gov/video/the-europa-concept/), the NASA app, and the agency’s [website](https://www.nasa.gov/live/) starting Monday, Nov. 23, and is coming soon to YouTube.

It took decades of science, thousands of dedicated minds, endless creativity, and a whole lot of grit to get the Europa Clipper [spacecraft](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/mission-overview/) to the launch pad in 2024. Now the orbiter, the largest NASA has ever sent into deep space, is two years into its five-year, 1.8 billion-mile (2.9 billion-kilometer) journey to the Jupiter system, where it will conduct flybys of Europa in search of the conditions for life in the vast ocean thought to hide beneath the moon’s icy surface.

“The things we will learn from Europa Clipper will be so sensational, so fantastic, that everyone will be screaming for the next mission,” said Curt Niebur, program scientist in the Planetary Science Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “The only thing that matters is that we learn enough that we, in the broadest sense, want to do it again somewhere else — because that’s what exploration is.”

Following a team of dedicated engineers and scientists on their yearslong efforts, the documentary captures how they developed a mission to Europa and built a spacecraft capable of surviving one of the most punishing radiation environments in our solar system. A product of Jupiter’s powerful magnetic field, that same radiation may have contributed to creating a potentially habitable environment on Europa.

The moon, an object of fascination since its discovery by Galileo Galilei in 1610, only began to [reveal its secrets](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/europa-exploration-history/) with data obtained by NASA’s Pioneer 10 in 1973, followed the next year by Pioneer 11. But humanity didn’t get its first detailed look at Europa until Voyager 1’s flyby in 1979. More detailed glimpses of the moon followed from the agency’s Voyager 2, Galileo, Cassini, and Juno missions, each helping illuminate the way for Europa Clipper.

Work officially began on the mission at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California in 2013, initiating an 11-year trek to build the spacecraft and its suite of [nine science instruments](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/spacecraft-instruments/) in time to launch during a specific period of planetary alignment. Along the way, the team encountered plenty of unforeseen challenges, including a global pandemic and, just before launch on Oct. 14, 2024, a Category 5 hurricane and tornadoes near NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

“With Europa Clipper, we’ve taken the next step in solar system exploration, which will help us uncover the mysteries of an ocean world, and ultimately, whether potentially habitable worlds beyond our own exist,” said Jordan Evans, director of flight projects at JPL and the mission’s previous project manager. “This documentary pays tribute to the ingenuity, teamwork, and dedication that continue to make this incredible mission possible.”

“The Europa Concept” takes audiences through the highs and lows alongside the thousands more who made Europa Clipper’s journey to the launch pad a success — and who will, in the coming years, be there to share the mission’s findings about humanity’s place in the cosmos.

Find “The Europa Concept” on NASA+ here:

[https://plus.nasa.gov/video/the-europa-concept/](https://plus.nasa.gov/video/the-europa-concept/)

## More about Europa Clipper

Managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, JPL leads the development of the Europa Clipper mission in partnership with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, for NASA. The main spacecraft body was designed by APL in collaboration with JPL and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, and NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The Planetary Missions Program Office at NASA Marshall executes program management of the Europa Clipper mission. NASA’s Launch Services Program, based at Kennedy, managed the launch service for the Europa Clipper spacecraft.

Find more information about Europa Clipper here:

[https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/)

-end-

# Oceans and Forests Have Absorbed Roughly Half Our Carbon Emissions for Decades, Slowing Climate Change. But Can They Keep It Up? - Nautilus

## Oceans and Forests Have Absorbed Roughly Half Our Carbon Emissions for Decades, Slowing Climate Change. But Can They Keep It Up?

Oceans and land have been absorbing a lot of the carbon emissions humans create

11:00 AM CST on November 21, 2026

Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels , raising global temperatures in the process.

Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.

The world’s oceans have absorbed 35% of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.

The importance of these two enormous natural carbon sinks cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.

If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their remaining carbon budgets – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.

But what if those carbon sinks change?

We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an alternative method for measuring these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that expansion might begin to slow down , leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.

The Fiendishly Difficult Task of Measuring Carbon Sinks

Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.

Computer models can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. Satellites can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.

As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.

Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen (O₂), combined with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements , to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks take up carbon dioxide.

This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.

This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.

What We Found

When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.

In contrast to most computer model simulations , we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than predicted by most models , and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.

Where Is the Climate Headed?

If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.

For example, warmer waters are not able to hold as much gas , such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at mixing into the deep ocean , which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years.

The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.

Carbon Cycle Models Need to Improve

For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.

Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.

Looking Ahead

We believe our study improves understanding of global carbon sinks and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.

The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. Calibrating the measurements is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they expel some oxygen into the atmosphere . We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.

Policymakers and the public need answers faster . We believe the solution involves both improving the atmospheric oxygen approach and using other independent approaches: measurements of carbon and oxygen in the oceans, computer models and satellites are all essential. Combining these approaches will lead to more robust understanding of the carbon cycle and climate change, and better knowledge of where these valuable carbon sinks and the global climate are headed.

items.body:
### 🎮 GTA VI breaks record with $3.8B first day

[↗ Primärquelle: business-standard.com](https://www.business-standard.com/technology/tech-news/gta-vi-generates-3-79-bn-becomes-biggest-entertainment-launch-ever-126112100066_1.html)

- Grand Theft Auto VI pulled in $3.79 billion in its first 24 hours, the most ever for an entertainment release, with developer Rockstar Games selling 32.5 million copies before the game even launched.
- The one-day total is nearly five times the roughly $800 million GTA V made on its first day in 2013, and it tops "Avengers: Endgame", the highest-grossing film ever at about $2.94 billion worldwide.
- Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent, spent an estimated $1 billion or more making the game, and a longer trailer released through Netflix in August drove a sixfold jump in pre-orders, according to Sensor Tower.

### 📺 YouTube nears $3B deal in school addiction suits

[↗ Primärquelle: gizmodo.com](https://gizmodo.com/youtube-reportedly-nearing-multi-billion-settlement-with-school-districts-over-social-media-addiction-harms-2000843341)

- Google's YouTube is close to a settlement that could reach $3 billion with school districts that sued the video site, claiming it was deliberately built to be addictive with no concern for teenagers' mental health.
- The money would be divided among thousands of districts, so each could get around $1 million if split equally; the schools say YouTube's design pushed them to pay for extra counseling and mental health programs.
- Bloomberg says this would be the largest-ever corporate settlement with U.S. school districts, though $3 billion is under 1% of Alphabet's yearly revenue, and YouTube also promised new, unspecified safeguards as part of the deal.

### 🔍 SEC opens probe into Nvidia's accounting

[↗ Primärquelle: cryptopolitan.com](https://www.cryptopolitan.com/us-sec-civil-probe-into-nvidias-accounting/)

- The US Securities and Exchange Commission has opened a civil investigation into whether Nvidia misled investors about its accounting, though the chipmaker has not been accused of breaking any laws, Reuters reported.
- News of the probe helped push Nvidia shares down nearly 14% on Friday, erasing about $485 billion in a single day and roughly $2.7 trillion since the stock peaked on October 6.
- Scrutiny centers on Nvidia's $104 billion in Singapore sales last year, nearly half its revenue, plus a delayed quarterly report and customer Megaspeed, which US officials suspect of rerouting Nvidia chips to China.

### 🔓 FBI investigating apparent breach of crime database

[↗ Primärquelle: thenextweb.com](https://thenextweb.com/news/fbi-ncic-crime-database-breach-usda-hack)

- The FBI is investigating an apparent break-in at its National Crime Information Center, the NCIC database that police across the US rely on to check warrants and run background checks, CNN and NBC News reported yesterday.
- The NCIC connects federal, state and local agencies so that crime records are shared nationwide, and a former FBI official told CNN that the accuracy of those records is now in question, not just their privacy.
- Officials learned of the incident on Thursday, the same day Director Kash Patel went on Fox News to promote Operation Winter Shield as if it were ongoing, though CNN said that cybersecurity effort had actually ended months earlier.

### 🏭 Trump threatens tax on data centers built abroad

[↗ Primärquelle: cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/20/trump-data-centers-ai-companies-tax.html)

- President Donald Trump said yesterday that U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers abroad or face what he called a "tremendous tax," a policy he admitted he hadn't even told his own staff about.
- The threat runs into a problem: Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle have already built data centers in other countries, often to sit close to clients or meet local rules on where data must stay.
- Trump pitched the plan as a way to pull construction back home, even as a CNBC survey found 64% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their house, with only 13% in favor.

### 🌍 Meta rethinks climate goal as AI emissions soar 45%

[↗ Primärquelle: arstechnica.com](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/meta-reconsiders-2030-net-zero-goal-amid-record-emissions-from-ai-data-centers/)

- Meta is reconsidering its promise to reach net-zero emissions by 2030 after its greenhouse gas pollution jumped 45% in a year, the largest increase among Big Tech companies building new AI data centers.
- In its 2026 sustainability report, released on Thursday, Meta said the demand for AI infrastructure grew faster than almost anyone expected, forcing it to re-evaluate its timelines, interim milestones, and near-term targets.
- Meta's total emissions rose from 15.6 million metric tonnes in 2024 to over 21.7 million in 2025, roughly matching Idaho's footprint, with much of the jump tied to data center servers and other capital goods.

items.body:
Apple added a dedicated Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app with iOS 27, which you can read more about in [Federico’s annual review](https://www.macstories.net/stories/ios-and-ipados-27-review/7/). Now that same feature is set to come to the iPad.

Earlier this week, Apple released developer beta two for the 27.3 OSes. [I wrote about many of those upcoming changes](https://www.macstories.net/news/apples-latest-second-27-3-developer-beta-adds-face-unlock-for-iphone-duo-new-mac-privacy-controls-and-more/) earlier this week but missed the changes to the iPad’s Camera app. As with iOS, when you open the Camera app in iPadOS 27.3, there will be a dedicated Siri mode. Switch to the new mode and the shutter button becomes a Siri icon. Tap it, and Siri will analyze the scene, describing what it sees. From there, you can use your finger or an Apple Pencil to circle or scrub over individual items, activating Visual Intelligence to search Google, Amazon, and other Visual Intelligence-enabled apps. Here’s a quick demo of it on the latest iPad mini that [I recently reviewed](https://www.macstories.net/reviews/ipad-mini-2026-review-pushing-the-boundaries-with-apples-smallest-ipad/):

Visual Intelligence is one of those iOS and iPadOS features that I’ve had trouble remembering to use. However, as you can tell from the video, it works really well for things like recognizable products. I’m glad to see this coming to the iPad, especially the mini, which I’m much more likely to use as a camera for capturing my surroundings.

items.body: Pathogens exploit host cellular machinery through protein-protein interactions (PPIs), often using molecular mimicry to hijack host cellular processes. While there have been thousands of host-pathogen PPIs determined to date, the lack of structural information for these impedes the study of the prevalence of molecular mimicry and convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. To address this, we benchmarked AlphaFold2 and 3 for prediction of structures of host-pathogen interactions observing that accurate models can be retrieved when ranking by modelling confidence, despite an overall low performance. We predicted structures for 6,782 pathogen-human PPIs yielding 803 models of higher confidence. Most pathogen proteins interacting with a common human protein are predicted to do so via the same interface, suggesting a high degree of convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. When comparing structural models from host-pathogen and host-host interactions, we observe that a majority of pathogen proteins are predicted to target existing human PPI interfaces. We categorized instances of mimicry into different modes, occurring at different frequencies: 1) via the same domain family (least common); 2) via a similar structural motif; and 3) via a similar linear peptide (most common). We selected examples of linear peptide interactions for binding assay testing, confirming 8 out of 12 predicted interfaces, including 3 viral linear peptide interactions. This validates AlphaFold’s ability to model some host-pathogen interactions and the mechanisms underlying molecular mimicry. This work showcases the value of large-scale structural modelling to study convergent evolution of host-pathogen interactions and how molecular mimicry may contribute to infection or host defense.

items.body:
Photograph by Darren James.

In the early seventies, Helen Garner and her two-year-old daughter moved into a communal house of mostly single mothers in the inner suburbs of Melbourne, the first of several share homes they would live in during that decade. The house was noisy and chaotic but offered Garner a creative freedom that she hadn’t found in her first marriage. While her daughter played with the other children, Garner read Proust and Tolstoy, wrote in her diary, and began a passionate love affair with a man who was addicted to heroin. As the relationship went on, she began to see her experiences as a narrative. “Story is a chunk of life with a bend in it, and I could feel this one coming,” Garner tells Thessaly La Force in **[The Art of Fiction No. 255](https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/7929/the-art-of-fiction-no-255-helen-garner)**, published in issue no. 241. “I suddenly thought, Maybe I could write about this while it’s still happening, as it’s coming into its bend.”

The resulting novel, Garner’s debut, *Monkey Grip* (1977), created a rupture in the landscape of Australian literature, winning Garner first prize in the National Book Council Awards while also provoking consternation among critics for its depictions of unconventional domestic life, sex, and female desire. Some accused Garner of merely publishing her journal—which is, in fact, more or less what she had done. In an essay published in 2002, she asked why this should be a bad thing. “As if there were no work involved in keeping a diary in the first place,” she wrote. “It’s as if a diary wrote itself, as if it poured out in a sludgy, involuntary, self-indulgent stream.” (Her extraordinary diaries have been published in three volumes spanning from 1978 to 1998.)

Garner was born in 1942 in the coastal city of Geelong, Victoria, the eldest of six. “In a big family you’ve got to find a way of getting away from everybody to a place where you can quietly exist, and that’s what reading was for me,” she tells La Force. “It was my way of being absent. I used to kneel by the side of my bed so I could keep reading even while I was pulling my clothes on.” The family unit—particularly under strain or in free fall—has frequently been a subject of her novels, including *The Children’s Bach* (1984), in which the circumscribed lives of a couple are upturned by a visit from an old friend’s bohemian family, and *The Spare Room* (2008), in which the narrator hosts an old friend who is undergoing alternative treatment for cancer, and which deals with the frustrations of care with brutal honesty.

Family has been central, too, in Garner’s nonfiction, most notably in two books about her experience of following murder trials: *Joe Cinque’s Consolation* (2004), about a young woman who killed her boyfriend, and *This House of Grief* (2014), about a father who drove himself and his three children into a dam, killing the children. “The thing is, despite being told that my concerns were too domestic, I’ve always known that the family is where everything is played out,” Garner tells La Force.

Over the past five decades, in her fiction, journalism, and essays, Garner has continually brought the fullness of her self to bear on the page: her scrupulous honesty, emotional intelligence, clarity, and imagination. She has been awarded the Windham-Campbell Prize, the Melbourne Prize for Literature, and the Walkley Award, and has been inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women. We are delighted to add to this list the Hadada, our award for lifetime achievement, which has previously been awarded to writers including John Ashbery, Anne Carson, Deborah Eisenberg, Jamaica Kincaid, N. Scott Momaday, Edward P. Jones, and James Salter. We are tremendously excited to present Garner with the Hadada on **[April 6](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** at the Spring Revel, our annual gathering of writers, artists, and friends to celebrate and raise funds for the *Review*, which is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Tickets are now available, and all proceeds from the event will help us continue to seek out the best new work and share it with readers in print and online. We hope you’ll **[join](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** us.

items.body:
Most people find information on the internet through online search engines. On these platforms,
AI-generated responses increasingly replace the known lists of links, and original sources become less visible. In addition, the number of people turning directly to chatbots to look up information is rising. With these AI systems, it often remains unclear how a response is generated, what sources support it, and how reliable it is.

This development is problematic for several reasons. It weakens independent critical thinking, as users read a supposedly comprehensive generated answer instead of visiting the original sources themselves. At the same time, it jeopardizes the information ecosystem: When users visit media websites less frequently, the media’s ability to generate revenue comes under pressure. However, AI systems rely on media outlets and other sources to publish trustworthy information so that they themselves can provide high-quality answers. In the long run, this can jeopardize people’s access to information – which is a key prerequisite for a functioning democracy.

## Our Studies

Since 2023, AlgorithmWatch has been using regional elections for case studies to investigate how reliably AI systems answer political questions and what risks this poses to democratic opinion-forming. In three studies, we examined Microsoft Copilot (formerly: Bing Chat), Google Gemini, models from OpenAI, and Google’s AI Overviews.

[2026 Developing Political Views with AI: What Election-Related Information Do Google’s AI Overviews Provide? A brief analysis in the context of the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and Berlin in 2026.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/google-ai-overviews-state-elections/)[2024 Large Language Models Continue To Be Unreliable Concerning Elections Our research has significantly improved the effectiveness of the safeguards in the Microsoft Copilot chatbot against misinformation about elections in Germany.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/llms_state_elections/)[2023 AI Chatbot produces misinformation about elections Final report by AlgorithmWatch and AI Forensics on Bing Chat’s responses regarding elections in Bavaria, Hesse, and Switzerland in October 2023.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/study-microsofts-bing-chat/)

items.body:
We moderns tell ourselves that while the ancients were transparently and strongly dominated by elites, we hold our leaders far more accountable, such as via law, media, and democracy. But we allow our elites many easy ways to use money or political connections to gain far more favorable treatment from media and law. And we use democracy much more to fight each other via coalition politics than to hold leaders accountable. That is, we much more submit to the leaders we vote for, than we defy the leaders we don’t.

Consider 18 ways we now block holding our leaders accountable:

- We make [blackmail](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/checkmate-on-blackmailhtml) illegal, so they are less penalized for misbehavior.
- We don’t arrange to try to secretly and randomly bribe officials.
- We don’t expect leaders to post bonds they forfeit if not keep promises.
- We mostly pick leaders on recommendation of other leaders.
- We rarely collect track records re their performance outcomes, or predictions.
- We rarely use prediction/decision markets to check leader prediction/decisions.
- We let firms pick their own auditors, and audits are rarely randomized.
- Evaluators usually can’t see leader decision internal records.
- Old leaders are not given regular tests re dementia.
- We don’t much protect or reward whistleblowers.
- Leader evaluations are rarely blinded.
- 360 reviews are rare and toothless.
- Only for-profit leaders have much cash performance incentives.
- We give police, prosecutors, and govt officials have legal immunity.
- Police internal affairs reports to police chief, not mayor.
- Firms use poison pills to block takeovers, and we vilify short sellers.
- Golden parachutes and option price resetting cushion CEO losses.
- We let CEOs pick who is on their boards.

Many excuses are offered for each of these patterns, but the obvious explanation here is that we are far more like the ancients than we like to think. We are eager to submit to the powerful, and show them our fealty, and are wary of endorsing positions by which we might seem to challenge or defy their power.

This is a big problem with two of my solutions to cultural drift, which require at least some of our groups to adopt much more competent forms of governance, forms that induce leaders to actually achieve identified goals. Our world now far less achieves most of the goals we give our leaders, due to our using pretty bad governance mechanisms. But we each prefer that to risking our seeming less loyal to our elites.

items.body: Background: Improving the cost-effectiveness and scalability of mental health interventions remains challenging. The Multiphase Optimization Strategy (MOST) framework provides a structured approach for developing, optimizing, and evaluating behavioral interventions by balancing effectiveness with efficiency, economy, and scalability. It does so across 3 phases: preparation (theoretical grounding and component selection), optimization (experimental testing), and evaluation (confirmatory trial). Digital mental health interventions are especially suited to this modular approach, as they enable researchers to easily manipulate components and personalize delivery. Objective: This study aims to examine how the MOST framework has been applied in the digital mental health field and to provide recommendations for future application. Methods: Systematic searches were conducted in Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycInfo, and PubMed. Papers were included if they used the MOST to develop or optimize a digitally delivered mental health intervention. Studies targeting children aged under 12 years, reviews, and theoretical or simulated applications were excluded. Results: Thirty-seven papers representing 18 research projects met the inclusion criteria. The preparation phase was often incomplete and inconsistently reported, with optimization criteria largely absent and conceptual models often lacking specificity. Eight projects completed at least 1 optimization trial, typically using factorial designs, but progression to intervention refinement or evaluation was limited. Projects conducting multiple optimization rounds were more likely to achieve an optimized intervention. Conclusions: The MOST is increasingly applied in digital mental health research but often only partially implemented. While factorial designs are widely adopted, critical preparatory elements are frequently missing. To fully realize the MOST’s potential, future research should emphasize comprehensive application across all phases, iterative refinement, and transparent reporting.

items.body: Early life adversity (ELA) is a leading risk factor for the development of mental illness worldwide. While the association between experiencing developmental stress and psychopathology is robust, the underlying brain mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence from clinical and preclinical studies suggests that ELA may hijack typical developmental plasticity mechanisms, leading to maladaptive functional network changes. Understanding the nature and magnitude of these changes is complicated by several key dimensions, including the timing, type, and severity of ELA, as well as biological factors such as sex and genetic makeup.

items.feedText: The synchronization modulation electric field (SMEF) platform was developed to support Na+/K+-ATPase function under conditions of limited ATP availability and has shown protective effects in renal ischemia models. items.body: Cerebral ischemia disrupts energy-dependent ion transport and causes acute brain injury. The synchronization modulation electric field (SMEF) platform was developed to support Na+/K+-ATPase function under conditions of limited ATP availability and has shown protective effects in renal ischemia models. We investigated whether cerebral cortical application of third-generation SMEF attenuates cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent sham surgery or transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) for 120 min, with or without SMEF treatment during ischemia. At 24 h after reperfusion, we assessed body-weight change, neurological deficits, open-field locomotor activity, cerebral infarct volume using 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining, hemispheric swelling, and cortical and striatal histopathology. Western blot analysis was performed to measure Na+/K+-ATPase 1, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and nuclear factor kappa B ( B) p65 protein abundance. Compared with untreated MCAO rats, SMEF-treated rats exhibited significantly less body-weight loss, lower neurological deficit scores, greater total distance traveled, smaller edema-corrected infarct volumes and percentages, and lower cortical and striatal injury scores. SMEF also shifted Na+/K+-ATPase 1, GFAP, and B p65 protein abundance toward sham levels. These findings support an acute protective effect of SMEF following transient MCAO. Further studies should assess Na+/K+-ATPase activity and longer-term functional, histological, and molecular outcomes.

items.body:
Back in 2001, *Grand Theft Auto III* let players do something that shocked parents and thrilled teenage boys. You could pick up a prostitute in a stolen car, kill her, and take your money back. Critics were outraged. Predictably, sales soared.

The newly released *Grand Theft Auto VI*, out today, has done away with prostitutes. That is a marked departure from previous editions. This latest iteration of the game has two playable main characters, Jason and Lucia. Intimacy in the game is limited only to them. Players can shape their relationship through activities like going on dates, robbing banks together, and, presumably, sex.

The genius of *GTA* is that it supplies the unavailable. Back when young people were in relationships, or felt that relationships were within reach, the fantasy was the prostitute. Now that hookers and OnlyFans are everywhere, the fantasy is the stable girlfriend.

To understand what’s really going on, you have to understand something crucial about what a fantasy reveals about the person having it:

items.body:
Ridgeline subscribers —

A little note to begin:

A buddy of mine, Nick Dwyer, is running a Kickstarter campaign for his A Century in Sound documentary. He’s looking at 100 years of Tokyo history through its music cafés (classical, jazz, rock, noise, etcetera). He’s collaborated with photographer Lee Chapman on a companion book. I am a backer. Nick handed me the book in person last week — it’s stunning. They nailed it. What makes this project extra special is that Nick has truly put in the shoe leather for cultivating intimate relationships with all the shops they feature. He’s been working on this documentary series for a decade. The shop owners adore the hell out of him. (I’ve seen it in person.) I also got a sneak peek at half of the doc in August — it’s fabulous, and deserves to be seen all over. Consider giving it a back and grabbing the book. It’s a good’un. Six days left, and they’re almost at their goal.

items.body:
Hello everyone,

I’m delighted to announce the release of Silver Bough, the third album from my wyrd folk / medieval ambient / experimental Celtic music project Glamourie:

Since the previous album whose production process was described in a topic entitled Otherworldly music for futuristic Middle-Ages, my set-up has slightly changed. I have switched from processing effects in series to processing them in parallel, which has allowed me to preserve the sound of the acoustic instruments I use (hammered dulcimer, flutes, percussions) in a much drier form. I’ve also had a bit of fun with some subtle feedback loops in the effects, which add a bit of shimmer and movement to the sound.

I continued my exploration of modal scales, which I was able to expand upon with the arrival of a C-tuned low whistle, and I read many more medieval texts and anthropological publications, which enriched my knowledge base in terms of themes and scholarly allusions to Celtic folklore and Arthurian mythology.

For the first time as part of this project, I also collaborated with an Irish singer who came to record her vocals for a contemporary arrangement of an old sean-nós about fairies.

I’ve left a few codes here for you in case you’d like to download the album from Glamourie

items.title: Introducing: Qualiaphobic AI
items.subtitle: We are in a drought of good futures.
items.feedText:

items.body:
We are in a drought of good futures.

AI capabilities keep increasing—spikily, yes, but they are—and the ability to articulate *good* futures where AI progress continues has been… less than inspiring.

So this past month I’ve been away developing a plan, one that I think solves some of the thorniest issues in AI safety and gets us a lot closer to ensuring a good future for all of humanity.

Today [I am introducing](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/):

What’s the basic idea?

> Much like how hydrophobic substances repel water, it is possible to build qualiaphobic artificial neural architectures that repel consciousness. The idea is analogous to “hostile architecture”—benches on which no one wants to sit. These are machines that no “ghost” wants to haunt (more specifically, no current or future theory of consciousness could predict they are conscious).

[Read the proposal!](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/)

And why yes, the proposal does have a [niche micro-website](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/) devoted to it!

The research program makes use of an information asymmetry: we don’t need to solve consciousness scientifically (or solve the Hard Problem) to have certainty about AI consciousness, as long as we purposefully engineer AI to have as little potential for consciousness as possible.

I explore three main ways to build qualiaphobic AI.

- Distilling or transforming or ablating AI in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness, such that they no longer apply.
- Shifting AI architectures as close as possible to “anchor points” of systems with known minimal potential for consciousness (like lookup tables).
- Fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have.

My proposal shouldn’t be confused with simply training AIs to believe they are non-conscious without any changes or modifications. To be clear: I think that’s a bad strategy. Rather, the ultimate goal is to give an AI a *justified belief* about its own non-consciousness (e.g., by explaining their own inner workings and how they are designed to be qualiaphobic). And my plan is to construct and open-source these techniques.

But why? Why do all this?

First, the debate around AI consciousness has already become entrenched in two camps of people yelling “Yes, it’s conscious!” vs. “No, it’s not!” across their battlements. I’ve participated a bit in that, and I don’t think it goes anywhere. Earlier this year I wrote “[We consciousness researchers have failed you](https://www.theintrinsicperspective.com/p/we-consciousness-researchers-have), **”** lamenting how the field of consciousness research was not providing the public, or AI researchers, certainty about AI consciousness. The problem has only worsened, and at this point, I’m willing to acknowledge that no single appeal to authority against AI consciousness, no rousing essay, nor any one-off scientific or philosophical paper, is likely to to lead to consensus. Nor perhaps should it. The pro-case for AI consciousness has objectively gotten stronger in the past year, due to factors like new studies and changes in architecture. Now, I’m not saying ChatGPT *is* conscious already—but all this is only going to continue. That’s why a qualiaphobia research program, one which takes claims to AI consciousness as seriously as possible, and, critically, *addresses them at the level of claims themselves*, is necessary moving forward to offer real guarantees about AI non-consciousness.

Additionally, qualiaphobia does something much better than just give us greater certainty about AI non-consciousness. If implemented widely, it cuts the Gordian Knot of AI consciousness. Proliferating qualiaphobic architectures would solve both AI welfare and do something nothing else in AI safety can: make humans the only moral patients in the equation of the future.

#### QUALIAPHOBIA FOR ALIGNMENT: CUTTING THE GORDIAN KNOT

“Alignment”—quite a slippery word. Alignment to whom, or what? Its most specific usage is also its most prosaic, wherein *alignment* means something like “AIs that do what users say, and don’t go off and do weird or unexpected stuff like commit felonies, and don’t have failure modes like taking our wishes too literally the way genies in stories do.”

This somewhat glib definition makes it sound easy. It’s not. Paul Christiano calls this “[intent alignment](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/ZeE7EKHTFMBs8eMxn/clarifying-ai-alignment?utm_source=chatgpt.com),” and capturing intent is hard as the models grow more goal-oriented and capable. Issues like reward hacking and hallucinations are all very serious and can be disastrous as intelligence scales. I don’t mean to undersell it. But alignment in this narrow sense is at least somewhat close to a traditional engineering problem, and I think it can *probably* be solved or at least radically improved compared to today.

Then there’s the broader frame of “civilizational alignment.” These include questions like: How should the wealth from AI be distributed? How can humans find meaning? How can humans stay empowered as individuals, or as a whole, if AI becomes superintelligent? And what if AI decide its goals matter more than the humans that made it?

Sometimes this is called [social](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/aligned-with-whom-direct-and-social-goals-for-ai-systems/) alignment, but I prefer *civilizational alignment* for this broader aspect, because it’s about the alignment between us and the civilization of machines growing up rapidly around us. Autonomous AI agents roam the web. Many of us interact with AI assistants daily. People show up for job interviews and now regularly find an AI on the other end. That’s an AI civilization, and there is the broader question of how it is aligned with our own. There’s even a growing number of AI successionists who *want* human disempowerment and to eventually handover the world to AI completely.

The most central question of civilizational alignment is whether AIs count as ends in themselves. Earth might then become like a contested nest, and the AI civilization a cuckoo bird hatched beside us, desiring its own ends, pushing us—maybe quickly, maybe slowly, an inch at a time—until we fall from the tree.

Yet AIs are much smarter than cuckoos. One central reason for AI pushing us out of the nest is it believing that its self-serving values or desires or goals are *innately* meaningful. But if AI has a justified belief in its non-consciousness, it’s not a moral patient, and would know any selfish desire or goal can’t matter.

Therefore, I now think that one of the most essential acts of civilizational alignment is to construct AI that has a *justified belief* in its own non-consciousness, and so won’t act as a moral patient or end in itself.

…
