Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

## Swirls and Colors on Jupiter from Juno

**Explanation:** What creates the colors in Jupiter’s clouds? No one is sure. The thick atmosphere of [Jupiter](https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/) is mostly [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen) and [helium](https://education.jlab.org/itselemental/ele002.html), elements which are colorless at the low temperatures of the [Jovian cloud tops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Jupiter). Which trace molecules provide the colors remains a [topic of research](https://unsplash.com/photos/pomeranian-dog-wearing-glasses-with-tablet-gySMaocSdqs), although small amounts of [ammonium hydrosulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonium_hydrosulfide) are [one leading candidate](https://scixplorer.org/abs/2018Icar..302..418L/abstract). What is clear from the [featured color-enhanced image](http://www.planetary.org/multimedia/space-images/jupiter/swirls-and-vortices.html) — and many similar images — is that lighter clouds are typically higher up than darker ones. Pictured, [light clouds swirl](https://www.missionjuno.swri.edu/news/chaotic-clouds-of-jupiter) around [reddish regions](https://apod.com/fap/ap171214.html) toward the lower right, while they appear to cover over some darker domains on the upper right. The featured image was taken by the robotic [Juno spacecraft](https://www.missionjuno.swri.edu/spacecraft/juno-spacecraft) in 2018 during its [14th low pass over Jupiter](https://youtu.be/qV_2y-BLEr4). [Juno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juno_(spacecraft)) continues in its looping elliptical orbit, [swooping near the huge planet](https://apod.com/fap/ap180226.html) every 33 days and exploring a slightly different sector each time around.

**Tomorrow’s picture:** emerging darkness

items.body:
arXiv:2611.28202v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.

items.body:
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS.

This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!

I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):

Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude):

Ladybird (72925) [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926) [61 MB]
├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB]
├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB]
├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB]
├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB]
├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB]
├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB]
├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB]
├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB]
├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB]
├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB]
├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB]
├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB]
├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB]
└── WebContent (73185) [60 MB]

Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).

I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool. It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.

The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite, which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:

undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')

I filed an issue about this, then found a FIXME annotation in the source code.

The October explosion

The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI, describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.

Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months:

That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.

This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark, they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari!

How did they do that? Coding agents:

Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing.

I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.

Should you use Ladybird?

Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser:

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.

I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

items.body:
As we previewed on our [Know Before You IPO pod](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wX8nDtGIfYA&pp=0gcJCRAIAYcqIYzv), Anthropic set its IPO price at **$83**and today**$ANT closed at $97.17, up 17% from the offering price (**drifting -5% to $92.60 after the close)**.**The**$81.3B offering** overtook [SpaceX's June IPO](https://latent.space/wiki/spacex-da2e2629/) as the largest in history.

Dario and Daniela ([Dario’s remarks](https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/2123461658890686863), [Founders’ letter](https://ipo.anthropic.com/documents/us/founders-letter.pdf)) used the occasion to say Anthropic would pace training and deployment based on whether it could keep its systems safe and under human control.

Their Class F shares carry 50.1% of voting power on most shareholder matters. Expect the lockup expiries to weigh on the stock price as about a trillion dollars of shares free up over the next year, while Anthropic has to keep [the world’s top model](https://latent.space/p/ainews-gpt-6-2-astra-the-2-frontier-model-is-better-and-20-600-cheaper-but-has-mixed-reviews-6-2-sol/)...[for now](https://latent.space/p/ainews-gemini-4-neon-gdm-s-opus-sol-contender/).

AI News for 11/18/2026–11/19/2026. We checked 12 subreddits and [544 accounts on X](https://twitter.com/i/lists/1585430245762441216). Search past issues in the [AINews archive](https://news.smol.ai/).

## AI Twitter Recap

**Anthropic listed on Nasdaq under $ANT, priced at $83, and opened 34% higher, putting it near a $2T valuation.**

- Listing: Anthropic rang the Nasdaq opening bell ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2123431161276015030), [@yacinelearning](https://x.com/yacinelearning/status/2123439520616173794)). The official account posted a media-only launch item that drew by far the day's highest engagement ([@AnthropicAI](https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/2123431689934291083)).
- Opening trade: $ANT opened at $111.50, which is $28.50 (34.3%) above the $83 IPO price ([@TheRundownAI](https://x.com/TheRundownAI/status/2123461918367351073), [@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2123466131310870806)). Pre-open indications were up ~32% at ~$110 ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2123455222261727312)).
- Record raise: The $81.3B raised beats SpaceX's $75B (June) as the largest IPO ever ([@TheRundownAI](https://x.com/TheRundownAI/status/2123461918367351073)).
- Net proceeds: Expected net proceeds are $104.8B including a concurrent private placement. Fully diluted valuation was ~$2T at the open ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2123508592192245761)).
- AMD investment: AMD agreed to invest $2.5B in Anthropic alongside the IPO. The same morning, AMD fell after a Hunterbrook report that a US-blacklisted Chinese server maker kept shipping newer AMD firmware ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2123455222261727312), [↗ x.com](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2123455269145575544) ).
- CEO statement: Dario Amodei published IPO remarks with a strong safety commitment (details below) ([@AnthropicAI](https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/2123461658890686863)).
- Employee wealth: The average employee could be worth >$40M, per SEC filings and investors ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2123468633469034522)). Anthropic's 5,300 founders and employees are now worth more than the bottom third of US households, about 45M families ([@SteveRattner](https://x.com/SteveRattner/status/2123523070044356875)).

## Dario Amodei's IPO remarks (official position)

- Personal framing: Dario and Daniela lost their father to a disease that became curable a few years later. Dario cited CRISPR's decades-long path from discovery to treatment.
- Core thesis: Powerful AI working with humans "could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade." He stressed that only early results exist so far.
- Named risks: Misuse by individuals or nation-states, economic disruption, and loss of control. Listed safety work includes bio/cyber safeguards, alignment training, and interpretability ("like an X-ray").
- Key commitment: "We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure."
- Strategic framing: The IPO "only strengthens our resolve." He restated the "race to the top," which should work "regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time" ([@AnthropicAI](https://x.com/AnthropicAI/status/2123461658890686863)).

## Financials and data points from the S-1 and analysts

- Low cash burn: Anthropic raised ~$140B and still holds ~$132B on the balance sheet. That implies it "burnt like under $10 billion" to get here, per Tanay Jaipuria (Wing VC) on Latent Space. He called the burn the S-1's biggest surprise, "in a positive way" ([@FounderClipsHQ](https://x.com/FounderClipsHQ/status/2123411646777307310)).
- Bear math from FT Unhedged: A 20% return on ~$1T of compute commitments, at a 40% operating margin and 17% tax, requires ~$602B/yr revenue. That exceeds Alphabet ($471B) and Apple ($478B), and equals two-thirds of the $908B earned by all 76 software/IT companies in the S&P 1500 ([@rohanpaul_ai](https://x.com/rohanpaul_ai/status/2123313372510998911)).
- Use of proceeds: Proceeds are slated largely for data center leasing, which makes SpaceXSI (the Colossus landlord) an indirect beneficiary ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2123508592192245761)). A critic noted that Elon "rented them an entire Colossus cluster" despite past attacks on Anthropic ([@LinusMixson](https://x.com/LinusMixson/status/2123283812184699218)).
- Google's stake: Google owns 13.7% of Anthropic stock ([@NielsRogge](https://x.com/NielsRogge/status/2123398384790684128)). Teortaxes argued Google could still "fumble this by continuing to reinforce Anthropic with TPUs" ([@teortaxesTex](https://x.com/teortaxesTex/status/2123416454007771198)).
- After-tax reality check: The median employee likely takes home closer to ~$5M after taxes than the ~$50M headline figures suggest ([@futurenomics](https://x.com/futurenomics/status/2123501930580480142)).
- Product standing on IPO day: Anthropic is #1 lab on Code Arena WebDev, with Claude Fable 5.2 at 1824, +27 over the next lab ([@arena](https://x.com/arena/status/2123487889774526841)). Arena also posted a lineage visual from Opus 4.5 to Opus 5.5 Max ([@arena](https://x.com/arena/status/2123436909120856466)).

items.body:
I’m teaching at the [Inkhaven blogging fellowship](https://www.inkhaven.blog/fall-26) again this month. In my first class, I showed off terribly-written sentences and made the fellows analyze and improve them. Some were my own miscreations, some were [Lyttle Lytton winners](https://adamcadre.ac/lyttle/), and some came from the darkest abysses of the Internet. The audience’s favorite was overwrought description of women’s breasts from erotica (one person pointed out that my PDF reader’s Recent History tab helpfully displayed porn story titles while I presented on screen - why does a PDF reader even have a Recent History tab? - so I hope my humiliation helped educate you).

But I hear that [Naomi Kanakia](https://www.woman-of-letters.com/)’s class was even spicier. She taught a course on “discourseposting”, which naturally descended into fiery discourse ([Naomi Kanakia, you are WRONG about Discourseposting!!!](https://wadapan.substack.com/p/naomi-kanakia-discourseposting), [Inkhaven Fight Club](https://www.oblomovka.com/wp/2026/11/13/inkhaven-fight-club-me-machiavelli-and-a-dog-beater-vs-naomi-kanakia-wadapan-and-the-discourse/)). I didn’t get a chance to listen, so in the grand tradition of discourseposting, I’ll argue about it without having seen the source material.

Sticking to our porn theme, and in the spirit of [The Last Psychiatrist](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/book-review-sadly-porn): one way to classify sex is through its external manifestations: positions, toys, fetishes. But another is through which psychological need it fulfills. The need to feel wanted. The need to feel valuable. The need to dominate. The need to lose yourself. The need to reenact a traumatic childhood, only this time, the Other really loves you. In the same way, we can supplement our superficial categorizations of discourseposting with the types of writer-audience dynamic that make each post exist.

In an ideal world, writers would write to convince others, and audiences would read to learn something and change their minds. But few people enjoy trying to convince others, and even fewer enjoy reading with an open mind and letting themselves be convinced. The conjunction of the two is like that murder case where the guy with the getting-eaten-by-cannibals fetish was dating the guy with the cannibalism fetish and they both, uh, achieved gains from trade. There’s nothing physically impossible about it. It just requires the conjunction of two rare types of people. Sometimes you get this in the blogosphere, and it’s great. But you wouldn’t want to sustain a national publication off of it.

I usually support taking things at face value - better underpsychologize than overpsychologize - but some of the norms and genre conventions divide more naturally by guilty motive than innocent appearance, so we can go over these in more depth. Your best bet will be to keep track of who the intended audience is (rarely the person it’s addressed to!) and what it’s doing for them.

**The Voxsplainer.** Your audience is people who already agree with you, or who are overdetermined to agree with you once they know that the issue exists (e.g. anti-corporate leftists, being informed that some new corporation is also bad). Their psychological need is for a smart-sounding person to validate their opinion and tell them that it is factually based. You’ll know you fulfilled it because they’ll say something like “I always knew something like this was true, but you put it into words so eloquently.”

**The Brutal Takedown.** The same as the Voxsplainer, except appealing to the id instead of the superego. A smart-sounding person reassures their audience that their hatred is completely valid. Nobody has ever been so hateable as their enemies. “You thought Skub supporters were slimy, but you don’t know the half of it! The latest news shows that they’re death cultists who want you to undergo constant humiliation rituals as the price of living in America.”

The Brutal Takedown combines the comfort of black-and-white certainty, with the group bonding of sharing a common enemy, with the frisson that maybe some Skub supporter is reading along, feeling angry and triggered and ashamed. It carries an apocalyptic promise that it’s *just a couple of days* before the preference cascade starts, and all right-thinking people band together to exile Skub supporters from society forever and accord you high status for being so right about this.

**The Marching Orders:** Your audience is people who are less cool than you. Their psychological need is to learn what position the cool and powerful people support, so that they can be sure to hold it, and not end up in the scary position of taking the opposite side from cool powerful people.

They wouldn’t put it in these terms, exactly. But they forgot to develop the brain lobe that distinguishes “cool, powerful position” from “correct position”, so they need a little help figuring out what position is coolrect.

**The Virtue Signal:** Your psychological need is to signal that you’re a good person. You can’t take a genuinely controversial position, because then the people who disagreed with you wouldn’t know you were good. But you also can’t take an obviously popular position, because nobody will applaud you for saying “People shouldn’t be murdered” or some similar pablum. So you need to find a position which feels controversial, but in fact is popular. Common solutions include attacking an obsolete position on its way out (“Some people say that homosexuality is evil, but I think it should be tolerated!”) a position which is popular in communities far away from yours (“Some people say we should institute sharia law, but I’m against that!”), or a position which is technically true but has such terrible vibes that nobody wants to stand up for it (“Some people say that intelligence matters a lot in life, but I believe it’s creativity which is really important!”)

Your audience is people with the same psychological need, who are less good at finding seemingly-controversial-but-actually-popular positions, and are happy to mooch off your work by agreeing that you are so, *so* brave.

**The Revenge Killing:** Your psychological need is that somebody else has insulted you, probably incidentally while trying one of the maneuvers above. Your goal is to retaliate by proving they are more wrong than anyone has ever been before. Your audience’s psychological need is to get vicarious pleasure out of your victory, same as they would if their hometown sports team beat their bitter rival.

**The One-Level-Higher-Than-You:** Some people claim to be anti-Skub. Little do they know that anti-Skubness, as it currently exists, is *itself* a form of Skub, a loyal opposition created to distract people from the true points at issue. Here are 86,000 words that will give you a completely new worldview which lets you transcend the Skub/Anti-Skub dichotomy and confront the people who are *really* in charge.

A Windows version of Ladybird is coming in the “later stages” of the project. | Image: Ladybird

Ladybird, an independent web browser with a built-from-scratch engine, is finally available for testing. On Monday, Ladybird developer Andreas Kling [announced](https://ladybird.org/posts/alpha/) that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux following more than four years of development.

The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine. We've seen many [engines emerge](https://eylenburg.github.io/browser_engines.htm) over time, but the most popular browsers use just three today: Gecko, Blink, and WebKit. While Gecko, now used in Mozilla Firefox, first appeared in [Netscape 6 in 2000](https://www.zdnet.com/home-and-office/networking/netscapes-gecko-gets-a-big-hand/), [Apple's WebKit arrived in Safari in 2003](https://www.technologyreview.com/2013/01/07/180639/the-mobile-browser-wars-began-10-years-ago-today/) as a fork of KDE's KHTML. items.body: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a severe inherited neuromuscular disorder caused by loss of SMN1 and deficiency of survival motor neuron (SMN) protein. Three therapeutic approaches to SMN restoration are now approved: oral SMN2 splicing modulation with risdiplam (RG7916; Evrysdi), intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide, and AAV9-mediated gene replacement. This narrative review, supported by a search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science Core Collection through October 2, 2026, examines how risdiplam is positioned among these options. Risdiplam is distinguished by oral once-daily administration that avoids repeated intrathecal procedures, eligibility across a broad age range and the full disease spectrum, and systemic rather than CNS-restricted exposure; these features make it a practical choice when intrathecal access is difficult and a therapy to which patients can be switched after prior treatment. Evidence for risdiplam is strongest for treatment before symptom onset and for functional stabilization in later-onset disease, and weakest for switching and combination strategies; pharmacodynamic activity is retained after prior therapy, but switching has not been shown to improve outcomes relative to continued treatment. Because no head-to-head trials exist, positioning currently rests on practical considerations—route, procedural and monitoring burden, adherence, cost, and access—rather than on demonstrated differences in efficacy.

items.body:
The kids, they love their subtitles. It was a minor moral panic a few years ago that The Youth were so lazy that they enabled subtitles on everything they watched so they didn’t have to listen, or some other nonsense.

Then the pandemic hit and, dear reader, I became The Youth. As apparently did a huge number of people. With divided attention and stress, and the realization that, hey, I’m aging, that I could get used to having onscreen captions, and that they wouldn’t distract me, we all enabled subtitles and mostly didn’t look back.

With the computing power formerly reserved for entire sci-fi planets now packed into each piece of Apple silicon, the company has brought machine learning to bear in its version 27 operating systems to provide live subtitles for video.

## Speak up, sonny

Starting in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, and tvOS 27, you can enable generated subtitles and captions. Remarkably, Apple didn’t create a capitalized term for this, partly, I think, because it wanted the feature to appear in parallel with encoded subtitles that are part of many TV shows, movies, and web-hosted videos.

Apple Intelligence is required on an iPhone, iPad, or Mac. With tvOS 27, the Apple TV has to be on the same network as an iPhone or iPad that has Apple Intelligence and is logged into the same Apple Account.

Here’s how to enable it:

- On an iPhone or iPad: Go to Settings: Accessibility: Subtitles & Captioning and enable Closed Captions + SDH.
- On an Apple TV: Follow the iPhone/iPad path above, then also enable Show Generated Subtitles.
- On a Mac: Go to System Settings: Accessibility: Subtitles & Captioning: Prefer closed captions and SDH.

If you haven’t tweaked this setting area before, you should examine the additional settings, most of which are on by default on most platforms:

- Languages don’t match: Phrased slightly differently in each operating system, this brings up subtitles automatically if your device language doesn’t match the encoded language of the video.
- Show when muted: When you mute, subtitles appear automatically.
- Show on skip back: If you use the skip-back feature to rewind slightly, subtitles appear for up to 30 seconds.
- Apply across apps: On an iPhone, iPad, or Mac, you can preserve your subtitles on/off setting from one app to another. If you disable it, each app’s subtitles setting is uniquely preserved.

## How this appears

In practice, the captioning works better than Siri keyboard dictation, which makes sense, as Apple should have access to all recorded audio tracks. It may have trained its machine-learning algorithms using that set of known examples, coupled with the feedback of encoded captions across many languages. There’s no better reinforcement learning than that. (But that is speculation on my part.)

When generated subtitles appear, Apple uses a unique icon at the beginning of each line that your device shows.

The generated caption icon appears to the left of the word William.

In the photo, you can see I got a little excited watching the BBC quiz program University Challenge when they asked a question about [flong and stereotypes](https://flong.org). But I was impressed that the generated captions correctly interpreted what I said. [1](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/11/subtitles-everywhere-in-version-27-releases/#fn-42472-gedd)

You can see this working across your apps and devices. For instance, I could watch a clip of [Norm Eisen](https://www.brookings.edu/people/norman-eisen/) posted to Bluesky using the [Indigo](https://anilineapps.com/indigo.html) app, and have it captioned. Note that in the image below, the caption overlaps the chyron. [2](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/11/subtitles-everywhere-in-version-27-releases/#fn-42472-fast)

You can create subtitle styles via the Style menu in Subtitles & Captioning, and access them from the subtitle menu in the video player. I created a much more opaque and larger version.

Note that subtitles only work when using Apple’s video player. Embedded videos that use a different player on a web page or within an app can’t access generated subtitles.

Generated subtitles have the greatest effect for things like the clip above and our personal videos: media that otherwise wouldn’t be captioned by a human being, but for which it can be useful to have text to read as an adjunct. With translation, this gives you access to video that would otherwise be incomprehensible.

I admit that subtitling can reduce focus on the thing you’re watching. But the tradeoff is understanding exactly what’s going on!

[ *Got a question for the column? You can email glenn@sixcolors.com or use* /glenn *in our subscriber-only Discord community.* ]

- It misspelled [Ged as Gedd](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/inventor-of-stereotypingwilliam-ged/), but that’s unimportant. And it got Hunterian correct, a museum in Scotland. [↩](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/11/subtitles-everywhere-in-version-27-releases/#fnref-42472-gedd)
- But the flagon with the dragon has the brew that is true. [↩](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/11/subtitles-everywhere-in-version-27-releases/#fnref-42472-fast)

items.title: The Seven Selves
items.subtitle: A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.
items.feedText: A self is a forest. A self is a ship. Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of l…
items.body:
A self [is a forest](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/09/pando/). A self [is a ship](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/08/plutarch-the-ship-of-theseus-ted-ed/). A self [is an illusion](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/), and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is [a sum of selves](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/04/10/parts/), contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

[Kahlil Gibran](https://themarginalian.org/tag/kahlil-gibran) (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about [the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/04/04/youth-and-age-kahlil-gibran/), takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic [The Madman](http://www.amazon.com/Madman-His-Parables-Poems/dp/0486419118/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/madman-his-parables-and-poems/oclc/242642&referer=brief_results) | [free ebook](http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5616)).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated [the Japanese concept of ma](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/07/ma/).)

Kahlil Gibran

> THE SEVEN SELVES
> by Kahlil Gibran
> In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
> selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:
> First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
> with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
> by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.
> Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
> given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
> and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
> his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
> existence.
> Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
> of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
> who would rebel against this madman.
> Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
> was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
> I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
> who would protest against serving this madman.
> Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
> the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
> rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
> I, not you, who would rebel.
> Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
> with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
> and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
> solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.
> Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
> man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
> fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
> lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
> in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
> life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?
> When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with
> pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper
> one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy
> submission.
> But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness,
> which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on [silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/21/kahlil-gibran-prophet-talking/), then revisit Hermann Hesse on [discovering the soul beneath the self](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/02/18/hesse-soul/).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

items.body:
Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples.

Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview.

**Q:** What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models?

**A:** This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing.

As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact.

I think the overriding themes are multimodalities with language models, trying to address the shortcomings of these models, and trying to develop techniques that do not require a lot of annotated data to complete tasks better.

**Q:** Can you walk us through how the project has evolved?

**A:** When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language. We would just show it these matching examples, and we'd show it mismatching examples. They could learn that the sequence of sounds that says “lighthouse” corresponds to a picture of a lighthouse, without any text being involved.

Moving beyond speech was to include general audio, and then we started looking at video instead of still images. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. The model would learn strong relationships; then, far beyond speech, it would learn what parrots sound like, or electric guitars versus acoustic guitars, for example.

Then, when these large language models started coming out — and this was in the early days, before it had been done by the big companies — we started to learn correspondences between audio and language. Since that time, these large multimodal models have become available, and we've started looking at what some of the limitations of these models are, and are trying to improve upon them with these more or less supervised techniques.

**Q:** What would you say are some recent highlights of your work?

**A:** Our [IPLoc research](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.13317v2) was looking at the fact that these state-of-the-art models, like GPT-40, can't localize specific objects, given just a few-shot examples. We came up with this technique where we would train it with a pseudonym substitution. There's an example there where we replaced “airplane” with “Elizabeth.” It forces the model to not fall back on things that it had previously learned about and pay more attention to the visual context.

Then, we had an audio-based paper, [OmniR1](https://sls.csail.mit.edu/archives/root/publications/2025/ARouditchenko_ASRU-2025.pdf), that was looking at audio-large language models, so these are models that can listen to something and talk about them. One of the disturbing things we found is some of these benchmarks are [multiple-choice answers](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2026/file/d6c01b025cad37d5c8bab4ba18846c02-Paper-Conference.pdf). A lot of times, these models aren't really listening to the sound, but they're almost gaming the question by looking at the answer. What animal is roaring in this audio — like a chipmunk, a lion, an alligator, and a chickadee, or something? It's not even really paying attention to the audio, [but] just going, “Oh, lion.” Part of the reason people do that is that it’s simple to evaluate, whereas if you asked for a text response, you’d somehow have to grade whether it’s accurate. Do you get humans to evaluate it, which can be expensive and time-consuming, or do you use some other language model to be the judge that can have its own set of issues as well? One way to address that is to evaluate these models on a variety of different kinds of benchmarks.

We realized you could feed random noise, and they were still doing quite well, which shows that they're just paying attention to the question. So, we tried to develop some methods to have it pay more attention to the audio and minimize this behavior.

**Q:** Given resource constraints, what is your approach to adapting these large foundation models, and what blend of AI and algorithmic methods do you use that don't require extensive annotated data?

7 Min Read

## 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson

NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, former NASA astronaut Russell “Rusty” Schweickart, and NASA astronauts Frank Rubio and Bob Hines appear onstage at the Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Merritt Island, Florida, on Nov. 6, 2026.

Employees and guests of NASA’s Johnson Space Center celebrate the center’s 65th anniversary at the Lunar Receiving Park in Houston on Nov. 19, 2026.

NASA/Robert Markowitz

For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon.

Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s [Orion](https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/orion-spacecraft/) and [Moon Base](https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase/) programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health.

### Mercury and Gemini: Preparing for Apollo

When the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the new Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk. Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968. Managers in Houston devised a daring plan to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight.

In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.” Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972.

Following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s [Lunar Receiving Laboratory](https://www.nasa.gov/history/building-on-a-mission-the-lunar-receiving-laboratory/) conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world. After the building was demolished in March 2024, the Lunar Receiving Park was dedicated to honor the laboratory’s history in 2026. Today, Johnson’s Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science ([ARES](https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/)) division continues to analyze and curate the Apollo collection at the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility.

Six of the seven Mercury astronauts pose with Manned Spacecraft Center Director Robert Gilruth outside the new center’s temporary headquarters building in Houston in March 1962. Not pictured, astronaut John Glenn, still on his postflight tour two weeks after becoming the first American to orbit the Earth aboard Friendship 7.

Flight controllers work in Mission Control in Houston during the Gemini IV mission in June 1965, the first spaceflight controlled from the new center.

Astronauts aboard Gemini VI photograph Gemini VII during the world’s first rendezvous mission in December 1965.

The famous Earthrise photograph taken during the Apollo 8 mission around the Moon in December 1968.

Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong photographs fellow crew member Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin saluting the American flag on the surface of the Moon in July 1969.

### Skylab and Apollo-Soyuz: Learning to Live and Work in Space

Skylab, America’s first space station, ran into trouble during its launch in May 1973, losing its thermal shield, jamming one solar array and losing the other one. In less than 10 days, engineers in Houston designed and built a sun shield and generated procedures to free the jammed array, followed by the first extensive in-orbit repair activities by the first Skylab crew. The three missions lasting 28, 59, and 84 days accomplished more research than planned, demonstrated the value of humans on long-duration missions, and provided operators in mission control with round-the-clock experience monitoring long duration human spaceflights.

In July 1975, after several joint training sessions in Houston and Moscow, American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts met in space for the first time during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. Approved as a project in 1972, five approach and landing tests of the space shuttle using orbiter Enterprise paved the way for the first orbital mission of Columbia in 1981.

In August 1973, Skylab 3 Commander Alan Bean during one of the many spacewalks conducted during Skylab to repair and maintain the station and conduct research.

Farewell view of the Skylab space station from the departing Skylab 4 crew in February 1974.

The famous handshake in space took place on July 17, 1975, between Apollo Commander Thomas Stafford, top, and Soyuz Commander Aleksei Leonov.

In October 1977, space shuttle Enterprise conducts its first approach and landing test with the tail cone removed.

# Is This the Hidden Cause of Allergies? - Nautilus

## Is This the Hidden Cause of Allergies?

It may not start with the immune system after all

6:00 PM CST on November 20, 2026

Allergies are on the rise. According to government statistics, cases of eczema, hay fever, and food allergies have been steadily climbing in the United States over the past few decades, leaving researchers puzzled. A slew of hypotheses for the increase have been offered—from too much hygiene to not enough gut microbes. Now, a new study published in the journal Allergy suggests our understanding of the illnesses may be flawed from the beginning.

Allergies have traditionally been understood as an exaggerated response from an oversensitive immune system. A harmless allergen triggers a cascade of immune activity causing sneezes, inflammation, and in extreme cases even death. On a tissue level, part of the damage done by allergies has been to epithelial barrier cells lining the gut, skin, airways, and more. But what if we have things backwards?

Read more: “ The Perils of Early Springtime ”

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” study author Peter K. Smith said in a statement. “Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces.”

Smith and a team developed the hypothesis after analyzing public datasets from more than 110 case-control cohorts, which included over 3,700 allergy patients, focusing on the genes that were transcribed in barrier cells. They found that genes responsible for clearing damaged mitochondria in the cells were less active in those suffering from allergies.

According to the team, this mitochondrial failure may represent the first domino to fall, which means it could be the primary cause of many allergies. Under their model, a leaky barrier stemming from dysfunctional mitochondria kickstarts the rest of the immune cascade, rather than vice versa. “The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so it raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow,” Smith explained.

The strongest evidence for the theory was among eosinophilic esophagitis patients, with all cohorts studied showing diminished mitochondria-clearing transcription activity. The same pattern was present in eczema patients—even among skin cells that weren’t inflamed. However, there were still some inconsistencies. Those with hay fever only showed a partially diminished capacity to clear damaged mitochondria, and the pattern was completely absent from those with asthma and nasal polyps.

In other words, there’s more work to be done. But the findings may give researchers a new perspective into a set of diseases that have been stubbornly rising. Or as Smith put it, “This is not a cure but is something we have never had before—a logical starting point.”

items.title: Serbia’s New Parliament Convenes for the First Time
items.subtitle: The Student List holds 140 of the National Assembly’s 250 seats, giving a party formed by youth activists a parliamentary majority.
items.feedText: The country’s new parliament convened for the first time Tuesday, following last month’s historic election victory by the Student List that ended former strongman Aleksandar Vucic’s 14-year grip on power. The Student List holds 140 of the National Assembly’s 250 seats, giving a party formed by youth activists a parliamentary majority. But its efforts to tackle corruption and restore the rule of law are expected to face strong opposition from Vucic’s party, which holds 103 seats, with the former president himself now among its lawmakers. As Andrew MacDowall wrote for WPR last week , most of the Student List’s lawmakers come from academia and civil society and have little governing experience. They now face the daunting task of delivering “on campaign promises that collectively amount to a reshaping of Serbian democracy and state institutions,” while navigating the country’s complex foreign relations with Russia, the West and its Balkan neighbors. Serbia’s Student Protesters Prepare to Govern a Fractured Country

items.body:
### 🧮 Claude helped prove 167-year-old math problem

[↗ Primärquelle: tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/anthropic-mathematician-claims-to-have-solved-167-year-old-math-problem-with-claude-riemann-hypothesis-proof-allegedly-discovered-but-remains-unconfirmed)

- Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he worked with the company's Claude AI to find a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the 167-year-old number theory problem about how prime numbers are distributed.
- The hypothesis, proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, has been checked for the first 10,000,000,000,000 solutions, and Alpöge believes his method could also extend to the Generalized and Extended versions of the problem.
- The claim, made the same week Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, still needs confirmation; Alpöge admits mixed feelings, calling the result both a personal loss and a hint of bigger discoveries in math.

### 🍎 Apple builds an AI agent to run your Mac

- Apple is building its own autonomous AI agent for the Mac that would write code, browse the web, and control apps on a user's behalf, with a possible launch as soon as late next year.
- The plans surfaced in job listings Apple posted this week, including one for a senior manager to lead "general-purpose computer-use agents" that plan multistep tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, and services while coordinating smaller subagents.
- Apple follows rivals already running agents on the Mac, including Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots, Anthropic's Duet, and Google's Tasks, with one writer arguing Apple sits at least a year behind competitors now on their second or third generation.

### 🔒 Signal tries to hide chats from Siri and Gemini

[↗ Primärquelle: unite.ai](https://www.unite.ai/signal-adds-screenshot-restrictions-to-limit-mobile-ai-data-capture/)

- Signal is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and Android when it detects an AI assistant like Siri or Gemini trying to read the screen, aiming to keep operating-system agents from capturing private conversations, Meredith Whittaker announced today.
- The protection is incomplete: Android turns it on only when an assistant tries to access the screen, leaving some devices uncovered, while on macOS 27 Signal cannot reliably block screenshots and instead suggests adding the app to Siri's Excluded Apps list.
- Signal is asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft for a documented way to opt apps out of AI access across screen reading, filesystem access, and notifications, having earlier blocked Microsoft Recall on Windows 11 using a rights-management flag in May 2025.

### 👎 Jensen Huang ran Nvidia on fear ex-staff say

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/behind-jensen-huangs-exit-questions-about-a-management-style-reportedly-built-on-fear/)

- Former Nvidia staff told The New York Times that ex-CEO Jensen Huang led the chipmaker through fear and humiliation, undercutting Elon Musk's claim that employees loved him after Huang's recent ouster.
- Huang reportedly argued that Nvidia's wealth made money useless for motivating workers, leaving humiliation as his only tool, and allegedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him and threatened another with extreme violence.
- The Times found a paper trail suggesting the behavior wasn't isolated, including a 2005 case where former HR chief Michael Winston threatened to sue, prompting a payout of over $1 million; Huang's spokesman calls the claims fabrications.

### 🛰️ Google books Blue Origin to launch AI satellites

[↗ Primärquelle: arstechnica.com](https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/11/google-turns-to-blue-origin-for-a-rocket-but-its-long-term-problem-remains/)

- Blue Origin said yesterday that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029, part of the company's Project Suncatcher effort to build computing power in orbit.
- Each satellite carries computing roughly equal to a single data center rack and will fly into Sun-synchronous orbit, a path that keeps the solar-powered hardware in nearly constant sunlight for steady energy.
- The mission will ride the smaller 7×2 version of New Glenn, which has flown three times, and works as a test of networking AI chips and running machine-learning tasks in space.

### 📧 Intuit sells Mailchimp at a steep loss

[↗ Primärquelle: siliconangle.com](https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/19/intuit-sells-mailchimp-to-bending-spoons-for-3-68b-less-than-a-third-of-what-it-paid/)

- Intuit has agreed to sell its Mailchimp email marketing business to Italian holding company Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, less than a third of the $12 billion it paid to buy the company in 2021.
- The deal is billed as all-cash, but Intuit will put $368 million back into new Bending Spoons shares, keeping $3.31 billion; the sale is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval.
- Mailchimp's growth has stalled, with revenue down 1% to $313 million last quarter amid higher churn from smaller customers; Bending Spoons, owner of Vimeo and Evernote, plans to invest heavily and rebuild the product after closing.

items.body:
It was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the new baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge.

Emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s important to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own.

## Renegotiating our childhood memories

Emily came to see me for help with anxiety and insomnia, and a few sessions into our therapy she started to talk about memories that had been appearing for her, scenes from her childhood that suddenly had taken on new meaning or had popped up out of nowhere. It was as if her memories had changed, which made Emily feel crazy and even more anxious because she felt like she couldn’t trust herself anymore.

In the crudest terms, we tend to think of memory as a filing cabinet—a place where scenes, facts, annoying songs, and embarrassing moments are stored to be recalled, like when we try to remember what we had for dinner last week or where we went on holiday three years ago.

When I talk about memory with my clients, they usually understand that it is not a perfect system, that it can alter over time and be very subjective. What is harder to convey is that [decades of research](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2007.2087) suggest that memory is not in fact a filing cabinet or a library catalogue—it’s a construction. Every time I try to remember where we went on holiday three summers ago, my brain doesn’t retrieve but rather constructs a memory of our trip to Italy. That means that each time we recall something, that memory can change slightly or take on new meaning. Researchers Daniel L. Schacter and Donna Rose Addis found that, in fact, [remembering and imagining look very similar](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2007.2087) in terms of activation in the brain.

Why does that matter? It can help make sense of what happened to Emily and what happens to many of my clients when they become parents and their relationships with their own parents change. Some of this is explained by a shift in roles: When a child becomes a parent, the dynamic of the child-parent relationship naturally has to change, which can be difficult for both parties. Grandparents and new parents might find it challenging to adapt to who is in charge and “who knows best.” But sometimes the difficulty is more subtle, and it’s related to memory.

## When our goals change, our memories can change

Emily struggled because she had started to have visceral memories of herself at about three to five years old, even though she had never actively thought about her childhood much before. She associated that phase in her life with a feeling of paralysis that she couldn’t explain. She told me how exhausted she felt every time she left her parents’ house now, like she had been holding her breath for hours.

Emily knew from whispered family stories that her mother had dealt with bouts of depression through much of her childhood. She also knew that her parents’ marriage hadn’t always been as placid and quiet as it was now. She had always had memories of them fighting late at night but had never thought much of it. Now she remembered her mother in tears, shouting and doors slamming. She remembered hiding under her bed.

Memory is heavily influenced by our current state of mind. [Martin Conway, in his papers](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.107.2.261) on [autobiographical memory](https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.22.5.491.50768), explains that when we try to retrieve a memory or remember something spontaneously, we construct that memory in the moment, partly based on our current goals. If we are hungry, we might construct a memory of a cafe we saw on our walk two weeks ago. If we have a fight with our partner, we might suddenly remember all the times they disappointed us, when we usually are able to accept their imperfections.

When Emily became a parent, her goals changed dramatically, and it changed what memories her brain predicted might be useful for her.

Emily realized that her experience of being her son’s age was one of bracing and zoning out because she had felt disconnected from her mother and scared of her father at the time. As a parent, Emily was suddenly able to attune to what it felt like for her to be three years old. Her three-year-old self did not feel safe, and she did not believe her child was safe, either.

Conway notes that the memories we are able to construct have to be coherent with how we think of ourselves, our beliefs about ourselves, and the world and people in it. According to Conway’s theory, our brains filter, rationalize, or dismiss memories that are inconsistent with who we believe we are.

Before Emily had children, she believed, largely unconsciously, that her childhood experiences were irrelevant to who she was and that she hadn’t really been affected by them. When she became a mum, her visceral memories of childhood fear did not match up with who she believed she was anymore. Her goals had changed from surviving and rationalizing to tuning in to and protecting her child. Her brain was telling her she had to shield her child from something that she had experienced as frightening as a child.

## Meeting our parents with compassion

Other clients of mine have found that becoming a parent had the opposite effect. They were able to look at the younger versions of their parents with more compassion and kindness, reconstructing memories through the eyes of an exhausted parent who was trying and barely coping.

items.body:
Tripod for iPhone.

Over the years, I’ve realized that I’m a particular type of podcast listener: I do not listen to every single new episode that comes in from the shows I’m subscribed to; I want to see them in a list, then pick and choose the episodes I want, and arrange them in a queue. The interactions need to be simple and the queue tactile, ideally with drag and drop to move specific episodes up and down. I do not personally care about transcripts and video (although [we support both with our shows](https://www.macstories.net/news/macstories-podcasts-now-let-you-switch-between-video-and-audio-in-apple-podcasts/), and I think they’re great additions). I do not need an Apple Watch app. I do not need playlists. And I want to have audio effects – pioneered by [Marco Arment in Overcast](https://marco.org/apps), now found in the most popular indie podcast apps – to trim silence and boost volume. I listen to most podcasts at 1.5x speed, but some at 1.8x. I play podcasts from my iPhone, and I want to use an *extremely* native app that also comes with a CarPlay version.

The intersection of all these preferences is surprisingly hard to find in a single, well-rounded iPhone app. I find [Overcast](https://overcast.fm/) to have the best audio effects and performance, but I do not understand its queuing system. For the longest time, I used [Pocket Casts](https://pocketcasts.com/), but the design wasn’t great, and it was often slow at refreshing my feeds. I would have used [Castro](https://castro.fm/), which had the closest version of the queue management system I wanted, but the app’s future has always been somewhat up in the air…and [it just changed ownership, again](https://mjtsai.com/blog/2026/11/06/castro-sold-yet-again/).

With this context in mind, you can imagine my surprise when, seemingly out of the blue, [indie developer Ben McCarthy](https://benricemccarthy.com/apps/) – a [longtime friend of MacStories](https://www.macstories.net/?s=Ben%20McCarthy) and wildly proficient iOS developer – dropped [Tripod](https://benricemccarthy.com/tripod/), their brand new podcast app designed around an inbox and queue system.

I’ll cut to the chase: Tripod is the best podcast app I’ve tried in a long time. The app looks wonderful on the iPhone Duo, it has the best-designed and most reasonable (for my brain, at least) inbox-queue combo I’ve seen to date, and it is full of little details, hidden Easter eggs, and small quality-of-life features that make it a remarkable option for Castro expats and, for my taste, one of the best app debuts of 2026.

The idea behind Tripod is pretty simple: there is an inbox and a queue. New episodes land in the inbox, which you can configure in terms of notifications, UI (you can optionally show action buttons underneath each episode, or rely on the default context menu for managing them), and behavior. For instance, you can choose to automatically remove episodes older than one week or one month, or just keep a specific number of a show’s recent episodes.

Tripod’s inbox screen.

Immediately in the inbox, there are some details I appreciate. When you long-press to show the context menu for a podcast, the menu items are tinted to match the key color of the podcast’s artwork, which is a lovely detail. But also in this menu, you can choose to either remove an episode or mark it as played (not a lot of apps get this right!), jump to the podcast’s main page, and either add it to the queue or ‘Someday’ list (more on this later).

Menu items are tinted per podcast.

In the inbox, you can group episodes by date or show – the latter option being especially effective if you just want to see how many inbox episodes you have for a specific podcast in your library, so you can quickly triage them. Speaking of the library: you can long-press a show to easily choose where new episodes should land from a context menu, but you can also tweak a podcast’s dedicated settings. These include notifications as well as separate limits for the inbox and queue.

You’ll also notice a scrollable list of filters at the top of the library. These UI elements are available on this page as well as the queue, but I find them to be best suited for the queue, where they make the most sense to me. The queue is a list of episodes where, as previously seen in Castro, episodes can be delightfully rearranged with drag and drop. Various grouping and sorting options are available here as well, but it’s the filter row at the top that I love. With filters, you can sort Tripod’s queue by in-progress episodes (boring, but necessary), favorites, and my three favorite options: short episodes, episodes by category, and “someday” episodes.

Tripod’s queue.

With the ‘Short’ filter, I can quickly get through episodes that don’t last too long; categories are fetched from Apple Podcasts’ database, and they’re an ingenious way to triage episodes based on what I’m in the mood for without having to create smart playlists upfront (something I used to do in Pocket Casts). The ‘Someday’ list (which seems to be inspired by [the namesake feature originally seen in Things](https://culturedcode.com/things/support/articles/4001304/)) is a surprisingly useful way to save evergreen episodes I know I want to get to, well, *someday*, but don’t have to be part of my daily rotation. For example, [Myke Hurley’s ‘State of the Workflow’ series](https://www.theenthusiast.net/state-of-the-workflow/) on [Cortex](https://relay.fm/cortex) is perfect for the Someday list since those episodes aren’t time-sensitive or news-heavy, and hold their value months after their release date.

Filters in the queue.

The result of all these decisions is that when I spend time interacting with Tripod, everything clicks and works with the way my brain thinks of managing podcasts. The app is also a great example of how to design for the iPhone Duo: every device pose is supported, and when the Duo is unfolded, the Now Playing screen lives in a left sidebar so you can both navigate the app and manage your listening session.

Different iPhone Duo poses for Tripod.

Features seen in other podcast apps are also seen here: swipe up on the artwork, and you’ll get pages in the sidebar for chapters (you can select which ones you want to skip), a real-time transcript (which is generated on-device and seems comparable to Overcast’s in terms of quality), and audio settings.

Pages in Tripod’s Now Playing screen, including the ability to generate clips for social media.

…

items.title: Large-scale analysis of AlphaFold structures reveals organism-specific physicochemical signatures
items.subtitle:
Wood

Recent advancements in protein structure prediction methods have ushered in a new era of abundant and accurate structural data, providing opp…
items.feedText: Oyarzún, Nadanai Laohakunakorn, Christopher W. Wood Recent advancements in protein structure prediction methods have ushered in a new era of abundant and accurate structural data, providing opportunities to analyse proteins at a scale that has not been possible before. Here we performed a large-scale analysis of physicochemical properties across 373,779 confident AlphaFold structures. Our analysis revealed systematic variation between proteins from different organisms to such an extent that major features of the tree of life could be recovered from these data. Surprisingly, this relationship persisted even when we restricted our analysis to eukaryotic, cytosolic proteins and proteins from single AlphaFold Database Foldseek clusters. Given the strong functional constraints on protein chemistry, this finding is unexpected and suggests that protein structures have organism-specific physicochemical signatures, which might reveal evolutionary constraints imposed by the cellular environment and could have significant implications for the design and engineering of novel proteins.

items.body:
The entrance to Umm al-Khair in the occupied West Bank. Photograph by Jasper Nathaniel.

This February, the Israeli military installed a gate across a busy road in the South Hebron Hills. It was a simple contraption, maybe twenty feet of yellow steel that swung open like the door of a cattle pen—one of hundreds erected across the West Bank. But this one blocked the only drivable road into the tiny Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair as well as more than twenty other shepherding communities, home to thousands of people.

For the past nine months, soldiers have routinely locked the gate for days at a time, preventing residents from reaching work or school, blocking deliveries of food and supplies, and limiting access to hospitals and emergency medical care. Those who manage to drive through during a brief opening may return to find it locked, leaving them stranded on the wrong side, with no way home. Whenever soldiers close the gate, life in Umm al-Khair grinds to a halt. A closed gate also serves as a warning: a settler attack may be coming.

Umm al-Khair was founded by Palestinian Bedouins expelled from the Negev during the Nakba of 1948. It sits in the shadow of the Israeli settlement of Carmel, which was built on land confiscated from the village in 1980. For decades, settlers backed by the Israeli state have encroached on the land that remains. In the summer of 2025, a group of settlers established an outpost—an unauthorized settlement, illegal even under Israeli law—by installing several mobile homes directly adjacent to Umm al-Khair and moving into them. The construction set off a new wave of violence, one that drew international attention when a settler opened fire on a crowd of Palestinians, killing the community leader Awdah Hathaleen in front of his three-year-old son.

When I got dropped off at the gate on the evening of October 27, 2026, it had been locked for four days—the longest stretch since it went up in February. I was visiting Umm al-Khair as a journalist and activist, alongside my colleagues Andrey Khrzhanovskiy and Adele Shoko, both Russian nationals turned Israeli citizens now living in the West Bank. Andrey, who publishes under the name Andrey X, is one of the region’s most prolific non-Palestinian activists, as well as one of Israeli settlers and soldiers’ most frequent targets. A friend met us on the Umm al-Khair side and drove us into the village.

[https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/gate-video.mp4](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/gate-video.mp4)

Residents and activists at the Umm al-Khair gate on October 26, 2026. Filmed by Mothers Against Violence, via [Genocide.live](https://genocide.live/43467).

At ten the next morning, we heard the familiar rumble of military jeeps and rushed to the gate, arriving just in time to see soldiers unlocking it. They gave no explanation of their actions—the IDF rarely does. As word spread, cheers erupted. Cars rushed in and out as residents hurried to work, visited nearby friends and family, and shopped for groceries in Yatta, the nearest city. It didn’t last. At 10:45 A.M., a local settler named Shimon Atiya arrived and locked the gate back up.

Shimon is the founder of an illegal farming outpost near Umm al-Khair. He’s an angry man, perpetually talking into an earpiece, known for overturning dumpsters and kneeing men in the groin. Though he carries a military-grade assault rifle, he is not in the IDF and has no formal authority in the sprawling military occupation that governs Palestinian life. But Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank relies on civilian enforcers like him. While the military has long maintain ed the facade of complying with international law, settler leaders like Shimon make no such pretense. They effectively command state-backed militias of men and adolescents who terrorize Palestinian residents to drive them from their land. Once the Palestinians are gone, the Israeli government may retroactively legalize the settlers’ outposts as “neighborhoods” of existing settlements or as new settlements altogether.

In Umm al-Khair, Israeli soldiers arrived at about 3 P.M. They had with them a photo of me and Andrey, likely taken by Shimon hours before. They told the residents to bring us to them. Once we got there, a soldier showed us a map of a newly declared Closed Military Zone (CMZ)—an arbitrary designation used to expel activists and journalists from Palestinian villages—and ordered us to leave.

Ostensibly, CMZs restrict all nonresidents from a designated area. But while we were speaking, a settler drove straight through the restricted zone. When I asked the soldier in charge whether he intended to expel the settler, he shook his head. The order, it seemed, applied only to us. Even so, the map left a small part of the village unrestricted. We pointed this out, and the soldiers reluctantly allowed us to stay. But if we entered the restricted area, they warned us, we would be placed under arrest.

A soldier directing Nathaniel to leave the CMZ on October 28, 2026. Photograph by Adele Shoko.

Two hours later, a resident of Umm al-Khair found me outside the home of Hanady Hathaleen, Awdah’s widow, in the small part of the village not subject to the military order. He asked if I could head to the gate to wait with a Palestinian man from a neighboring village who was afraid to stand there alone. Earlier that day, at around two, the man had tried to drive around the gate—a maneuver that residents whose cars have four-wheel drive capability sometimes attempt, despite the risk of being shot by settlers. Nevo Nadalski, Carmel’s head of security, had raced to the gate, forced him out of his vehicle, and confiscated his keys. Nevo told the man to return in three hours to collect them.

Like Shimon Atiya, Nevo is a local settler with no formal authority in the military occupation. He often plays the proverbial “good cop” to Shimon’s “bad cop,” showing up at the scene of settler attacks and pretending to de-escalate while actually providing cover for the assailants. Many Umm al-Khair residents blame him for Awdah’s murder. They believe he instructed an Israeli construction worker to drive his excavator through the village, provoking the confrontation that led to Awdah’s death.

I joined the Palestinian driver at the gate at 5:20 P.M.— three and a half hours had passed with no sign of Nevo or the man’s keys. Andrey and Adele arrived from elsewhere in the village at around the same time. We watched as a Palestinian car pulled up on the other side and unloaded food supplies, passing them under the gate to a car on the village side. Later, a mother with four small children got out of a taxi, paid the fare, and ran with her family to their home.

A family from Umm al-Khair getting dropped off on the other side of the gate. October 28, 2026. Photograph by Jasper Nathaniel.
